articles.title: Darboux's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $U$ be an open subset of the model
space $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, and let $\alpha$ be a field of continuous alternating 2-forms on
$\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ that is symplectic on $U$. Then for every $x \in U$ there is an open partial
homeomorphism $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ whose source contains $x$ and is contained in $U$, such
that $\varphi$ is $C^\infty$ on its source, $\varphi^{-1}$ is $C^\infty$ on its target, and for
every $z$ in the target the pullback of $\alpha(\varphi^{-1}(z))$ by the derivative
$D\varphi^{-1}(z)$, namely
$(v, w) \mapsto \alpha(\varphi^{-1}(z))(D\varphi^{-1}(z)\, v, D\varphi^{-1}(z)\, w)$, is in Darboux
normal form.

## Sources

- J. G. Darboux, Sur le problème de Pfaff, Bull. Sci. Math. 6 (1882), 14-36, 49-68. Listed as §39 in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `darboux` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Model space $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ for Darboux's theorem
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the model
space is $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, the Euclidean space of dimension $2n$ with coordinates indexed by
$0, 1, \dots, 2n - 1$ and the standard inner product.

articles.title: Index of the $i$-th $p$-coordinate in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$
articles.statement:
For $i \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$,
the index of the $i$-th $p$-coordinate among the coordinates $0, \dots, 2n - 1$ of
$\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is $i$ itself.

articles.title: Index of the $i$-th $q$-coordinate in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$
articles.statement:
For $i \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$,
the index of the $i$-th $q$-coordinate among the coordinates $0, \dots, 2n - 1$ of
$\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is $i + n$.

articles.title: Darboux normal form
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $e_0, \dots, e_{2n-1}$ be the
standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$. A continuous alternating 2-form $\omega$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$
is in Darboux normal form if for all $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ we have
$\omega(e_i, e_{n+j}) = 1$ when $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise, $\omega(e_i, e_j) = 0$, and
$\omega(e_{n+i}, e_{n+j}) = 0$.

By antisymmetry these conditions determine the form uniquely: it is the standard symplectic form
$\omega_0 = \sum_i dx_i \wedge dx_{n+i}$.

articles.title: Symplectic 2-form fields
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and $U$ a subset of
$\mathbb{R}^{2n}$. A field $\alpha$ of continuous alternating 2-forms on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is
symplectic on $U$ if $\alpha$ is $C^\infty$ on $U$, its exterior derivative $d\alpha$ vanishes
at every point of $U$, and $\alpha$ is non-degenerate at every point of $U$: for every $x \in U$
and every nonzero $v \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ there is $w \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ with
$\alpha(x)(v, w) \neq 0$.

articles.title: Holomorphic maps on a connected manifold that agree on a nonempty open set are equal
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a connected complex manifold without boundary, modeled on a complex normed space with
complex $C^1$ (that is, holomorphic) transition maps, and let $F$ be a complex normed space. If
two holomorphic (everywhere complex differentiable) maps $f, g : M \to F$ agree on a nonempty
open subset $U \subseteq M$, then $f = g$.

articles.title: Identity theorem for holomorphic maps
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a connected complex manifold without
boundary, modeled on a complex normed space with complex $C^1$ (that is, holomorphic) transition
maps, and let $F$ be a complex normed space. If two holomorphic (everywhere complex
differentiable) maps $f, g : M \to F$ agree on a nonempty open subset $U \subseteq M$, then
$f = g$.

## Sources

- O. Forster, Lectures on Riemann Surfaces, identity theorem for holomorphic maps; Lean states connected-complex-manifold vector-valued form. It is `MDifferentiable.eq_of_eqOn_of_isOpen`, kept under the source's name.

articles.title: Open mapping theorem for Riemann surfaces
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be complex manifolds without
boundary modeled on complex normed spaces of dimension one, with complex $C^1$ (that is,
holomorphic) transition maps, and suppose $M$ is connected. Then every holomorphic (everywhere
complex differentiable) map $f : M \to N$ that is not constant is an open map.

## Sources

- O. Forster, Lectures on Riemann Surfaces, open mapping theorem for Riemann surfaces; Lean states one-complex-dimensional specialization. It is `MDifferentiable.isOpenMap_of_finrank_eq_one`, kept under the source's name.

articles.title: Open mapping theorem for one-dimensional complex manifolds
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be complex
manifolds without boundary modeled on complex normed spaces of dimension one, with complex $C^1$
(that is, holomorphic) transition maps, and suppose $M$ is connected. Then every holomorphic
(everywhere complex differentiable) map $f : M \to N$ that is not constant is an open map.

articles.title: The model space $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ of the Liouville–Arnold theorem
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$n$, $E_n$ is the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, with coordinates indexed by
$0, \dots, 2n-1$ and the standard inner product.

articles.title: Liouville–Arnold coordinates: index of $p_i$
articles.statement:
For $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the
coordinate $p_i$ of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is coordinate number $i$: this map sends $i$ to the same
number $i$, regarded as an index in $\{0, \dots, 2n-1\}$.

articles.title: Liouville–Arnold coordinates: index of $q_i$
articles.statement:
For $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the
coordinate $q_i$ of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is coordinate number $n + i$: this map sends $i$ to
$n + i \in \{0, \dots, 2n-1\}$.

articles.title: Liouville integrable system on a subset of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$
articles.statement:
Functions
$F_0, \dots, F_{n-1} \colon \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}$ are Liouville integrable on a set
$U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ if each $F_i$ is $C^\infty$ on $U$, the Poisson brackets
$\{F_i, F_j\}$ vanish at every point of $U$ for all $i, j$, and at every $x \in U$ the
Fréchet derivatives $dF_0(x), \dots, dF_{n-1}(x)$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$.

The set $U$ is not required to be open; the Liouville–Arnold theorem assumes this separately.

articles.title: Common level set of $n$ functions on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$
articles.statement:
For functions
$F_0, \dots, F_{n-1} \colon \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}$ and values
$c_0, \dots, c_{n-1} \in \mathbb{R}$, the common level set is
$\{x \in \mathbb{R}^{2n} : F_i(x) = c_i \text{ for all } i\}$.

articles.title: Liouville–Arnold theorem
articles.statement:
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ be open and let
$F_0, \dots, F_{n-1} \colon \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}$ be Liouville integrable on $U$. For
$c = (c_0, \dots, c_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, let
$M_c = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{2n} : F_i(x) = c_i \text{ for all } i\}$ be the common level set. If
$M_c \subseteq U$ and $M_c$ is compact and connected (in particular nonempty), then $M_c$ is
homeomorphic to the $n$-torus $(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^n$.

The hypotheses *compact* and *connected* on the level set, and its
containment in the open set where the derivatives are independent,
restore standard regularity assumptions that Knill elides; without them
the conclusion fails.

## Sources

- V. I. Arnold, *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics* (2nd ed., 1989), Theorem 49.A.1 (the standard modern reference). The result is due to Liouville (1855) for the local existence of action-angle coordinates and Arnold (1963) for the compact-connected-component topology. Listed as §45 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `liouville_arnold` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Standard Poisson bracket on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$
articles.statement:
Write the coordinates of a point
$x \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ as $p_i = x_i$ and $q_i = x_{n+i}$ for $i = 0, \dots, n-1$. For functions
$F, G \colon \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}$, the Poisson bracket for the symplectic form
$\omega_0 = \sum_i dp_i \wedge dq_i$ is the function

$$
\{F, G\}(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial p_i}(x)
\frac{\partial G}{\partial q_i}(x) - \frac{\partial F}{\partial q_i}(x)
\frac{\partial G}{\partial p_i}(x) \right).
$$

Partial derivatives are read off the Fréchet derivative, which is taken to be zero at points
where the function is not differentiable.

articles.title: Model space $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ for the Newlander–Nirenberg theorem
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$n$, $E_n$ is the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, the model space carrying the almost complex
structure.

articles.title: Almost complex structure on a subset of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number,
let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ and let $J$ assign to each point $y \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ a real
linear map $J(y) : \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$. Then $J$ is an almost complex structure
on $U$ if $J$ is $C^\infty$ on $U$ and $J(x)(J(x)v) = -v$ for every $x \in U$ and every
$v \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}$.

articles.title: Newlander–Nirenberg theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n}$
be open and let $J$ be an almost complex structure on $U$ whose Nijenhuis tensor vanishes on $U$.
Then every $x \in U$ has holomorphic coordinates for $J$: there are open sets
$S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ and $T \subseteq \mathbb{C}^n$ with $x \in S \subseteq U$ and a
homeomorphism $\varphi : S \to T$ such that $\varphi$ is $C^\infty$ on $S$, $\varphi^{-1}$ is
$C^\infty$ on $T$ (both as maps of real vector spaces), and for every $y \in S$ and every
$v \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ the real derivative of $\varphi$ satisfies
$D\varphi(y)(J(y)v) = i \, D\varphi(y)v$.

## Sources

- A. Newlander and L. Nirenberg, `Complex analytic coordinates in almost complex manifolds`, Annals of Math, 65 (3) 1957, 391-404. Problem `newlander_nirenberg` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Vanishing of the Nijenhuis tensor on a set
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let
$U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n}$, let $J$ assign to each point $y \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ a real linear
map $J(y) : \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$, and write $N$ for the Nijenhuis tensor of $J$.
The Nijenhuis tensor of $J$ vanishes on $U$ if $N(V, W)(x) = 0$ for all $C^\infty$ vector fields
$V, W : \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ and every $x \in U$.

The vector fields range over globally smooth fields, which is the textbook hypothesis. Whenever
$U$ is open and $J$ is an almost complex structure on $U$ this is equivalent to the pointwise
condition: the tensor is bilinear over functions, and constant vector fields already realize
every pair of tangent vectors.

articles.title: Nijenhuis tensor
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ assign to each point
$y \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ a real linear map $J(y) : \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$, and let
$V, W : \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ be vector fields. Write $JV$ for the vector field
$y \mapsto J(y)V(y)$ and $[V, W]$ for the Lie bracket of vector fields. The Nijenhuis tensor of
$J$ at a point $x \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is

$$N(V, W)(x) = [JV, JW](x) - J(x)[JV, W](x) - J(x)[V, JW](x) - [V, W](x).$$

For an almost complex structure the last term is $J^2[V, W]$, so this is the usual torsion of
$J$. When $J$ is an almost complex structure on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n}$, the
expression is $C^\infty(U)$-bilinear in $V$ and $W$ on $U$: the terms involving the derivatives
of $V$ and $W$ cancel using $J^2 = -1$, so the value at a point $x$ of $U$ depends only on
$V(x)$, $W(x)$ and the derivative of $J$ there.

articles.title: Radó's theorem
articles.statement:
Every connected Riemann surface is second countable: if $X$ is a
connected Hausdorff topological space with an atlas of charts to $\mathbb{C}$ whose transition
maps are of class $C^1$ over $\mathbb{C}$ (that is, holomorphic), then the topology of $X$ is
second countable.

## Sources

- John Hamal Hubbard, *Teichmüller theory and applications to geometry, topology, and dynamics. Vol. 1*, §1.3. Problem `rado_riemannSurface` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Vector fields with a closed orbit
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold (possibly with boundary or
corners) and let $R$ assign to each point $x \in M$ a tangent vector $R(x) \in T_xM$. We say that
$R$ has a closed orbit when there are a curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to M$ and a real number
$T > 0$ such that $\gamma$ is $T$-periodic, $\gamma$ is a smooth integral curve of $R$, and
$\gamma$ is not constant.

The main theorem applies this to a Reeb vector field, whence the name closed Reeb orbit.

articles.title: Contact condition for a one-form
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a one-form and $d\alpha$ a two-form on
$M$. The pair satisfies the contact condition when $d\alpha$ is the exterior derivative of
$\alpha$ and, at every point $x \in M$, the covector $\alpha_x$ is nonzero and there are tangent
vectors $u, v \in T_xM$ with $\alpha_x(u) = \alpha_x(v) = 0$ and $d\alpha_x(u, v) \ne 0$.

When $M$ has dimension $3$, this says that $\alpha$ vanishes nowhere and $d\alpha$ is
nondegenerate on the plane $\ker \alpha_x$, which is equivalent to $\alpha \wedge d\alpha$
vanishing nowhere.

articles.title: Exterior derivative of a one-form
articles.statement:
A two-form $d\alpha$ on $M$ is the exterior derivative
of a one-form $\alpha$ on $M$ when, for all smooth vector fields $X, Y$ on $M$ and every point
$x \in M$,

$$
d\alpha_x(X_x, Y_x) = X_x\big(\alpha(Y)\big) - Y_x\big(\alpha(X)\big) - \alpha_x\big([X, Y]_x\big),
$$

where $\alpha(Y)$ is the function $y \mapsto \alpha_y(Y_y)$, $X_x(f)$ is the derivative of a
function $f$ at $x$ in the direction $X_x$, and $[X, Y]$ is the Lie bracket of $X$ and $Y$.

This coordinate-free identity determines $d\alpha$ uniquely.

articles.title: Integral curves
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold (possibly with boundary or corners) and let
$R$ assign to each point $x \in M$ a tangent vector $R(x) \in T_xM$. A curve
$\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to M$ is an integral curve of $R$ when $\gamma$ is smooth and
$\gamma'(t) = R(\gamma(t))$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Reeb vector fields
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a one-form and $d\alpha$ a two-form on $M$. An
assignment $R$ of a tangent vector $R(x) \in T_xM$ to each point $x \in M$ is a Reeb vector field
for $(\alpha, d\alpha)$ when, at every point $x \in M$, $\alpha_x(R(x)) = 1$ and
$d\alpha_x(R(x), v) = 0$ for all $v \in T_xM$.

articles.title: Smooth one-forms
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold (possibly with boundary or corners).
A smooth one-form on $M$ is a smooth section of the cotangent bundle of $M$: a smooth choice of
a linear map $\alpha_x : T_xM \to \mathbb{R}$ at each point $x \in M$.

articles.title: Smooth vector fields
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold (possibly with boundary or
corners). A smooth vector field on $M$ is a smooth section of the tangent bundle of $M$: a smooth
choice of a tangent vector $X_x \in T_xM$ at each point $x \in M$.

articles.title: Two-forms as fields of bilinear forms
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold (possibly with
boundary or corners). A two-form on $M$ is here a smooth section of the bundle whose fiber at
$x \in M$ is the space of bilinear maps $T_xM \times T_xM \to \mathbb{R}$; antisymmetry is not
required.

articles.title: Weinstein conjecture in dimension three (Taubes)
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a nonempty compact Hausdorff
smooth manifold without boundary, modelled on a real vector space of dimension $3$. Let $\alpha$
be a smooth one-form and $d\alpha$ a smooth two-form on $M$ satisfying the contact condition:
$d\alpha$ is the exterior derivative of $\alpha$ and, at every point $x$, $\alpha_x \ne 0$ and
$d\alpha_x(u, v) \ne 0$ for some $u, v \in \ker \alpha_x$. Let $R$ be a Reeb vector field for
$(\alpha, d\alpha)$. Then $R$ has a closed orbit: a nonconstant smooth integral curve of $R$
that is periodic with some positive period.

## Sources

- C.H. Taubes, 'The Seiberg–Witten equations and the Weinstein conjecture', Geom. Topol. 11 (2007) 2117–2202; arXiv:math/0611007. Conjecture: A. Weinstein, 'On the hypotheses of Rabinowitz' periodic orbit theorems', J. Differential Equations 33 (1979) 353–358. §141 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `weinstein_conjecture_dim3` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Borsuk's conjecture in a given dimension
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, Borsuk's conjecture
in dimension $n$ is the statement that the Borsuk number of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$
is at most $n + 1$.

Equivalently, every bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with at least two points is covered by
$n + 1$ sets, each of extended diameter strictly smaller than that of the set.

articles.title: Upper bounds on the Borsuk number of a Euclidean space
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$,
the Borsuk number of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is at most $k$ if and only if every
bounded subset $s$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with at least two points has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover,
that is, $s$ is covered by $k$ sets, each of extended diameter strictly smaller than that of
$s$.

articles.title: Borsuk number of a Euclidean space
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the Borsuk number of the
Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the supremum, in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, of the Borsuk
numbers of the bounded subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with at least two points.

articles.title: When the first Borsuk failure dimension is infinite
articles.statement:
The first Borsuk failure dimension
is $\infty$ if and only if, for every positive integer $n$, the Borsuk number of the Euclidean
space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is at most $n + 1$.

articles.title: First Borsuk failure dimension
articles.statement:
The first Borsuk failure dimension is the least positive
integer $n$ such that the Borsuk number of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is greater than
$n + 1$, and $\infty$ if there is no such $n$.

articles.title: Borsuk covers by closed sets
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, a set $s$ in the Euclidean
space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover if and only if there are $k$ closed subsets of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ whose union contains $s$, each of extended diameter strictly smaller than that
of $s$.

articles.title: Borsuk covers by subsets
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, a set $s$ in the Euclidean
space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover if and only if there are subsets
$c_1, \dots, c_k$ of $s$ with $s = c_1 \cup \dots \cup c_k$, each of extended diameter strictly
smaller than that of $s$.

articles.title: Enlarging a Borsuk cover
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $k$ and $l$ be natural numbers with $k \le l$. If a
nonempty set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover, then $s$ has
an $l$-piece Borsuk cover.

Repeating an existing piece enlarges the cover to the larger size.

articles.title: Borsuk covers of nonempty sets have at least one piece
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural
numbers. If a nonempty set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk
cover, then $0 < k$.

articles.title: Borsuk covers
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a set in an extended pseudometric space and let $k$ be a
natural number. The set $s$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover if there are $k$ sets whose union
contains $s$, each of extended diameter strictly smaller than that of $s$.

articles.title: Two-distance sets
articles.statement:
A set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a two-distance set
if there are reals $0 < a < b$ such that the distance between any two distinct points of $s$ is
$a$ or $b$, and both $a$ and $b$ occur as the distance between some two points of $s$.

articles.title: Bounds on the Borsuk number of a set
articles.statement:
For a nonempty set $s$ in the Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and a natural number $k$, the Borsuk number of $s$ is at most $k$ if and only if
$s$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover.

articles.title: A Borsuk cover bounds the Borsuk number
articles.statement:
If a set $s$ in the Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover for a natural number $k$, then the Borsuk number of
$s$ is at most $k$.

articles.title: Borsuk number of a set
articles.statement:
The Borsuk number of a set $s$ in the Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is the least natural number $k$ such that $s$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover, that
is, $s$ is covered by $k$ sets each of strictly smaller extended diameter than $s$; it is
$\infty$ if no such $k$ exists.

articles.title: Two-distance Borsuk number in dimension $n$
articles.statement:
The two-distance Borsuk number in dimension
$n$ is the supremum, taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, of the Borsuk numbers of all bounded
two-distance sets with at least two points in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: Brunn–Minkowski inequality
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $A$ and $B$ be nonempty compact subsets of
$\mathbb{R}^n$, let $A + B = \{a + b : a \in A,\ b \in B\}$ be their Minkowski sum, and let
$\mathrm{vol}$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then

$$\mathrm{vol}(A + B)^{1/n} \ge \mathrm{vol}(A)^{1/n} + \mathrm{vol}(B)^{1/n}.$$

## Sources

- H. Brunn, Über Ovale und Eiflächen (1887); H. Minkowski, Geometrie der Zahlen (1896); modern formulation R. J. Gardner, Bull. AMS 39 (2002), 355–406, DOI 10.1090/S0273-0979-02-00941-2.

articles.title: Prékopa–Leindler inequality
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 0$ and $0 < t < 1$, and let
$f, g, h : \mathbb{R}^n \to [0, \infty]$ be Borel measurable functions on Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $f(x)^{1-t} g(y)^t \le h((1-t)x + ty)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$.
Then, with all integrals taken over $\mathbb{R}^n$ against Lebesgue measure,

$$\Big(\int f(x)\,dx\Big)^{1-t} \Big(\int g(x)\,dx\Big)^{t} \le \int h(x)\,dx.$$

## Sources

- A. Prékopa, Acta Sci. Math. 32 (1971), 301–316; H. J. Brascamp and E. Lieb, J. Funct. Anal. 22 (1976), 366–389, DOI 10.1016/0022-1236(76)90004-5.

articles.title: Colorful Carathéodory theorem in finite-dimensional inner product spaces
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension $n$, and let $S_0, \dots, S_n$ be
finite subsets of $V$ such that $0$ lies in the convex hull of each $S_l$. Then there are
points $t_0 \in S_0, \dots, t_n \in S_n$ such that $0$ lies in the convex hull of
$\{t_0, \dots, t_n\}$.

## Sources

- I. Barany, Discrete Math. 40 (1982), 141-152, DOI 10.1016/0012-365X(82)90115-7.

articles.title: Colorful Carathéodory theorem for finite sets
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 0$ and let $S_0, \dots, S_d$ be
finite subsets of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that the origin lies in the convex hull
of each $S_i$. Then there are points $c_0 \in S_0, \dots, c_d \in S_d$ such that the origin lies
in the convex hull of $\{c_0, \dots, c_d\}$.

## Sources

- I. Barany, Discrete Math. 40 (1982), 141-152, DOI 10.1016/0012-365X(82)90115-7.

articles.title: Colorful Carathéodory theorem
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 0$ and let $S_0, \dots, S_d$ be subsets of the
Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that the origin lies in the convex hull of each $S_i$. Then
there are points $c_0 \in S_0, \dots, c_d \in S_d$ such that the origin lies in the convex hull of
$\{c_0, \dots, c_d\}$.

## Sources

- I. Barany, Discrete Math. 40 (1982), 141-152, DOI 10.1016/0012-365X(82)90115-7.

articles.title: Equichordal point theorem
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a compact convex subset of the Euclidean plane
with nonempty interior. Then $K$ does not have two distinct equichordal points: there are no
points $P \ne Q$ of the plane such that both $P$ and $Q$ are equichordal points of $K$.

## Sources

- M. R. Rychlik, A complete solution to the equichordal point problem of Fujiwara, Blaschke, Rothe and Weizenböck, Invent. Math. 129 (1997). Listed as §205 in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Knill, §205. Problem `equichordal_point_unique` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Equichordal point
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a subset of the Euclidean plane. A point $P$ is an
equichordal point of $K$ if $P$ lies in the interior of $K$ and there is a real $L > 0$ such
that for every unit vector $u$ there are reals $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ for which $P + a u$ and
$P - b u$ lie in the boundary (frontier) of $K$, the open segment between $P - b u$ and
$P + a u$ lies in the interior of $K$, and the distance between $P + a u$ and $P - b u$
equals $L$.

The open segment condition makes $P + a u$ and $P - b u$ the endpoints of the chord through $P$
in direction $u$, ruling out other boundary crossings for nonconvex star-shaped domains.

articles.title: Euclidean plane for the equichordal point problem
articles.statement:
The Euclidean plane is the space
$\mathbb{R}^2$ of pairs of real numbers with the Euclidean inner product and norm.

articles.title: Model space for convex bodies
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $E_n$ is the real Euclidean
space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with its standard inner product and Euclidean norm.

articles.title: Hadwiger's theorem
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the real vector space of continuous
invariant valuations on the convex bodies of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (continuous, additive, and invariant
under linear isometries and translations) is finite-dimensional of dimension $n + 1$.

## Sources

- H. Hadwiger (1937). Listed as §31 in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `hadwiger` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Continuous invariant valuation
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, a real-valued function $f$ on
the convex bodies (nonempty compact convex subsets) of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a
continuous invariant valuation if: $f$ is continuous for the Hausdorff metric;
$f(A) + f(B) = f(C) + f(D)$ for all convex bodies $A, B, C, D$ with $A = C \cup D$ and
$B = C \cap D$; $f(e(A)) = f(A)$ for every convex body $A$ and every linear isometry $e$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$; and $f(A + t) = f(A)$ for every convex body $A$ and every $t \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: The space of continuous invariant valuations
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the continuous
invariant valuations on the convex bodies of $\mathbb{R}^n$ form a real linear subspace of the
vector space of all functions from the convex bodies of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Hanner polytopes are convex
articles.statement:
Every Hanner polytope $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
convex.

articles.title: Hanner polytopes live in positive dimension
articles.statement:
If $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a Hanner
polytope, then $0 < n$.

articles.title: The Hanner cross-polytopes are Hanner polytopes
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner
cross-polytope $P_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a Hanner polytope.

articles.title: Hanner cross-polytope
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cross-polytope
$P_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is defined by recursion on $n$: $P_0$ is the centered unit
segment $[-1, 1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^1$, and $P_{n+1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ is the
$\ell_1$ sum of $P_n$ and the centered unit segment.

articles.title: The Hanner cube is the coordinate cube
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cube
$C_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ equals the coordinate cube
$\{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} : -1 \le x_i \le 1 \text{ for every } i\} = [-1, 1]^{n+1}$.

articles.title: The Hanner cubes are Hanner polytopes
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cube
$C_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a Hanner polytope.

articles.title: Hanner cube
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cube $C_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is
defined by recursion on $n$: $C_0$ is the centered unit segment $[-1, 1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^1$,
and $C_{n+1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ is the $\ell_\infty$ sum of $C_n$ and the centered
unit segment.

articles.title: $\ell_\infty$ sum of bodies
articles.statement:
For sets $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and
$L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, the $\ell_\infty$ sum of $K$ and $L$ is the set of points of
$\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ whose first $m$ coordinates form a point of $K$ and whose last $n$
coordinates form a point of $L$; that is, the product $K \times L$ under the identification
$\mathbb{R}^{m+n} = \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: $\ell_1$ sum of bodies
articles.statement:
For sets $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,
the $\ell_1$ sum of $K$ and $L$ is the convex hull in $\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ of
$(K \times \{0\}) \cup (\{0\} \times L)$, where $\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ is identified with
$\mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n$ by splitting off the first $m$ coordinates.

articles.title: Centered unit segment
articles.statement:
The centered unit segment is the closed unit ball
$\{x \in \mathbb{R}^1 : \|x\| \le 1\}$, that is, the segment $[-1, 1]$. It is the
one-dimensional leaf in the recursive definition of Hanner polytopes.

articles.title: Hanner polytopes are compact
articles.statement: Every Hanner polytope is compact.

articles.title: Hanner polytopes
articles.statement:
For $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, identify
$\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ with $\mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n$ by splitting off the first $m$
coordinates; the $\ell_\infty$ sum of $K$ and $L$ is $K \times L$, and their $\ell_1$ sum is the
convex hull of $(K \times \{0\}) \cup (\{0\} \times L)$, both viewed as subsets of
$\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$. The Hanner polytopes are the smallest family of subsets of the Euclidean
spaces $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that: the unit segment $[-1, 1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^1$ is a Hanner
polytope; if $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a Hanner polytope and
$e \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is an invertible linear map, then $e(K)$ is a Hanner
polytope; and if $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ are Hanner polytopes
with $m, n > 0$, then their $\ell_\infty$ sum and their $\ell_1$ sum are Hanner polytopes.

articles.title: Membership in the $\ell_\infty$ Hanner sum
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and
$L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. A point $x \in \mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ lies in the $\ell_\infty$ Hanner
sum of $K$ and $L$ if and only if $(x_1, \dots, x_m) \in K$ and
$(x_{m+1}, \dots, x_{m+n}) \in L$.

articles.title: Membership in the Hanner unit segment
articles.statement:
A point $x \in \mathbb{R}^1$ lies in the Hanner
unit segment if and only if every coordinate $x_i$ of $x$ satisfies $|x_i| \le 1$.

articles.title: Hanner polytopes are centrally symmetric
articles.statement:
Every Hanner polytope $K$ is centrally
symmetric about the origin: $-K = K$.

articles.title: Negation preserves membership in a Hanner polytope
articles.statement:
For every Hanner polytope
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $-x \in K$ if and only if $x \in K$.

articles.title: Hanner polytopes contain the origin in their interior
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
every Hanner polytope $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, the origin is an interior point of $K$.

articles.title: Hanner polytopes contain the origin
articles.statement: The origin belongs to every Hanner polytope.

articles.title: Hyperplane slicing theorem
articles.statement:
There is a constant $c > 0$ such that for every $n \ge 1$ and
every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a convex compact set with nonempty interior) of
Lebesgue volume $1$ there exist a hyperplane $H \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a set
$\{x : f(x) = t\}$ for a nonzero linear functional $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and some
$t \in \mathbb{R}$) and an isometry $\varphi \colon \mathbb{R}^{n-1} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with image
$H$ such that the $(n-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue volume of $\varphi^{-1}(K \cap H)$ is at least $c$.

This is Bourgain's slicing conjecture, proved by Klartag and Lehec building on Guan's bound
(Theorem 1.1); equivalently, the isotropic constant of convex bodies is bounded by a universal
constant.

## Sources

- B. Klartag, J. Lehec, Affirmative resolution of Bourgain's slicing problem using Guan's bound, Geometric and Functional Analysis (2025), arXiv:2412.15044, https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15044.

articles.title: Hyperplane slicing conjecture
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a constant $c > 0$ such that
for every $n \ge 1$ and every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a convex compact set with
nonempty interior) of Lebesgue volume $1$ there exist a hyperplane $H \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a
set $\{x : f(x) = t\}$ for a nonzero linear functional $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and some
$t \in \mathbb{R}$) and an isometry $\varphi \colon \mathbb{R}^{n-1} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with image
$H$ such that the $(n-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue volume of $\varphi^{-1}(K \cap H)$ is at least $c$.

## Sources

- `OWR-12337-001` (DOI 10.4171/owr/2013/09), where it is posed as an open problem; it has since been resolved.

articles.title: Convex bodies in $\mathbb{R}^n$
articles.statement:
A set $K$ in the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is a convex body when it is convex, compact and has nonempty interior.

## Sources

- `OWR-12337-001` (DOI 10.4171/owr/2013/09): "convex body `K ⊆ ℝⁿ`".

articles.title: Hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^n$
articles.statement:
A set $H$ in the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is a hyperplane when $H = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : f(x) = t\}$ for some nonzero
linear functional $f \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ and some $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- `OWR-12337-001` (DOI 10.4171/owr/2013/09): "hyperplane section".

articles.title: Isoperimetric inequality
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a continuous, $1$-periodic, Lipschitz map from
$\mathbb{R}$ to the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ that is injective on $[0, 1)$, so that its
image $C = g(\mathbb{R})$ is a simple closed curve, and suppose $C$ has finite
one-dimensional Hausdorff measure. Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded, connected open
set whose boundary is $C$. Let $L$ be the one-dimensional Hausdorff measure of $C$ (its
length) and $A$ the Lebesgue measure of $U$ (its area). Then $4 \pi A \le L^2$, and
$4 \pi A = L^2$ if and only if $C$ is a circle, that is, $C = \{x : \lVert x - c \rVert = r\}$
for some point $c \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and some real $r > 0$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isoperimetric_inequality.

articles.title: Jung's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $s$ be a bounded subset of the Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ with diameter $\operatorname{diam} s$. Then there is a point $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$
such that $s$ is contained in the closed ball with center $c$ and radius
$\sqrt{n / (2(n + 1))} \cdot \operatorname{diam} s$.

## Sources

- H. Jung, Über die kleinste Kugel, die eine räumliche Figur einschließt, J. Reine Angew. Math. 123 (1901) 241–257 original theorem; D. Gale sharp Euclidean formulation; standard modern reference M. Berger, Geometry I & II.

articles.title: Kirchberger's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets of points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Then $A$
and $B$ are strictly separated by a hyperplane, that is, there are a nonzero vector
$w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $\beta$ with $\langle w, a \rangle < \beta$ for all $a \in A$
and $\beta < \langle w, c \rangle$ for all $c \in B$, if and only if for every set
$C \subseteq A \cup B$ of at most $d + 2$ points, the sets $A \cap C$ and $B \cap C$ are strictly
separated by a hyperplane in the same sense.

Proof: The reverse implication applies Helly's theorem to tagged strict half-spaces in one higher
dimension, following the route of Rademacher and Schoenberg (1950) from Kirchberger (1903).

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirchberger%27s_theorem.
- Paul Kirchberger, "Über Tchebychefsche Annäherungsmethoden," Mathematische Annalen 57 (1903), 509–540, DOI 10.1007/BF01445182, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01445182.

articles.title: Feasible region of a linear program
articles.statement:
The feasible region of a linear program with
$m$ variables, constraint matrix $A$ and right-hand side $b$ is the set of vectors
$x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with $A x \le b$ and $x \ge 0$, both inequalities holding componentwise.
It is a convex polyhedron in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

articles.title: Linear program
articles.statement:
A linear program in standard inequality form with $m$ variables and
$n$ constraints is given by an objective vector $c \in \mathbb{R}^m$, a right-hand side
$b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and an $n \times m$ real constraint matrix $A$; it stands for the problem
of maximising $c \cdot x$ over $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ subject to $A x \le b$ and $x \ge 0$.

articles.title: Maximum principle for linear programming
articles.statement:
Consider a linear program with $m$ variables
and objective vector $c \in \mathbb{R}^m$, let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be its feasible region
and $f(x) = c \cdot x$ its objective function, and let $x \in P$ be a local maximiser of $f$ on
$P$, that is, $f(y) \le f(x)$ for all $y \in P$ in some neighbourhood of $x$. Then $x$ is a
global maximiser of $f$ on $P$, and if $c \ne 0$ then $x$ lies on the topological boundary of
$P$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

## Sources

- G. B. Dantzig (1947), simplex algorithm. Listed as §101 in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `lp_maximum_principle` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Objective function of a linear program
articles.statement:
The objective function of a linear program
with $m$ variables and objective vector $c \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is the map
$f \colon \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $f(x) = c \cdot x = \sum_i c_i x_i$.

articles.title: Optimal vertices of linear programs
articles.statement:
Consider a linear program with $m$ variables and
objective vector $c \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be its feasible region
and $f(x) = c \cdot x$ its objective function. If $P$ is nonempty and bounded, then some
$x \in P$ maximises $f$ on $P$ and is an extreme point of $P$, that is, $x$ does not lie in the
open segment between two distinct points of $P$.

## Sources

- G. B. Dantzig (1947), simplex algorithm. Listed as §101 in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `lp_maximum_principle` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Strong linear programming duality
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a real $m \times n$ matrix, and let
$b \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$; inequalities between vectors are componentwise.
Suppose some $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies $x \ge 0$ and $Ax \le b$, and that $c \cdot x$ is
bounded above over all such $x$. Then there exist $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$
with $x \ge 0$, $Ax \le b$, $y \ge 0$, $A^{\mathsf{T}} y \ge c$ and $c \cdot x = b \cdot y$.

By weak duality, such $x$ and $y$ are optimal solutions of the primal problem of maximizing
$c \cdot x$ subject to $x \ge 0$, $Ax \le b$ and of the dual problem of minimizing $b \cdot y$
subject to $y \ge 0$, $A^{\mathsf{T}} y \ge c$.

Informal source: George B. Dantzig, *Linear Programming and Extensions*,
Princeton University Press, 1963, strong duality theorem.

articles.title: Rado's centerpoint theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of
$\mathbb{R}^d$, not necessarily distinct. Then some point $x$ in the convex hull of
$\{p_1, \dots, p_n\}$ has at least $n/(d+1)$ of the points in every closed halfspace containing
it: for all $v \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$ with $\langle v, x \rangle \le t$, the
number of indices $i$ with $\langle v, p_i \rangle \le t$ is at least $n/(d+1)$.

## Sources

- R. Rado, J. London Math. Soc. s1-21 (1946), 291-300, DOI 10.1112/jlms/s1-21.4.291.

articles.title: Convex hull of a compact set is compact
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed
space. If $K \subseteq E$ is compact, then the convex hull of $K$ is compact.

articles.title: Restriction of a convex function to a line
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed space with
continuous dual $E^*$, and let $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex. For all $x, v \in E^*$, the
function $s \mapsto h(x + s v)$ is convex on $\mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Mazur's theorem for support functions
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space
with continuous dual $E^*$, let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact set with support function
$h_K$, and write $h_K'(\ell; v)$ for the directional derivative of $h_K$ at $\ell$ in direction
$v$. Then the Gateaux points of $h_K$, that is, the functionals $\ell \in E^*$ with
$h_K'(\ell; v) + h_K'(\ell; -v) \le 0$ for every $v \in E^*$, form a dense subset of $E^*$.

articles.title: Opposite directional derivatives have nonnegative sum
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed space
with continuous dual $E^*$, let $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex, and write $h'(x; v)$ for the
directional derivative of $h$ at $x$ in direction $v$. For all $x, v \in E^*$,
$h'(x; v) + h'(x; -v) \ge 0$.

articles.title: Continuity of the directional derivative of a support function in the direction
articles.statement:
Let
$E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact
set with support function $h_K$, and write $h_K'(x; w)$ for the directional derivative of $h_K$
at $x$ in direction $w$. For every $x \in E^*$, the map $w \mapsto h_K'(x; w)$ is continuous on
$E^*$.

articles.title: Subadditivity of the directional derivative
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed space with
continuous dual $E^*$, let $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex, and write $h'(x; v)$ for the
directional derivative of $h$ at $x$ in direction $v$. For all $x, v, w \in E^*$,
$h'(x; v + w) \le h'(x; v) + h'(x; w)$.

articles.title: Strict sublevel sets of the symmetrized directional derivative are open
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact set with
support function $h_K$, and write $h_K'(x; v)$ for the directional derivative of $h_K$ at $x$ in
direction $v$. For every $v \in E^*$ and every real $c$, the set of $x \in E^*$ with
$h_K'(x; v) + h_K'(x; -v) < c$ is open.

articles.title: Lipschitz bound on directional derivatives of a support function
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real
normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact set with
support function $h_K$, and write $h_K'(x; w)$ for the directional derivative of $h_K$ at $x$ in
direction $w$. If $C$ is a real number with $h_K(\ell_1) - h_K(\ell_2) \le C \|\ell_1 - \ell_2\|$
for all $\ell_1, \ell_2 \in E^*$, then $h_K'(x; w) \le C \|w\|$ for all $x, w \in E^*$.

articles.title: Directional derivative in direction zero
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous
dual $E^*$ and let $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ be any function. For every $x \in E^*$, the directional
derivative of $h$ at $x$ in direction $0$ is $0$.

articles.title: Directional derivative
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$. For
$h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ and $x, v \in E^*$, the directional derivative of $h$ at $x$ in
direction $v$ is the infimum of the difference quotients,
$h'(x; v) = \inf_{t > 0} \frac{h(x + t v) - h(x)}{t}$, which is taken to be $0$ when these
quotients are not bounded below.

For convex $h$ the quotients are bounded below, so this is the usual one-sided directional
derivative.

articles.title: Difference quotients of a convex function are bounded below
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed
space, $E^*$ its continuous dual, and $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ a convex function. For all
$x, v \in E^*$, the set of difference quotients $\{(h(x + t v) - h(x))/t : t > 0\}$ is bounded
below.

The bound comes from comparing slopes of $h$ on the line through $x$ in direction $v$.

articles.title: Difference quotients
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed space and $E^*$ its continuous dual. For
$h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ and $x, v \in E^*$, the difference quotients of $h$ at $x$ in direction
$v$ form the set $\{(h(x + t v) - h(x))/t : t > 0\}$.

When $h$ is convex this set is bounded below, and its infimum is the one-sided directional
derivative of $h$ at $x$ in direction $v$.

articles.title: Gateaux points
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real normed space, $E^*$ its continuous dual, and
$h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$. For $x, v \in E^*$ let $h'(x; v)$ be the infimum of the difference
quotients $(h(x + t v) - h(x))/t$ over $t > 0$, taken to be $0$ when they are unbounded below.
A point $x \in E^*$ is a Gateaux point of $h$ when $h'(x; v) + h'(x; -v) \le 0$ for every
$v \in E^*$.

articles.title: Maximizers at a Gateaux point of the support function are unique
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a
nonempty compact subset of a real normed space $E$, and let $h_K(l) = \sup_{y \in K} l(y)$ be its
support function on the continuous dual $E^*$. If $l \in E^*$ is a Gateaux point of $h_K$ and
$z_1, z_2 \in K$ satisfy $l(z_1) = h_K(l)$ and $l(z_2) = h_K(l)$, then $z_1 = z_2$.

articles.title: A maximizer bounds the directional derivative of the support function from below
articles.statement:
Let
$K$ be a nonempty compact subset of a real normed space $E$, let $h_K(l) = \sup_{y \in K} l(y)$
be its support function on the continuous dual $E^*$, and write $h_K'(u; v)$ for the
directional derivative of $h_K$ at $u$ in direction $v$. If $u \in E^*$ and $z \in K$ satisfy
$u(z) = h_K(u)$, then $v(z) \le h_K'(u; v)$ for every $v \in E^*$.

articles.title: Straszewicz's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let
$A \subseteq E$ be a compact convex set. Then every extreme point of $A$ lies in the closure of
the set of exposed points of $A$.

articles.title: The support function of a compact set is attained
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset
of a real normed space $E$, and let $h_K(l) = \sup_{x \in K} l(x)$ be its support function on the
continuous dual $E^*$. For every $l \in E^*$ there is $x \in K$ with $l(x) = h_K(l)$.

articles.title: The support function of a compact set is continuous
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty compact
subset of a real normed space $E$. Its support function $h_K(l) = \sup_{x \in K} l(x)$ is
continuous on the continuous dual $E^*$ with the operator norm.

articles.title: The support function of a compact set is convex
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of
a real normed space $E$. Its support function $h_K(l) = \sup_{x \in K} l(x)$ is a convex function
on the whole continuous dual $E^*$.

articles.title: The support function of a compact set is Lipschitz
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset
of a real normed space $E$, and let $h_K(l) = \sup_{x \in K} l(x)$ be its support function on the
continuous dual $E^*$. There is a constant $C \ge 0$ such that
$h_K(l_1) - h_K(l_2) \le C \|l_1 - l_2\|$ for all $l_1, l_2 \in E^*$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the
operator norm.

articles.title: Support function
articles.statement:
For a set $K$ in a real normed space $E$, the support function of $K$
sends a continuous linear functional $\ell$ on $E$ to the supremum $\sup_{x \in K} \ell(x)$ of the
values of $\ell$ on $K$.

The supremum is taken in $\mathbb{R}$, so it is $0$ when $K$ is empty or $\ell$ is unbounded
above on $K$; for nonempty compact $K$ it is attained.

articles.title: A unique maximizer of a linear functional is an exposed point
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a nonempty
compact set in a real normed space $E$, let $\ell$ be a continuous linear functional on $E$, and
let $h_K$ be the support function of $K$. If $z \in K$ satisfies $\ell(z) = h_K(\ell)$ and every
$y \in K$ with $\ell(y) = h_K(\ell)$ equals $z$, then $z$ is an exposed point of $K$.

articles.title: Tverberg's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $d, r$ be natural numbers with $r \ge 1$ and let $N = (d+1)(r-1)+1$.
For any points $p_1, \dots, p_N$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, not necessarily distinct, there are pairwise
disjoint sets $P_1, \dots, P_r \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ whose union is $\{1, \dots, N\}$ and a
point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ that lies in the convex hull of $\{p_i : i \in P_j\}$ for every $j$.

## Sources

- H. Tverberg, J. London Math. Soc. s1-41 (1966), 123-128, DOI 10.1112/jlms/s1-41.1.123.

articles.title: Ulam's flat-sections problem in dimension three
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ be a compact
set homeomorphic to the closed unit ball. Suppose that for every nonzero continuous linear
functional $F : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ and every real $c$ such that the plane
$\{x : F(x) = c\}$ meets the interior of $K$, the intersection of this plane with the boundary
(frontier) of $K$ is homeomorphic to the unit circle. Then $K$ is convex.

Only planes meeting the interior of $K$ are constrained: a supporting plane can meet the
boundary in a single point, as the plane $\{x : x_1 = 1\}$ does for the closed unit ball, so
requiring a circle for every plane would make the hypothesis impossible. Allowing empty or
one-point sections for the other planes would still exclude convex bodies such as the cube,
whose face planes meet its boundary in a square.

## Sources

- S. Ulam, Problem 68 of the Scottish Book, asking to prove that a manifold whose every hyperplane section of its boundary is a sphere is convex. Montejano gave a complete solution, settling the problem affirmatively: L. Montejano, "About a problem of Ulam concerning flat sections of manifolds", Comment. Math. Helv. 65 (1990), 462–473; see also Montejano, "Three old problems from the Polish school of mathematics", Bol. Soc. Mat. Mex. (3) 30 (2024).

articles.title: Body of revolution
articles.statement:
A body of revolution in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is given by real numbers
$R_1, R_2$ and a function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that vanishes outside the interval
$[-R_1, R_2]$, is infinitely differentiable on the open interval $(-R_1, R_2)$ and is concave on
$[-R_1, R_2]$. The dimension $d$ is only a parameter; these data do not depend on it.

articles.title: Solid of revolution
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 1$ and let a body of revolution in $\mathbb{R}^d$ be given
by $R_1$, $R_2$ and $f$. Writing points of $\mathbb{R}^d$ as $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{d-1})$, its solid
is the set of all $x$ with $x_0 \in [-R_1, R_2]$ and $x_1^2 + \dots + x_{d-1}^2 \le f(x_0)^2$.

articles.title: Center of mass
articles.statement:
The center of mass of a set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is the average
$\frac{1}{\operatorname{vol}(K)} \int_K x \, dx$, where $dx$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$.
By convention it is $0$ when $\operatorname{vol}(K)$ is $0$ or infinite, or when $x \mapsto x$ is
not integrable on $K$. For a compact convex body this is the usual center of mass.

articles.title: Cutting hyperplane at a level
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, let $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be
a unit vector and let $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$. A cutting hyperplane of $K$ in direction $\xi$ at
level $\delta$ is a real number $t$, standing for the hyperplane
$\{p \in \mathbb{R}^d : \xi \cdot p = t\}$, such that the volume of
$K \cap \{p \in \mathbb{R}^d : \xi \cdot p \le t\}$ equals $\delta$. Here a set of infinite volume
is assigned volume $0$.

articles.title: Floating in equilibrium in a direction
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, let
$\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be a unit vector and let $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$. We say that $K$ floats in
equilibrium in direction $\xi$ at level $\delta$ if, for every cutting hyperplane
$\{p : \xi \cdot p = t\}$ of $K$ in direction $\xi$ at level $\delta$, the center of mass of $K$
minus the center of mass of $K \cap \{p : \xi \cdot p \le t\}$ is a real multiple of $\xi$
(possibly zero); that is, the line through the two centers of mass is parallel to $\xi$ when they
differ.

articles.title: Floating in equilibrium in every orientation
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ floats in
equilibrium in every orientation at level $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$ if it floats in equilibrium in
direction $\xi$ at level $\delta$ for every unit vector $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

articles.title: Lower half-space
articles.statement:
For a unit vector $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$, the
closed lower half-space is $H^-(\xi) = \{p \in \mathbb{R}^d : \xi \cdot p \le t\}$.

## Sources

- D. Ryabogin, A negative answer to Ulam's Problem 19 from the Scottish Book, Annals of Math. 195 (3) 2022, Equation (1).

articles.title: Centrally symmetric set
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is centrally symmetric if there
is a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that the translate $K - p = \{x - p : x \in K\}$ is
origin-symmetric, that is, $K - p = -(K - p)$.

articles.title: Origin-symmetric set
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is origin-symmetric if $K = -K$,
where $-K = \{-x : x \in K\}$.

articles.title: Strictly convex body
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is a strictly convex body if it is
strictly convex (for distinct $x, y \in K$, every point of the open segment between $x$ and $y$
lies in the interior of $K$), compact, and has nonempty interior.

articles.title: Direction of the line through the centers of mass
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number, let
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, let $\xi$ be a unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, let
$\delta \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $H$ be a cutting hyperplane of $K$ in direction $\xi$ at level
$\delta$, with translation $t$, so that
$H^-(\xi) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \langle x, \xi \rangle \le t\}$. Writing $c(A)$ for the center
of mass of a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, the direction vector of the line $l(\xi)$ through the
center of mass of $K$ and the center of mass of the submerged part $K \cap H^-(\xi)$ is the vector
$c(K) - c(K \cap H^-(\xi))$.

articles.title: Unit sphere
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, the unit sphere
$S^{d-1} = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \|x\| = 1\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, centered at the origin.

articles.title: Ryabogin's negative answer to Ulam's floating body problem
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 3$. There exists a
body of revolution $K \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ that is a strictly convex body, is not centrally
symmetric, and floats in equilibrium in every orientation at the level $\operatorname{vol}(K)/2$.

## Sources

- D. Ryabogin, `A negative answer to Ulam's Problem 19 from the Scottish Book`, Annals of Math, 195 (3) 2022. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_ulam` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Local defining function
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real inner product space, $S \subseteq E$,
$\rho : E \to \mathbb{R}$ and $p \in E$. Then $\rho$ is a local defining function of $S$ at $p$
when $\rho(p) = 0$, $\rho$ is of class $C^2$ at $p$, its differential $D\rho(p)$ is nonzero, and
for all $x$ in some neighborhood of $p$, $x \in S$ if and only if $\rho(x) = 0$. In particular
$p \in S$.

Every point of a $C^2$ hypersurface has local defining functions, and every point of a regular
level set of a $C^2$ function is of this form.

articles.title: Hyperplanes have zero mean curvature
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product
space. For all $a \in E$, $c \in \mathbb{R}$ and $p \in E$, the mean curvature at $p$ of the level
set of $\rho(x) = \langle a, x \rangle - c$ through $p$ is $0$. In particular, for $a \neq 0$ the
hyperplane $\{x \mid \langle a, x \rangle = c\}$ has mean curvature $0$ at each of its points.

articles.title: Reversing the normal negates the mean curvature
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real
inner product space. For every $\rho : E \to \mathbb{R}$ and every $p \in E$, the mean curvature
at $p$ of the level set of $-\rho$ through $p$ is the negative of the mean curvature at $p$ of the
level set of $\rho$ through $p$: replacing $\rho$ by $-\rho$ reverses the unit normal and changes
the sign of the mean curvature.

articles.title: Positive rescaling preserves the mean curvature
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real
inner product space. For every $\rho : E \to \mathbb{R}$, every $p \in E$ and every real $c > 0$,
the mean curvature at $p$ of the level set of $c\rho$ through $p$ equals the mean curvature at $p$
of the level set of $\rho$ through $p$.

articles.title: Mean curvature under rescaling of the defining function
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional
real inner product space. For every $\rho : E \to \mathbb{R}$, every $p \in E$ and every real
$c \neq 0$, the mean curvature at $p$ of the level set of $c\rho$ through $p$ equals $c / |c|$
(the sign of $c$) times the mean curvature at $p$ of the level set of $\rho$ through $p$.

articles.title: Mean curvature of the unit sphere
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product
space of dimension $n$. For every $p \in E$ with $\|p\| = 1$, the mean curvature at $p$ of the
level set of $\rho(x) = \|x\|^2 - 1$ through $p$ is $n - 1$. That is, the unit sphere of $E$ has
mean curvature $n - 1$ with respect to the outward normal, the mean curvature being the sum (not
the average) of the principal curvatures.

articles.title: Mean curvature of a level set
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space,
$\rho : E \to \mathbb{R}$ and $p \in E$. Write $\nabla\rho(p)$ for the gradient of $\rho$ at $p$,
$D^2\rho(p)$ for the second derivative of $\rho$ at $p$ (a bilinear form on $E$), and
$\Delta\rho(p) = \sum_i D^2\rho(p)(e_i, e_i)$ for a fixed orthonormal basis $(e_i)$ of $E$. The
mean curvature at $p$ of the level set of $\rho$ through $p$, with respect to the unit normal
$\nu = \nabla\rho(p) / \|\nabla\rho(p)\|$, is
$H = (\Delta\rho(p) - D^2\rho(p)(\nu, \nu)) / \|\nabla\rho(p)\|$, and $H = 0$ when
$\nabla\rho(p) = 0$.

This is the trace of the second fundamental form on the tangent hyperplane $\nabla\rho(p)^\perp$,
the sum of the principal curvatures, and it equals
$\operatorname{div}(\nabla\rho / \|\nabla\rho\|)(p)$ when $\rho$ is $C^2$ near $p$ and
$\nabla\rho(p) \neq 0$. Since $D^2\rho(p)$ is bilinear, $\Delta\rho(p)$ does not depend on the
choice of orthonormal basis.

articles.title: Second fundamental form under rescaling of the defining function
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
finite-dimensional real inner product space. For every $\rho : E \to \mathbb{R}$, all
$p, u, v \in E$ and every real $c \neq 0$, the second fundamental form at $p$ of the level set of
$c\rho$ through $p$, evaluated at $(u, v)$, equals $c / |c|$ (the sign of $c$) times the second
fundamental form at $p$ of the level set of $\rho$ through $p$, evaluated at $(u, v)$.

articles.title: Second fundamental form of a level set
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner
product space, $\rho : E \to \mathbb{R}$ and $p \in E$. Write $\nabla\rho(p)$ for the gradient of
$\rho$ at $p$ and $D^2\rho(p)$ for the second derivative of $\rho$ at $p$ (a bilinear form on
$E$). The second fundamental form at $p$ of the level set of $\rho$ through $p$, with respect to
the unit normal $\nabla\rho(p) / \|\nabla\rho(p)\|$, is defined for all $u, v \in E$ by
$\mathrm{II}(u, v) = D^2\rho(p)(u, v) / \|\nabla\rho(p)\|$, and it is $0$ when $\nabla\rho(p) = 0$.
When $\rho$ is $C^2$ near $p$ and $\nabla\rho(p) \neq 0$, for tangent vectors $u$, $v$ (orthogonal
to $\nabla\rho(p)$) it equals $\langle D_u \nu, v \rangle$ for the unit normal field
$\nu = \nabla\rho / \|\nabla\rho\|$.

The formula is the second fundamental form (independent of the defining function, up to the sign
fixed by the normal) only for tangent $u$ and $v$: two defining functions of the same hyperplane
can give different values on the normal vector.

articles.title: A point with a local defining function lies in the set
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a real inner product
space, $S \subseteq E$, $\rho : E \to \mathbb{R}$ and $p \in E$. If $\rho$ is a local defining
function of $S$ at $p$, then $p \in S$.

articles.title: Doubly ruled graphs are planes or hyperbolic paraboloids
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real-valued
function of two real variables whose graph is doubly ruled; no continuity of $f$ is assumed. Then
there are real numbers $a, b, c, d, e, g$ such that
$f(x, y) = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 + dx + ey + g$ for all real $x$ and $y$, and either $a = b = c = 0$
(the graph is a plane) or $b^2 - 4ac > 0$ (the graph is a hyperbolic paraboloid).

This answers Steinhaus's Problem 44 of the Scottish Book, which asks whether such a surface, the
graph of a continuous function, must be a hyperbolic paraboloid, and whether this can be proved
without continuity. Banach answered both questions affirmatively, with a proof based on the remark
that any two lines on the surface either intersect or have parallel projections on the
$xy$-plane; planes are the degenerate doubly ruled case.

## Sources

- H. Steinhaus, Problem 44 of the Scottish Book; addendum in the Scottish Book, 30 July 1935: solved affirmatively by Banach, also without assuming continuity; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015).

articles.title: Doubly ruled graph
articles.statement:
The graph of a real-valued function $f$ of two real variables is
doubly ruled when for every point $(x_0, y_0) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ there are $(u_1, v_1, w_1)$ and
$(u_2, v_2, w_2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ such that the lines through $(x_0, y_0, f(x_0, y_0))$ with
directions $(u_1, v_1, w_1)$ and $(u_2, v_2, w_2)$ both lie in the graph of $f$, and $(u_2, v_2)$
is not a real multiple of $(u_1, v_1)$.

A line lying in the graph has a nonzero horizontal direction, so the last condition holds exactly
when the two lines are distinct.

articles.title: Line lying in a graph
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real-valued function of two real variables, and let
$x_0, y_0, u, v, w$ be real numbers. The line through $(x_0, y_0, f(x_0, y_0))$ with direction
$(u, v, w)$ lies in the graph of $f$ when $(u, v) \ne (0, 0)$ and
$f(x_0 + tu, y_0 + tv) = f(x_0, y_0) + tw$ for every real $t$.

articles.title: Acceleration of a space curve
articles.statement:
For a curve $r \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ and a real
number $t$, the acceleration of $r$ at $t$ is the derivative at $t$ of its velocity
$s \mapsto r'(s)$, that is $r''(t)$, where a derivative that does not exist is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: Curvature of a space curve
articles.statement:
For a curve $r \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ with velocity
$r'$ and acceleration $r''$, the curvature of $r$ at a real number $t$ is
$\kappa(t) = \lVert r'(t) \times r''(t) \rVert / \lVert r'(t) \rVert^3$, where $\times$ is the cross
product and $\lVert \cdot \rVert$ is the Euclidean norm; the quotient is $0$ when $r'(t) = 0$.

articles.title: Fáry–Milnor theorem
articles.statement:
Let $r \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a smooth knot, that is,
a real-analytic, $2\pi$-periodic curve that is injective on $[0, 2\pi)$ and has nonzero velocity
everywhere. If the total curvature of $r$ is at most $4\pi$, then $r$ is unknotted: there is a
real-analytic isotopy from $r$ to the standard circle through smooth knots.

## Sources

- I. Fáry, 'Sur la courbure totale d'une courbe gauche faisant un nœud', Bull. Soc. Math. France 77 (1949) 128–138; J. Milnor, 'On the total curvature of knots', Ann. of Math. (2) 52 (1950) 248–257. §161 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `fary_milnor` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Smooth knot
articles.statement:
A curve $r \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is a smooth knot when it is
real-analytic, periodic with period $2\pi$, injective on $[0, 2\pi)$, and regular, that is, its
velocity $r'(t)$ is nonzero for every real number $t$.

articles.title: Unknotted curve
articles.statement:
A curve $r \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is unknotted when there is
a real-analytic map $R \colon \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ such that
$R(t, 0) = r(t)$ and $R(t, 1) = (\cos t, \sin t, 0)$, the standard circle, for every real
number $t$, and for every $s \in [0, 1]$ the curve $t \mapsto R(t, s)$ is a smooth knot.

articles.title: Period of a parametrised knot
articles.statement:
The period used for parametrised knots is the real number
$2\pi$.

articles.title: Euclidean 3-space for the Fáry–Milnor theorem
articles.statement:
Euclidean 3-space is the real vector
space $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the Euclidean inner product and norm.

articles.title: Standard circle
articles.statement:
The standard circle is the curve $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ given by
$t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t, 0)$: the unit circle centred at the origin in the $xy$-plane.

articles.title: Total curvature of a space curve
articles.statement:
For a curve $r \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ with
velocity $r'$ and curvature $\kappa$, the total curvature of $r$ is the arc-length integral
$\int_0^{2\pi} \kappa(t) \, \lVert r'(t) \rVert \, dt$ over one period, where the integral is taken
to be $0$ if the integrand is not integrable.

articles.title: Velocity of a space curve
articles.statement:
For a curve $r \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ and a real
number $t$, the velocity of $r$ at $t$ is its derivative $r'(t)$, taken to be $0$ when $r$ is not
differentiable at $t$.

articles.title: Planar determinant for the Umlaufsatz
articles.statement:
For vectors $u = (u_0, u_1)$ and
$v = (v_0, v_1)$ in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, $\det(u, v) = u_0 v_1 - u_1 v_0$, the
signed area of the parallelogram spanned by $u$ and $v$.

articles.title: Hopf's Umlaufsatz
articles.statement:
Let $r : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a positively oriented simple
closed unit-speed plane curve: $r$ is continuously differentiable and $2\pi$-periodic, injective
on $[0, 2\pi)$, satisfies $\lVert r'(t) \rVert = 1$ for all $t$, and has positive signed area
$\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi} \det(r(t), r'(t))\,dt > 0$, where $\det(u, v) = u_0 v_1 - u_1 v_0$.
Let $\alpha : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuously differentiable tangent-angle lift of
$r$, that is, $r'(t) = (\cos \alpha(t), \sin \alpha(t))$ for all $t$. Then the total signed
curvature over one period is $2\pi$: $\int_0^{2\pi} \alpha'(t)\,dt = 2\pi$.

## Sources

- H. Hopf, *Über die Drehung der Tangenten...*, Compositio Math. 2 (1935). Knill, §170. Problem `hopf_umlaufsatz` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Positively oriented simple closed unit-speed curve
articles.statement:
A curve
$r : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ in the Euclidean plane is a positively oriented simple closed
unit-speed curve when it is continuously differentiable, periodic with period $2\pi$, injective on
$[0, 2\pi)$, has velocity of norm $\lVert r'(t) \rVert = 1$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, and has
positive signed area $\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi} \det(r(t), r'(t))\,dt > 0$, where
$\det(u, v) = u_0 v_1 - u_1 v_0$.

articles.title: Tangent-angle lift
articles.statement:
For a curve $r : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ in the Euclidean plane,
a function $\alpha : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a tangent-angle lift of $r$ when $\alpha$ is
continuously differentiable and the velocity of $r$ satisfies
$r'(t) = (\cos \alpha(t), \sin \alpha(t))$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Parameter period for the Umlaufsatz
articles.statement:
The parameter period of the closed curves in the
Hopf Umlaufsatz is the real number $2\pi$.

articles.title: Euclidean plane for the Umlaufsatz
articles.statement:
The Euclidean plane is the space $\mathbb{R}^2$ of
pairs of real numbers with the Euclidean inner product and norm.

articles.title: Signed area of a closed plane curve
articles.statement:
For a curve $r : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$, the
signed area is $\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi} \det(r(t), r'(t))\,dt$, where $r'$ is the velocity of
$r$ and $\det(u, v) = u_0 v_1 - u_1 v_0$ (Green's normalization). Its sign fixes the orientation
convention.

articles.title: Signed curvature
articles.statement:
For a function $\alpha : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and
$t \in \mathbb{R}$, the signed curvature of $\alpha$ at $t$ is the derivative $\alpha'(t)$, taken
to be $0$ where $\alpha$ is not differentiable at $t$.

When $\alpha$ is a tangent-angle lift of a unit-speed plane curve, this is the signed curvature
of the curve at $t$.

articles.title: Total signed curvature of a tangent-angle lift
articles.statement:
For a function
$\alpha : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the total signed curvature is $\int_0^{2\pi} \alpha'(t)\,dt$,
the integral of the signed curvature $\alpha'$ over one parameter period $[0, 2\pi]$.

articles.title: Velocity of a plane curve
articles.statement:
For a curve $r : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ in the Euclidean
plane and $t \in \mathbb{R}$, the velocity of $r$ at $t$ is its derivative $r'(t) \in \mathbb{R}^2$,
taken to be $0$ where $r$ is not differentiable.

articles.title: Aspect ratio
articles.statement:
For points $a = (a_1, a_2)$ and $b = (b_1, b_2)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, the
aspect ratio of the axis-aligned rectangle with opposite corners $a$ and $b$ is
$|a_1 - b_1| / |a_2 - b_2|$, the ratio of its horizontal side length to its vertical side
length; it is $0$ when $a_2 = b_2$.

articles.title: Axis-aligned rectangle
articles.statement:
For points $a = (a_1, a_2)$ and $b = (b_1, b_2)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$,
the axis-aligned (possibly degenerate) rectangle with opposite corners $a$ and $b$ is the list of
its four vertices $(a_1, a_2)$, $(b_1, a_2)$, $(b_1, b_2)$, $(a_1, b_2)$, in this order.

articles.title: Inscribed rectangle
articles.statement:
Let $\gamma$ be a map from the unit circle to $\mathbb{R}^2$. For
points $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and an angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, the rotated rectangle given by
$a$, $b$ and $\theta$ is inscribed in $\gamma$ when its four vertices are pairwise distinct and
each lies in the image of $\gamma$.

The map $\gamma$ need not be smooth, or even a Jordan curve, for this definition.

articles.title: Rotated rectangle with given opposite corners
articles.statement:
For $z, w \in \mathbb{C}$ and an angle
$\theta$, $R(z, w, \theta)$ is the list of four points $z e^{i\theta}$,
$(\operatorname{Re} w + i \operatorname{Im} z) e^{i\theta}$, $w e^{i\theta}$,
$(\operatorname{Re} z + i \operatorname{Im} w) e^{i\theta}$: the vertices, in order, of the
axis-parallel rectangle with opposite corners $z$ and $w$, rotated about the origin by $\theta$.
The rectangle is degenerate when $z$ and $w$ have the same real part or the same imaginary
part.

articles.title: Rotated rectangle
articles.statement:
For points $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and an angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$,
the rotated rectangle given by $a$, $b$ and $\theta$ is the list of four points obtained by applying
the rotation $(x, y) \mapsto (x \cos\theta + y \sin\theta, -x \sin\theta + y \cos\theta)$ about the
origin to each vertex, in order, of the axis-aligned rectangle with opposite corners $a$ and $b$.

articles.title: Rectangular peg theorem (Greene–Lobb)
articles.statement:
Let $\gamma : S^1 \to \mathbb{C}$ be a $C^\infty$
embedding of the unit circle (a smooth Jordan curve in the plane). For $z, w \in \mathbb{C}$ and
an angle $\theta$, write $R(z, w, \theta)$ for the list of the four points $z e^{i\theta}$,
$(\operatorname{Re} w + i \operatorname{Im} z) e^{i\theta}$, $w e^{i\theta}$,
$(\operatorname{Re} z + i \operatorname{Im} w) e^{i\theta}$, in this order: the vertices of the
(possibly degenerate) axis-parallel rectangle with opposite corners $z$ and $w$, rotated about
the origin by $\theta$. Then for all $z$, $w$, $\theta$ there exist $z'$, $w'$, $\theta'$ such
that $R(z, w, \theta)$ is similar to $R(z', w', \theta')$, meaning that for some real $r > 0$
the distance between the $i$-th and $j$-th vertices of $R(z, w, \theta)$ is $r$ times the
distance between the $i$-th and $j$-th vertices of $R(z', w', \theta')$ for all $i, j$, and all
four vertices of $R(z', w', \theta')$ lie on $\gamma$.

## Sources

- J. E. Greene and A. Lobb, `The rectangular peg problem`, Annals of Math, 194 (2) 2021. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_rectangular_peg_problem` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Hugelmeyer's theorem on aspect ratios of inscribed rectangles
articles.statement:
Let $\gamma$ be a smooth Jordan
curve, that is, a map from the unit circle to $\mathbb{R}^2$ that is a $C^\infty$ immersion and a
topological embedding, and let $X$ be the set of all $r \in [0, 1]$ such that some rectangle
inscribed in $\gamma$ has aspect ratio $\tan(r\pi/4)$. Then the Lebesgue measure of $X$ is at
least $1/3$.

## Sources

- C. Hugelmeyer, `Inscribed rectangles in a smooth Jordan curve attain at least one third of all aspect ratios`, Annals of Math, 194 (2) 2021. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_inscribed_rectangles` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Aspect-ratio parameters of inscribed rectangles
articles.statement:
For a map $\gamma$ from the unit circle
to $\mathbb{R}^2$, let $X(\gamma)$ be the set of all $r \in [0, 1]$ for which there are points
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and an angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ such that the rotated rectangle given
by $a$, $b$ and $\theta$ is inscribed in $\gamma$ and the axis-aligned rectangle with opposite
corners $a$ and $b$ has aspect ratio $\tan(r\pi/4)$.

articles.title: Fundamental domain of the Moebius band
articles.statement:
For a real number $a$, this is the set of points
$(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $0 \le x \le 1$ and $0 \le y < a$.

articles.title: Moebius embedding
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a real number, let $S = [0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}$ be the
unit strip and let $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$. Then $f$ is a Moebius embedding of
aspect ratio $a$ if $f(1 - x, y + a) = f(x, y)$ for every $(x, y) \in S$, $f$ is $C^\infty$ on
$S$, at every point of $S$ the derivative of $f$ within $S$ is a linear isometry
$\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$, and $f$ is injective on $[0, 1] \times [0, a)$.

This encodes the paper's smooth isometric embedding of a Moebius band: the strip is glued into
a band by the first condition, and injectivity on a fundamental domain makes the glued map an
embedding.

articles.title: Gluing map of the Moebius band
articles.statement:
For a real number $a$, this is the map
$\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ given by $(x, y) \mapsto (1 - x, y + a)$.

articles.title: Schwartz's optimal paper Moebius band theorem
articles.statement:
Let $a > 0$. If
$f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is a Moebius embedding of aspect ratio $a$, then
$a > \sqrt{3}$. That is, a smooth embedded paper Moebius band has aspect ratio greater
than $\sqrt{3}$.

## Sources

- R. E. Schwartz, `The optimal paper Moebius band`, Annals of Math, 201 (1) 2025. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_optimal_moebius` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Unit strip
articles.statement:
The unit strip is the set of points $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with
$0 \le x \le 1$, that is, $[0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Fréchet's Problem 117 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
There is a $1$-periodic continuous
map $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$, injective on $[0, 1)$, that has a tangent
line at every parameter $t$, such that no $1$-periodic continuous map
$p : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ that is injective on $[0, 1)$ and has the same image
as $\gamma$ is differentiable at every $t$ with $p'(t) \neq 0$.

Here $\gamma$ has a tangent line at $t$ when there is a unit vector $v$ such that for
every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with
$\|w - \langle w, v \rangle v\| \le \varepsilon \|w\|$, where $w = \gamma(s) - \gamma(t)$,
whenever $0 < |s - t| < \delta$.

## Sources

- M. Fréchet, Problem 117 of the Scottish Book; in general, no, by A. J. Ward, Fundamenta Mathematicae 28 (1937), cited in the typescript addendum Ad 117. Ward also gives a representation whose derivatives exist and are not all zero except on a null set of parameter values whose points have Carathéodory measure zero.

articles.title: Tangent line to a closed space curve
articles.statement:
A `1`-periodic continuous injective-on-`[0, 1)` curve `γ : ℝ → ℝ³`
has an (oriented) tangent line at `t` if there is a unit direction `v` such
that every nearby secant vector `γ s - γ t` is arbitrarily close, relative
to its length, to the line spanned by `v`.

articles.title: The claim of Fréchet's Problem 117
articles.statement:
The claim of Fréchet's Problem 117 from the Scottish
Book is the statement that for every $1$-periodic continuous map
$\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ that is injective on $[0, 1)$ and has a tangent line at
every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, there is a $1$-periodic continuous map
$p : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ that is injective on $[0, 1)$, has the same image as $\gamma$,
and is differentiable at every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ with $p'(t) \ne 0$.

articles.title: Classification of compact connected $1$-manifolds with boundary
articles.statement:
Every compact, connected,
Hausdorff, second-countable smooth $1$-manifold $M$ with (possibly empty) boundary is
diffeomorphic either to the circle $S^1$ or to the closed interval $[0, 1]$.

## Sources

- Classification of 1-manifolds with boundary; Hirsch, Differential Topology; J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., collar theorem; Lean states compact connected `𝓡∂ 1` with closed interval specialization.

articles.title: Classification of connected $1$-manifolds without boundary
articles.statement:
Every connected, Hausdorff,
second-countable smooth $1$-manifold $M$ without boundary is diffeomorphic either to the circle
$S^1$ or to the real line $\mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- Classification of connected boundaryless 1-manifolds; Milnor (1965); Hirsch; Lean states dichotomy specialization for `𝓡 1`.

articles.title: A closed simply connected topological 4-manifold with no smooth structure
articles.statement:
There
exists a compact, Hausdorff, simply connected topological space $M$ that admits an atlas of
charts modelled on $\mathbb{R}^4$, such that no atlas of charts on $M$ modelled on $\mathbb{R}^4$
makes $M$ a smooth ($C^\infty$) manifold.

## Sources

-. Problem `four_manifold_not_smooth` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Hadamard–Caccioppoli global inverse theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a proper map that is a $C^\infty$ local diffeomorphism.
Then $f$ is a global $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism: there is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism
$\Phi : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ whose underlying map is $f$.

## Sources

- J. Hadamard, Bull. Soc. Math. France 34 (1906) 71–84; R. Caccioppoli, Rend. Sem. Mat. Univ. Padova 3 (1932); F.-C. Plastock, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 200 (1974) extension to Banach spaces; J.
