Lee, Riemannian Manifolds? Lean states Euclidean `ℝⁿ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)` specialization with `IsProperMap` and `IsLocalDiffeomorph` hypotheses.

articles.title: Hairy ball theorem
articles.statement:
Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $E$ be a real inner product space of
dimension $2k + 1$, with unit sphere $S = \{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$. If $f : S \to E$ is
continuous and $\langle f(x), x \rangle = 0$ for every $x \in S$, then $f(x) = 0$ for some
$x \in S$.

## Sources

- H. Poincaré proved the 2-sphere case in 1885 and L. E. J. Brouwer extended it to higher even-dimensional spheres in 1912; J. Milnor, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint hairy ball; Guillemin-Pollack, Differential Topology; Lean states even-sphere ambient finite-dimensional inner-product specialization via `inner = 0`.

articles.title: Composition of immersions at a point over boundaryless models
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a
nontrivially normed field, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$
be charted spaces modelled through models with corners on normed spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, where
the models of $N$ and $N'$ are boundaryless. If $f : M \to N$ is a $C^n$ immersion at a point
$x \in M$ and $g : N \to N'$ is a $C^n$ immersion at $f(x)$, then $g \circ f$ is a $C^n$
immersion at $x$.

Here a map is a $C^n$ immersion at a point when, for some normed space $F$ over $\mathbb{K}$,
there are charts of the maximal $C^n$ atlases around the point and its image, the first mapped by
the map into the second, in which the map reads $u \mapsto \varphi(u, 0)$ for a continuous linear
isomorphism $\varphi$ from the product of the source model space with $F$ onto the target model
space.

articles.title: Composition of immersions with fixed complements
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially normed
field, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$ be charted spaces
modelled through models with corners on normed spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, where the models of $N$
and $N'$ are boundaryless. Let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be normed spaces over $\mathbb{K}$. If
$f : M \to N$ is a $C^n$ immersion with complement $F_1$ and $g : N \to N'$ is a $C^n$ immersion
with complement $F_2$, then $g \circ f$ is a $C^n$ immersion with complement $F_1 \times F_2$.

Here a map is a $C^n$ immersion with complement $F$ when for every point there are charts of the
maximal $C^n$ atlases around the point and its image, the first mapped by the map into the
second, in which the map reads $u \mapsto \varphi(u, 0)$ for a continuous linear isomorphism
$\varphi$ from the product of the source model space with $F$ onto the target model space.

articles.title: Composition of immersions over boundaryless models
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially
normed field, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$ be charted
spaces modelled through models with corners on normed spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, where the models
of $N$ and $N'$ are boundaryless. If $f : M \to N$ and $g : N \to N'$ are $C^n$ immersions, then
$g \circ f$ is a $C^n$ immersion.

Here a map is a $C^n$ immersion when there is a normed space $F$ over $\mathbb{K}$ such that for
every point there are charts of the maximal $C^n$ atlases around the point and its image, the
first mapped by the map into the second, in which the map reads $u \mapsto \varphi(u, 0)$ for a
continuous linear isomorphism $\varphi$ from the product of the source model space with $F$ onto
the target model space.

articles.title: Composition of immersions at a point with fixed complements
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a
nontrivially normed field, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$
be charted spaces modelled through models with corners on normed spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, where
the models of $N$ and $N'$ are boundaryless. Let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be normed spaces over
$\mathbb{K}$. If $f : M \to N$ is a $C^n$ immersion at a point $x \in M$ with complement $F_1$
and $g : N \to N'$ is a $C^n$ immersion at $f(x)$ with complement $F_2$, then $g \circ f$ is a
$C^n$ immersion at $x$ with complement $F_1 \times F_2$.

Here a map is a $C^n$ immersion at a point with complement $F$ when there are charts of the
maximal $C^n$ atlases around the point and its image, the first mapped by the map into the
second, in which the map reads $u \mapsto \varphi(u, 0)$ for a continuous linear isomorphism
$\varphi$ from the product of the source model space with $F$ onto the target model space.

articles.title: Composition of immersions at a point
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially normed field, let
$n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$ be $C^n$ manifolds without
boundary modeled on Banach spaces over $\mathbb{K}$. If $f : M \to N$ is a $C^n$ immersion at a
point $x \in M$ and $g : N \to N'$ is a $C^n$ immersion at $f(x)$, then $g \circ f$ is a $C^n$
immersion at $x$.

Here a map is a $C^n$ immersion at a point when, in suitable charts around the point and its
image, it reads $u \mapsto \varphi(u, 0)$ for a continuous linear isomorphism
$\varphi : E \times F \to E'$, where $E$ and $E'$ are the model spaces of the source and target
and $F$ is some normed space over $\mathbb{K}$.

Proof: Restrict the first immersion's codomain chart to the second immersion's domain chart, then
conjugate that chart transition through the second linear normal form. The normal forms compose
with the product of their complements.

## Sources

- J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 4.

articles.title: Injective differential gives an immersion
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or
$\mathbb{C}$, let $n \ge 1$ be a smoothness degree (possibly $\infty$ or $\omega$), and let
$M$ and $N$ be $C^n$ manifolds without boundary over $\mathbb{K}$, modelled on
finite-dimensional normed $\mathbb{K}$-vector spaces. If a map $f \colon M \to N$ is $C^n$ at
every point of some neighbourhood of a point $x \in M$ and its differential $df_x$ at $x$ is
injective, then $f$ is a $C^n$ immersion at $x$.

Proof: Choose a complement to the differential's range, apply the inverse function theorem to
the resulting product map in extended charts, and use its local inverse as a target chart.

## Sources

- J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 4.

articles.title: Composition of immersions
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially normed field, let
$n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$ be $C^n$ manifolds without
boundary modeled on Banach spaces over $\mathbb{K}$. If $f : M \to N$ and $g : N \to N'$ are
$C^n$ immersions, then $g \circ f$ is a $C^n$ immersion.

Here a map is a $C^n$ immersion when there is a normed space $F$ over $\mathbb{K}$ such that
around every point, in suitable charts around the point and its image, the map reads
$u \mapsto \varphi(u, 0)$ for some continuous linear isomorphism $\varphi : E \times F \to E'$,
where $E$ and $E'$ are the model spaces of the source and target.

Proof: Apply the pointwise composition construction using the product of the two global
complements, then package the resulting fixed-complement immersion.

## Sources

- J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 4.

articles.title: Injective differential with complemented range gives an immersion
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $n \ge 1$ be a smoothness degree (possibly $\infty$ or
$\omega$), and let $M$ and $N$ be $C^n$ manifolds without boundary over $\mathbb{K}$, modelled on
Banach spaces $E$ and $E'$. Let $f \colon M \to N$ be $C^n$ at every point of some neighbourhood
of a point $x \in M$, and suppose that its differential $df_x \colon E \to E'$ is injective and
that there is a continuous linear projection of $E'$ onto the range of $df_x$. Then $f$ is a
$C^n$ immersion at $x$.

articles.title: Alternating partial sum
articles.statement:
For a sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ of natural numbers and
$k \in \mathbb{N}$, the alternating partial sum of $a$ up to $k$ is the integer
$\sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^{k-j} a_j$.

articles.title: Smoothness of the Morse quadratic form
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$, the Morse
quadratic form $Q_{k,n} \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ of index $k$ is $C^\infty$.

articles.title: Morse function
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a $C^\infty$ manifold without boundary modelled on a real
normed space of finite dimension $d$. A function $f \colon M \to \mathbb{R}$ is a Morse function
if it is $C^\infty$ and, for every critical point $p$ of $f$ (a point where the differential
$df_p$ is zero), there exist an integer $0 \le k \le d$, a map $\varphi \colon M \to \mathbb{R}^d$
that is a local $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism at $p$ with $\varphi(p) = 0$, and an open set $U$
containing $p$ such that $f(q) = f(p) + Q_k(\varphi(q))$ for all $q \in U$. Here $Q_k$ is the
Morse quadratic form $Q_k(y) = -y_1^2 - \dots - y_k^2 + y_{k+1}^2 + \dots + y_d^2$ on
$\mathbb{R}^d$.

articles.title: Existence of Morse functions
articles.statement:
Every Hausdorff, second-countable $C^\infty$ manifold $M$
without boundary, modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, admits a Morse function
$f \colon M \to \mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- J. Milnor, Morse Theory, Ann. of Math. Studies 51 (1963); M. Hirsch, Differential Topology; J. Lee, Intro to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed.; Lean states boundaryless finite-dimensional second-countable specialization.

articles.title: Morse inequalities
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a compact Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary,
modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, and let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be a Morse
function: $f$ is $C^\infty$, has finitely many critical points, and the Hessian of $f$ at each
critical point, computed in the preferred chart, is a nondegenerate bilinear form. The Morse index
of a critical point is the largest dimension of a subspace on which this Hessian is negative
definite. For $j \in \mathbb{N}$ let $c_j$ be the number of critical points of $f$ of Morse index
$j$, and let $b_j$ be the dimension of the singular homology $H_j(M; \mathbb{R})$ (taken to be $0$
if infinite). Then for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$\sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^{k-j} b_j \le \sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^{k-j} c_j.$$

## Sources

- M. Morse, The Calculus of Variations in the Large, AMS Colloq. Publ. 18 (1934). Listed as §40 in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `morse_inequality` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Morse lemma
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be a $C^\infty$ function with
$Df(0) = 0$ whose Hessian at $0$ is nondegenerate: if $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies
$D^2 f(0)(v, w) = 0$ for all $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$, then $v = 0$. Then there exist an integer
$0 \le k \le n$, a map $\varphi \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ that is a local $C^\infty$
diffeomorphism at $0$ with $\varphi(0) = 0$, and an open set $U$ containing $0$ such that
$f(x) = f(0) + Q_k(\varphi(x))$ for all $x \in U$. Here $Q_k$ is the Morse quadratic form
$Q_k(y) = -y_1^2 - \dots - y_k^2 + y_{k+1}^2 + \dots + y_n^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

## Sources

- J. Milnor, Morse Theory, Ann. of Math. Studies 51 (1963) Lemma 2.2; M. Hirsch, Differential Topology; J. Lee, Intro to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Morse lemma; Lean states Euclidean origin finite-dimensional specialization with corrected nondegeneracy grouping `(∀ w, (fderiv (fderiv f) 0 v) w = 0) → v = 0`.

articles.title: The Morse quadratic form when the index is at least the dimension
articles.statement:
If $n \le k$, then the
Morse quadratic form $Q_{k,n}$ of index $k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies $Q_{k,n}(v) = -\|v\|^2$
for every $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$, where $\|v\|$ is the Euclidean norm of $v$.

articles.title: The Morse quadratic form of index zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the Morse quadratic
form $Q_{0,n}$ of index $0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies $Q_{0,n}(v) = \|v\|^2$ for every
$v \in \mathbb{R}^n$, where $\|v\|$ is the Euclidean norm of $v$.

articles.title: The Morse quadratic form vanishes at the origin
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$, the
Morse quadratic form $Q_{k,n}$ of index $k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies $Q_{k,n}(0) = 0$.

articles.title: Morse quadratic form
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, the Morse quadratic form of index
$k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, with coordinates $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$, is the function
$Q_{k,n} \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ given by
$Q_{k,n}(v) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \varepsilon_i v_i^2$, where $\varepsilon_i = -1$ if $i < k$ and
$\varepsilon_i = 1$ if $i \ge k$. In particular, if $k \ge n$ every coefficient is $-1$.

articles.title: Weak Morse inequalities
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a compact Hausdorff smooth ($C^\infty$) manifold
without boundary, modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, and let
$f \colon M \to \mathbb{R}$ be a Morse function, that is, a smooth function with finitely many
critical points, all of them non-degenerate. Then for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ the $k$-th Betti
number of $M$, the real dimension of the singular homology $H_k(M; \mathbb{R})$, is at most the
number of critical points of $f$ of Morse index $k$.

## Sources

- M. Morse, The Calculus of Variations in the Large, AMS Colloq. Publ. 18 (1934). Listed as §40 additional statement in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `weak_morse_inequality` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Local graph form of a level set near a regular point
articles.statement:
Let $E$, $G$ and $F$ be
finite-dimensional real normed spaces with $\dim E = \dim G + \dim F$, let $f \colon E \to F$ be
a $C^1$ map and let $x_0 \in E$ be a point at which the derivative $Df(x_0)$ is surjective. Then
there exist a continuous linear isomorphism $e \colon E \to G \times F$, a neighbourhood $U$ in
$G$ of the first component of $e(x_0)$, a map $g \colon G \to F$ that is $C^1$ on $U$, and a
neighbourhood $V$ of $x_0$ such that a point $x \in V$ satisfies $f(x) = f(x_0)$ if and only if
$e(x) = (u, g(u))$ for some $u \in U$.

articles.title: Graph maps are immersions
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be real normed spaces, let
$n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$ and let $h \colon E \to F$ be a $C^n$ map. Then the
graph map $x \mapsto (x, h(x))$ from $E$ to $E \times F$ is a $C^n$ immersion, where $E$ and
$E \times F$ are regarded as manifolds modelled on themselves.

articles.title: Regular level sets are locally graphs
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon \mathbb{R}^{k+m} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be a
$C^1$ map and let $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{k+m}$ be a point at which the derivative $Df(x_0)$ is
surjective. Then there exist a linear isomorphism
$e \colon \mathbb{R}^{k+m} \to \mathbb{R}^k \times \mathbb{R}^m$, a neighbourhood $U$ in
$\mathbb{R}^k$ of the first component of $e(x_0)$, a map $g \colon \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^m$
that is $C^1$ on $U$, and a neighbourhood $V$ of $x_0$ such that a point $x \in V$ satisfies
$f(x) = f(x_0)$ if and only if $e(x) = (u, g(u))$ for some $u \in U$.

Proof: A projection onto the derivative kernel supplies adapted linear coordinates. The
product-space implicit function theorem then identifies the level set with a local `C¹` graph
(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implicit_function_theorem).

## Sources

- J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 4 (rank theorem).

articles.title: Regular level sets are locally parametrized by immersions
articles.statement:
Let
$f \colon \mathbb{R}^{k+m} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be a $C^1$ map and let $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{k+m}$ be a
point at which the derivative $Df(x_0)$ is surjective. Then there exist an open set
$U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$, a point $u_0 \in U$, a map $\varphi \colon \mathbb{R}^k \to
\mathbb{R}^{k+m}$ that is $C^1$ and a $C^1$ immersion on all of $\mathbb{R}^k$, and a
neighbourhood $V$ of $x_0$ such that $\varphi(u_0) = x_0$ and
$\varphi(U \cap \varphi^{-1}(V)) = V \cap f^{-1}(f(x_0))$.

Proof: Apply the implicit function theorem in adapted linear coordinates, then use a smooth bump
to extend the local graphing function globally. A shear chart makes its graph map an immersion.

## Sources

- J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 4 (rank theorem).

articles.title: Bad parameter set
articles.statement:
Let $F \colon \mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a map
and $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$. For $a \in \mathbb{R}^p$ write $F_a = F(a, \cdot)$ for the slice
$\mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$. The bad parameter set of $F$ at $y$ is the set of
$a \in \mathbb{R}^p$ for which there is $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with $F(a, x) = y$ and the derivative
of $F_a$ at $x$ not surjective, that is, the set of $a$ for which $y$ is not a regular value of
$F_a$.

The derivative of a map at a point where it is not differentiable is taken to be zero.

articles.title: Critical points of a map to Euclidean space
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable
smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, and let
$f : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a map. The critical set of $f$ is the set of points $x \in M$ at which
the manifold derivative of $f$ at $x$, a linear map $T_xM \to \mathbb{R}^n$, is not surjective.

The derivative is taken to be $0$ at points where $f$ is not differentiable.

articles.title: Critical values of a map to Euclidean space
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable
smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, and let
$f : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a map. The set of critical values of $f$ is the image under $f$ of its
critical set, the set of points $x \in M$ at which the manifold derivative of $f$ at $x$ is not
surjective.

articles.title: Parametric Sard theorem for real analytic families
articles.statement:
Let $p, m, n$ be natural numbers, let
$F \colon \mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a real analytic ($C^\omega$) map
and let $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Suppose that the derivative of $F$ is surjective at every point
$(a, x)$ with $F(a, x) = y$. Then the bad parameter set of $F$ at $y$, the set of
$a \in \mathbb{R}^p$ for which some $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ has $F(a, x) = y$ and the derivative of
the slice $F(a, \cdot) \colon \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ at $x$ is not surjective, has
Lebesgue measure zero.

## Sources

- R. Abraham, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 69 (1963), 470–475, DOI 10.1090/S0002-9904-1963-10969-6 parametric transversality; V. Guillemin and A. Pollack, Differential Topology; J. Lee, Intro to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed.; Lean states Euclidean finite-dimensional measure-zero form with `fderiv ℝ F` surjective hypothesis.

articles.title: Sard's theorem on open subsets of finite-dimensional spaces
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be
finite-dimensional real normed spaces, let $\mu$ be an additive Haar measure on $F$ with its Borel
$\sigma$-algebra, let $U \subseteq E$ be open, and let $g : E \to F$ be $C^\infty$ on $U$. Then the
image under $g$ of the set of points $x \in U$ at which the derivative of $g$ is not surjective has
$\mu$-measure zero.

articles.title: Sard's theorem for maps into Euclidean space
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable smooth
manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, and let
$f : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a $C^\infty$ map. Then the set of critical values of $f$, the image
under $f$ of the points of $M$ at which the manifold derivative of $f$ is not surjective, has
Lebesgue measure zero.

## Sources

- A. Sard, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 48 (1942) 883–890 measure of critical values; J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed.; Guillemin-Pollack, Differential Topology; Lean states finite-dimensional manifold to `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)` specialization.

articles.title: Submersions at a point are closed under composition
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially
normed field, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$ be charted
spaces modelled, through models with corners, on normed spaces $E$, $E''$, $E'''$ over
$\mathbb{K}$, where the models of $M$ and $N$ have no boundary. If $f : M \to N$ is a $C^n$
submersion at $x \in M$ and $g : N \to N'$ is a $C^n$ submersion at $f(x)$, then $g \circ f$ is a
$C^n$ submersion at $x$.

Here $f$ is a $C^n$ submersion at $x$ when, for some normed space $F$ over $\mathbb{K}$, there are
charts $\varphi$ of $M$ around $x$ and $\psi$ of $N$ around $f(x)$ in the $C^n$ maximal atlases,
with $f$ mapping the domain of $\varphi$ into the domain of $\psi$, and a continuous linear
equivalence $e : E \to E'' \times F$ such that
$\hat\psi \circ f \circ \hat\varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ e$ on the image of $\hat\varphi$,
where $\hat\varphi$ and $\hat\psi$ denote the charts followed by the models with corners.

articles.title: Composition of submersions with chosen complements
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially
normed field, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$ be charted
spaces modelled, through models with corners, on normed spaces $E$, $E''$, $E'''$ over
$\mathbb{K}$, where the models of $M$ and $N$ have no boundary. Let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be normed
spaces over $\mathbb{K}$. If $f : M \to N$ is a $C^n$ submersion with complement $F_1$ and
$g : N \to N'$ is a $C^n$ submersion with complement $F_2$, then $g \circ f$ is a $C^n$
submersion with complement $F_2 \times F_1$.

Here $f$ is a $C^n$ submersion with complement $F$ when at every $x \in M$ there are charts
$\varphi$ of $M$ around $x$ and $\psi$ of $N$ around $f(x)$ in the $C^n$ maximal atlases, with
$f$ mapping the domain of $\varphi$ into the domain of $\psi$, and a continuous linear
equivalence $e : E \to E'' \times F$ such that
$\hat\psi \circ f \circ \hat\varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ e$ on the image of $\hat\varphi$,
where $\hat\varphi$ and $\hat\psi$ denote the charts followed by the models with corners.

articles.title: Submersions are closed under composition
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially normed
field, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$ be charted spaces
modelled, through models with corners, on normed spaces $E$, $E''$, $E'''$ over $\mathbb{K}$,
where the models of $M$ and $N$ have no boundary. If $f : M \to N$ and $g : N \to N'$ are $C^n$
submersions, then so is $g \circ f$.

Here $f$ is a $C^n$ submersion when there is one normed space $F$ over $\mathbb{K}$ such that at
every $x \in M$ there are charts $\varphi$ of $M$ around $x$ and $\psi$ of $N$ around $f(x)$ in
the $C^n$ maximal atlases, with $f$ mapping the domain of $\varphi$ into the domain of $\psi$, and
a continuous linear equivalence $e : E \to E'' \times F$ such that
$\hat\psi \circ f \circ \hat\varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ e$ on the image of $\hat\varphi$,
where $\hat\varphi$ and $\hat\psi$ denote the charts followed by the models with corners.

articles.title: Composition of submersions at a point with chosen complements
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a
nontrivially normed field, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$
be charted spaces modelled, through models with corners, on normed spaces $E$, $E''$, $E'''$ over
$\mathbb{K}$, where the models of $M$ and $N$ have no boundary. Let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be normed
spaces over $\mathbb{K}$. If $f : M \to N$ is a $C^n$ submersion at $x \in M$ with complement
$F_1$ and $g : N \to N'$ is a $C^n$ submersion at $f(x)$ with complement $F_2$, then
$g \circ f$ is a $C^n$ submersion at $x$ with complement $F_2 \times F_1$.

Here $f$ is a $C^n$ submersion at $x$ with complement $F$ when there are charts $\varphi$ of $M$
around $x$ and $\psi$ of $N$ around $f(x)$ in the $C^n$ maximal atlases, with $f$ mapping the
domain of $\varphi$ into the domain of $\psi$, and a continuous linear equivalence
$e : E \to E'' \times F$ such that
$\hat\psi \circ f \circ \hat\varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ e$ on the image of $\hat\varphi$,
where $\hat\varphi$ and $\hat\psi$ denote the charts followed by the models with corners.

articles.title: Changing the target chart of a submersion at a point
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially
normed field, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$ and $N$ be charted spaces
modelled, through models with corners, on normed spaces $E$ and $E''$ over $\mathbb{K}$, both
models without boundary. Let $f : M \to N$ be a $C^n$ submersion at $x \in M$ with complement $F$,
and let $e : E \to E'' \times F$ be the continuous linear equivalence chosen for it. Then for every
chart $\psi$ of $N$ in the $C^n$ maximal atlas with $f(x)$ in its domain there is a chart
$\varphi$ of $M$ in the $C^n$ maximal atlas with $x$ in its domain, such that $f$ maps the domain
of $\varphi$ into the domain of $\psi$ and
$\hat\psi \circ f \circ \hat\varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ e$ on the image of $\hat\varphi$,
where $\hat\varphi$ and $\hat\psi$ denote the charts followed by the models with corners.

Here $f$ is a $C^n$ submersion at $x$ with complement $F$ (a normed space over $\mathbb{K}$) when
there are charts of $M$ around $x$ and of $N$ around $f(x)$ in the $C^n$ maximal atlases, the
first mapped by $f$ into the second, in which $f$ reads $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ e$ on the image of
the first, for some continuous linear equivalence $e : E \to E'' \times F$; a witness of this
fixes one such $e$.

articles.title: Surjective differential into a finite-dimensional manifold gives a submersion
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$ with
$n \ge 1$, let $M$ be a $C^n$ manifold without boundary over $\mathbb{K}$ modelled on a Banach
space, and let $N$ be a $C^n$ manifold, possibly with boundary or corners, over $\mathbb{K}$
modelled on a finite-dimensional space. If $f : M \to N$ is $C^n$ at every point of some
neighbourhood of $x \in M$ and the manifold derivative of $f$ at $x$ is surjective, then $f$ is a
$C^n$ submersion at $x$: there are charts of the $C^n$ maximal atlases around $x$ and $f(x)$, the
first mapped by $f$ into the second, in which $f$ reads $(u, v) \mapsto u$ after a continuous linear
identification of the model space of $M$ with the product of the model space of $N$ and some
normed space.

articles.title: Composition of submersions at a point
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially normed field, let
$n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$ be $C^n$ manifolds without
boundary over $\mathbb{K}$ modelled on Banach spaces. If $f : M \to N$ is a $C^n$ submersion at
$x \in M$ and $g : N \to N'$ is a $C^n$ submersion at $f(x)$, then $g \circ f$ is a $C^n$
submersion at $x$. Here $f$ is a $C^n$ submersion at $x$ when there are charts of the $C^n$
maximal atlases around $x$ and $f(x)$, the first mapped by $f$ into the second, in which $f$ reads
$(u, v) \mapsto u$ after a continuous linear identification of the model space of $M$ with the
product of the model space of $N$ and some normed space.

Proof: Replace the first submersion's target chart by the second submersion's source chart, then
compose the two projection normal forms and use the product of their complements.

## Sources

- J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 4.

articles.title: Surjective differential gives a submersion between finite-dimensional manifolds
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$ with
$n \ge 1$, and let $M$ and $N$ be $C^n$ manifolds without boundary over $\mathbb{K}$ modelled on
finite-dimensional spaces. If $f : M \to N$ is $C^n$ at every point of some neighbourhood of
$x \in M$ and the manifold derivative of $f$ at $x$ is surjective, then $f$ is a $C^n$ submersion
at $x$: there are charts of the $C^n$ maximal atlases around $x$ and $f(x)$, the first mapped by
$f$ into the second, in which $f$ reads $(u, v) \mapsto u$ after a linear identification of the
model space of $M$ with the product of the model space of $N$ and some normed space.

Proof: Split the surjective derivative, augment the map by its kernel coordinate, and apply the
inverse function theorem to obtain charts in which the map is the first projection.

## Sources

- J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 4.

articles.title: Composition of submersions
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a nontrivially normed field, let
$n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty, \omega\}$, and let $M$, $N$, $N'$ be $C^n$ manifolds without
boundary over $\mathbb{K}$ modelled on Banach spaces. If $f : M \to N$ and $g : N \to N'$ are
$C^n$ submersions, then so is $g \circ f$. Here $f$ is a $C^n$ submersion when there is one normed
space $F$ such that at every $x \in M$ there are charts of the $C^n$ maximal atlases around $x$ and
$f(x)$, the first mapped by $f$ into the second, in which $f$ reads $(u, v) \mapsto u$ after a
continuous linear identification of the model space of $M$ with the product of the model space of
$N$ and $F$.

Proof: Apply the complement-level pointwise composition theorem using the two fixed global
complements, then package their product as the complement of the composite.

## Sources

- J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Ch. 4.

articles.title: Approximation by maps having zero as a regular value, compact case
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a compact,
Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real
normed space, let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be $C^\infty$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is
a $C^\infty$ map $g : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\lVert f(x) - g(x) \rVert < \varepsilon$ for
every $x \in M$ (Euclidean norm) and $0$ is a regular value of $g$, that is, the manifold
derivative of $g$ at $x$ is surjective for every $x \in M$ with $g(x) = 0$.

## Sources

- R. Thom, Comment. Math. Helv. 28 (1954) 17–86 transversality; M. Hirsch, Differential Topology; Guillemin-Pollack, Differential Topology; J. Lee, ISMs; Lean states compact-source uniform-approx regular-value-zero corollary.

articles.title: Approximation by maps having zero as a regular value
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Hausdorff,
second-countable smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed
space, let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be $C^\infty$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a
$C^\infty$ map $g : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\lVert f(x) - g(x) \rVert < \varepsilon$ for
every $x \in M$ (Euclidean norm) and $0$ is a regular value of $g$, that is, the manifold
derivative of $g$ at $x$ is surjective for every $x \in M$ with $g(x) = 0$.

No compactness is needed.

articles.title: Collar neighborhood theorem (topological form)
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $M$ be a Hausdorff,
second-countable smooth ($C^\infty$) manifold with boundary modeled on the closed half-space
$\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_1 \ge 0\}$, and let $\partial M$ be its boundary. Then there is an open
embedding $c : \partial M \times [0, 1) \to M$ such that $c(b, 0) = b$ for every $b \in \partial M$.

Proof: Local chart collars are glued by Brown's external-collar construction, following Hatcher,
*Algebraic Topology*, Proposition 3.42, and the locally finite extension of Connelly (1971).

## Sources

- M. Hirsch, Differential Topology, GTM 33; J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed.; Kosinski, Differential Manifolds; Lean states topological collar `IsOpenEmbedding` corollary for `EuclideanHalfSpace` model.

articles.title: Smooth retraction onto a closed embedded manifold in $\mathbb{R}^n$
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Hausdorff,
second-countable smooth ($C^\infty$) manifold without boundary, modelled on a finite-dimensional
real normed space, and let $e \colon M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a smooth embedding (a $C^\infty$
immersion that is a topological embedding) whose image $e(M)$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then
there exist an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ containing $e(M)$ and a $C^\infty$ map
$r \colon U \to M$ such that $r(e(x)) = x$ for every $x \in M$.

## Sources

- Tubular neighborhood theorem; M. Hirsch, Differential Topology; J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds; Lean states smooth-retraction corollary for closed embedding into `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)` via `Opens`.

articles.title: Sendov's solution of Blumenthal's minimax angle problem (Erdős Problem 504)
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $N$, let $\alpha_N$ be the minimax angle of $N$ points in the plane: the supremum of the
$\alpha \in [0, \pi]$ such that every set of $N$ points in the plane contains three distinct points
$x, y, z$ with $\angle xyz \ge \alpha$ (the angle at $y$). Then $\alpha_3 = \pi/3$,
$\alpha_4 = \pi/2$, and for all natural numbers $n \ge 2$ and $N$: if $2^n < N \le 2^n + 2^{n-2}$,
then $\alpha_N = \left(1 - \frac{2}{2n + 1}\right)\pi$, and if $2^n + 2^{n-2} < N \le 2^{n+1}$,
then $\alpha_N = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n + 1}\right)\pi$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #504, https://www.erdosproblems.com/504 (status SOLVED); resolution: Bl. Sendov, Minimax of the angles in a plane configuration of points, Acta Math. Hungar. 69 (1995), 27-46, main theorem, as stated in Zbl 0853.52009: α(N) = (1 - 2/(2n+1))π for 2^n < N ≤ 2^n + 2^{n-2} and (1 - 1/(n+1))π for 2^n + 2^{n-2} < N ≤ 2^{n+1}, n ≥ 2; α(3) = π/3, α(4) = π/2, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01874605.

articles.title: Blumenthal's minimax angle values (Erdős Problem 504)
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, let
$\alpha_N$ be the minimax angle of $N$ points in the plane: the supremum of the
$\alpha \in [0, \pi]$ such that every set of $N$ points in the plane contains three distinct
points $x, y, z$ with $\angle xyz \ge \alpha$ (the angle at $y$). The statement is Sendov's
answer: $\alpha_3 = \pi/3$, $\alpha_4 = \pi/2$, and for all natural numbers $n \ge 2$ and $N$,
if $2^n < N \le 2^n + 2^{n-2}$, then $\alpha_N = \left(1 - \frac{2}{2n + 1}\right)\pi$, and if
$2^n + 2^{n-2} < N \le 2^{n+1}$, then $\alpha_N = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n + 1}\right)\pi$.

articles.title: Minimax angle
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, the minimax angle $\alpha_N$ is the supremum of
the $\alpha \in [0, \pi]$ such that every set of $N$ points in the Euclidean plane contains three
distinct points $x, y, z$ with $\angle xyz \ge \alpha$, where $\angle xyz$ is the unoriented angle
at $y$.

For $N \le 2$ no set of $N$ points has three distinct points, so the set of such $\alpha$ is empty
and $\alpha_N$ is $0$ by the convention for the supremum of the empty set.

articles.title: Containment of a point pattern in d-dimensional grid cells
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number,
let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}^d$ be a set of cells and let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$. Then $A$
contains $P$ when there are maps $f_1, \dots, f_d : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that each $f_i$
is strictly increasing on the set $\{p_i : p \in P\}$ of $i$-th coordinates of points of $P$, and
$(f_1(p_1), \dots, f_d(p_d)) \in A$ for every $p \in P$.

For finite $P$ this is containment of the $d$-dimensional 0-1 matrix $M_P$ of $P$ in the 0-1
matrix whose ones are the cells of $A$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 5 (containment of `d`-dimensional 0-1 matrices and the matrix `M_P`).

articles.title: Containment of a point pattern in a set of grid cells
articles.statement:
A set of cells
$A \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, each cell written (column, row), contains a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ when there are maps $f_X, f_Y : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that
$f_X$ is strictly increasing on the set of $x$-coordinates of points of $P$, $f_Y$ is strictly
increasing on the set of $y$-coordinates of points of $P$, and $(f_X(x), f_Y(y)) \in A$ for every
$(x, y) \in P$.

For finite $P$ this is containment of the 0-1 matrix $M_P$ of $P$ (rows of $P$ listed bottom to
top; flipping the rows of both matrices preserves containment).

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (0-1 matrix containment and the matrix `M_P` of a finite point set).

articles.title: Every set in $\mathbb{R}^d$ contains the empty pattern
articles.statement:
For every natural number $d$ and
every set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, $S$ contains the empty set $\emptyset \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$
in the sense of containment of point sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 5 (definition of containment in `ℝ^d`).

articles.title: Containment of point sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number and let
$S, P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$. Then $S$ contains $P$ when there are maps
$f_1, \dots, f_d : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that expand distances between coordinates of points
of $P$, that is, $f_i(p_i) - f_i(q_i) \ge p_i - q_i$ for every $i$ and all $p, q \in P$ with
$p_i > q_i$, and such that $(f_1(p_1), \dots, f_d(p_d)) \in S$ for every $p \in P$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 5 (definition of containment in `ℝ^d`).

articles.title: Large sets of grid cells with no $r \times r$ all-ones submatrix
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers
$r \ge 2$ and $n \ge 1$ there is a set $S$ of cells of the $n \times n$ grid
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}^2$ with $|S| \ge \frac{1}{2} n^{2 - 2/(r+1)}$ that contains no $r \times r$
all-ones submatrix: there are no sets $R, C \subseteq \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with $|R| = |C| = r$
and $R \times C \subseteq S$.

In the language of 0-1 matrix extremal functions this says $\operatorname{ex}(n, J_{r,r}) \ge
\frac{1}{2} n^{2-2/(r+1)}$ for the $r \times r$ all-ones matrix $J_{r,r}$; it is the cited
Kővári–Sós–Turán-type lower bound, with the paper's explicit constant.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 4.4.

articles.title: Power saving for continuous Turán numbers of finite patterns in $\mathbb{R}^d$
articles.statement:
Let $d$
be a natural number and let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be finite. Then there is a real number
$\varepsilon > 0$ such that the $d$-dimensional continuous Turán number satisfies
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d) = O(n^{d - \varepsilon})$ as the natural number $n$ tends to infinity.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.14.

articles.title: Almost linear bound for patterns with at most one point in each row
articles.statement:
Let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a finite set whose points have pairwise distinct $y$-coordinates.
Then there is a natural number $t$ such that $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = O(n \cdot 2^{\alpha(n)^t})$
as the natural number $n$ tends to infinity, where $\operatorname{opx}$ is the continuous Turán
number and $\alpha$ is the inverse Ackermann function.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 3.8.

articles.title: Power saving for continuous Turán numbers of finite planar patterns
articles.statement:
Let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be finite. Then there is a real number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that the
continuous Turán number satisfies $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = O(n^{2 - \varepsilon})$ as the
natural number $n$ tends to infinity.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 3.6.

articles.title: The inverse Ackermann function at 8
articles.statement:
The inverse Ackermann function $\alpha$ satisfies
$\alpha(8) = 3$, since $A(2, 2) = 7 < 8 \le 61 = A(3, 3)$, where $A$ is the two-argument
Ackermann function.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 3.2 (the inverse Ackermann function `α(n)`).

articles.title: Upper bound for the inverse Ackermann function
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, if
$n \le A(k, k)$, where $A$ is the two-argument Ackermann function, then $\alpha(n) \le k$, where
$\alpha$ is the inverse Ackermann function.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 3.2 (the inverse Ackermann function `α(n)`).

articles.title: The inverse Ackermann function at 2
articles.statement:
The inverse Ackermann function $\alpha$ satisfies
$\alpha(2) = 1$, since $A(0, 0) = 1 < 2 \le 3 = A(1, 1)$, where $A$ is the two-argument
Ackermann function.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 3.2 (the inverse Ackermann function `α(n)`).

articles.title: Inverse Ackermann function
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the inverse Ackermann function
$\alpha(n)$ is the least natural number $k$ with $n \le A(k, k)$, where $A$ is the two-argument
Ackermann function, given for all natural numbers $m$ and $j$ by $A(0, j) = j + 1$,
$A(m + 1, 0) = A(m, 1)$ and $A(m + 1, j + 1) = A(m, A(m + 1, j))$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 3.2 (the inverse Ackermann function `α(n)` in Keszegh's bound quoted before Corollary 3.8).

articles.title: Saturating sets for a point pattern
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a real number and let $P$ and $S$ be
subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Then $S$ is saturating for $P$ in $[0, n]^2$ when $S$ is an open
subset of $[0, n]^2$ that does not contain $P$, while every open set $S'$ with
$S \subsetneq S' \subseteq [0, n]^2$ contains $P$. Here a set $T$ contains $P$ when there are
maps $f_X, f_Y : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $f_X(x) - f_X(x') \ge x - x'$ whenever
$x > x'$ are $x$-coordinates of points of $P$, likewise $f_Y(y) - f_Y(y') \ge y - y'$ whenever
$y > y'$ are $y$-coordinates of points of $P$, and $(f_X(x), f_Y(y)) \in T$ for every
$(x, y) \in P$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 6 (definition of saturating sets).

articles.title: Defining inequality of the inverse Ackermann function
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
$n \le A(\alpha(n), \alpha(n))$, where $\alpha$ is the inverse Ackermann function and $A$ is the
two-argument Ackermann function.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 3.2 (the inverse Ackermann function `α(n)`).

articles.title: Projection bound for the d-dimensional continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural
number, $n$ a real number and $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$, and let $\Pr(P)$ be the subset of
$\mathbb{R}^d$ obtained by dropping the last coordinate of every point of $P$. Writing
$\mathrm{opx}(n, Q, k)$ for the $k$-dimensional continuous Turán number, we have
$n \cdot \mathrm{opx}(n, \Pr(P), d) \le \mathrm{opx}(n, P, d + 1)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 5.5; `Pr(P)` as defined before it.

articles.title: Increment bound for the continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ and let
$n, \delta$ be real numbers with $n > 0$ and $0 < \delta < n$. Then the continuous Turán number
$\mathrm{opx}$ satisfies $\mathrm{opx}(n, P) \le \mathrm{opx}(n + \delta, P)$ and
$\mathrm{opx}(n + \delta, P) < \mathrm{opx}(n, P) + 3 n \delta$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 2.6.

articles.title: Continuity of the continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
For every $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, the
continuous Turán number $\mathrm{opx}(n, P)$ is a continuous function of $n$ on $(0, \infty)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Proposition 2.7.

articles.title: Increment bound for the d-dimensional continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$ be a
natural number, let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, and let $n, \varepsilon$ be real numbers with
$n > 0$ and $0 < \varepsilon < n$. Then the $d$-dimensional continuous Turán number
$\mathrm{opx}$ satisfies $\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d) \le \mathrm{opx}(n + \varepsilon, P, d)$ and
$\mathrm{opx}(n + \varepsilon, P, d) < \mathrm{opx}(n, P, d) + d (2n)^{d-1} \varepsilon$.

The hypothesis $d \ge 2$ is needed: for $d = 1$ and $P = \{0, L\}$ with $L > n + \varepsilon$,
every open subset of $[0, n + \varepsilon]$ avoids $P$, so
$\mathrm{opx}(n + \varepsilon, P, 1) = n + \varepsilon = \mathrm{opx}(n, P, 1) + \varepsilon$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 5.3.

articles.title: Continuity of the d-dimensional continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
For every natural number $d$
and every $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, the $d$-dimensional continuous Turán number
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d)$ is a continuous function of $n$ on $(0, \infty)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Proposition 5.4.

articles.title: Dilation bound for the d-dimensional continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural
number, let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be finite and let $c_1, c_2, q, n$ be real numbers with
$c_1 > 0$, $q > 1$ and $n > 0$. Suppose that for every coordinate $i$ and all $p, p' \in P$ with
$p_i < p'_i$ such that no $r \in P$ has $p_i < r_i < p'_i$, we have
$c_1 \le p'_i - p_i \le c_2$. Let $qP = \{q p : p \in P\}$ and
$m = \lceil q c_2 / c_1 \rceil + 1$. Then the $d$-dimensional continuous Turán number
$\mathrm{opx}$ satisfies

$$
\mathrm{opx}(n, qP, d) \le
m^d \, \mathrm{opx}(\lceil \lceil n / c_1 \rceil / m \rceil \, c_1, P, d).
$$

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 5.10.

articles.title: The higher-dimensional continuous Turán number of the empty pattern
articles.statement:
For every dimension
$d$ and every real number $n$, $\mathrm{opx}(n, \emptyset, d) = 0$: every set contains the empty
pattern, so no set is free of it.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 5 (definition of `opx(n, P, d)`).

articles.title: Patterns with a constant last coordinate
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ be a set
whose points all have the same last coordinate, and let $\mathrm{Pr}(P) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be
the set obtained by deleting the last coordinate of each point of $P$. Then for every real number
$n$, $\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d + 1) = n \cdot \mathrm{opx}(n, \mathrm{Pr}(P), d)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Proposition 5.6.

articles.title: Stacked graphs of increasing functions in three dimensions
articles.statement:
Let $a > 0$, $b$ and $c > 0$
be real numbers and let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be strictly increasing on $[0, a]$ with
$(f(t) - f(s)) / (t - s) \le b$ whenever $0 \le s < t \le a$. Let
$P = \{(t, f(t)) : t \in [0, a]\}$ be the graph of $f$ over $[0, a]$ and, for $k \ge 1$, let
$Q_{P,k,c} = \{(x, y, ic) : (x, y) \in P,\ i \in \{1, \dots, k\}\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$. Then,
as the real number $n \to \infty$, $\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_{P,2,c}, 3) = \Theta(n^{5/2})$ and
$\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_{P,3,c}, 3) = \Theta(n^{8/3})$.

The hypothesis $a > 0$ excludes the degenerate cases where the graph $P$ is a single point
($a = 0$) or empty ($a < 0$).

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.18.

articles.title: Upper bound for higher-dimensional grid patterns
articles.statement:
Let $X_1, \dots, X_d$ be finite sets of
real numbers, $k_i = |X_i|$, and $P = X_1 \times \dots \times X_d \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$. Put
$\alpha = \max_i k_i / \prod_i k_i$ if $d \ge 1$ and every $k_i$ is positive, and $\alpha = 0$
otherwise. Then $\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d) = O(n^{d - \alpha})$ as the natural number $n \to \infty$.

When some $k_i = 0$ the grid $P$ is empty and the bound reads $O(n^d)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.13.

articles.title: Higher-dimensional continuous Turán numbers versus extremal functions
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a
natural number and let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be finite. Then the $d$-dimensional continuous
Turán number $\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d)$ and the $d$-dimensional 0-1 matrix extremal function
$\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P, d)$ of $P$ satisfy $\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d) = \Theta(\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P, d))$
as the natural number $n$ tends to infinity, with constants depending on $P$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 5.11.

articles.title: Higher-dimensional continuous Turán numbers are monotone in the side length
articles.statement:
For every
set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and all real numbers $m \le n$,
$\mathrm{opx}(m, P, d) \le \mathrm{opx}(n, P, d)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 5.2.

articles.title: Higher-dimensional continuous Turán numbers are monotone under containment
articles.statement:
Let
$P, Q \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$. If $Q$ contains $P$, then
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d) \le \mathrm{opx}(n, Q, d)$ for every real number $n$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 5.1.

articles.title: Higher-dimensional continuous Turán numbers are nonnegative
articles.statement:
For every dimension $d$,
real number $n$ and set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, $\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d) \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 5 (definition of `opx(n, P, d)`).

articles.title: Nonempty open patterns in dimension at least two
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$, let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a nonempty open set, and let $Q_P$ be the set of points of $P$ all
of whose coordinates are rational. Then, as the real number $n \to \infty$,
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d) = \Theta(n^d)$ and $\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_P, d) = \Theta(n^d)$.

The paper states this without the hypotheses $P \neq \emptyset$ and $d \ge 2$; both are needed:
$\mathrm{opx}(n, \emptyset, d) = 0$, and for $d = 1$ the interval $P = (0, 1)$ has
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P, 1) \le 1$, since a $P$-free open set $S$ has Lebesgue measure at most $1$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.8.

articles.title: Upper bound for higher-dimensional permutation-type patterns
articles.statement:
For every $d$ there is a
real number $C$ such that for every real $c > 0$ there is a real number $K$ with the following
property. Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a finite set of $k$ points such that, for each
coordinate $i$, distinct points of $P$ have distinct $i$-th coordinates and consecutive values of
the $i$-th coordinate on $P$ differ by at most $c$. Then
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d) \le K \cdot 2^{Ck} \cdot n^{d-1}$ for every natural number $n$, where
$n^{d-1}$ means $1$ when $d = 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.12.

articles.title: Stacked permutation patterns in three dimensions
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a
finite set of at least two points with pairwise distinct $x$-coordinates and pairwise distinct
$y$-coordinates, and for $i \in \{2, 3\}$ let
$P_i = \{(x, y, j) : (x, y) \in P,\ j \in \{1, \dots, i\}\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$. Then, as $n$
tends to infinity through the natural numbers, $\mathrm{opx}(n, P_2, 3) = \Theta(n^{5/2})$ and
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P_3, 3) = \Theta(n^{8/3})$.

The requirement of at least two points is the paper's standing assumption on the permutation
matrix: for a single point, $P_2$ is two points on a vertical line and
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P_2, 3) \le n^2$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.15.

articles.title: Stacked plus signs in three dimensions
articles.statement:
Let $r > 0$ and $c > 0$, let
$P = \{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |x| \le r,\ |y| \le r,\ x = 0 \text{ or } y = 0\}$ be the plus
sign of size $r$, and for $t \in \{2, 3\}$ let
$Q_{P,t,c} = \{(x, y, ic) : (x, y) \in P,\ i \in \{1, \dots, t\}\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$. Then,
as the real number $n$ tends to infinity, $\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_{P,2,c}, 3) = \Theta(n^{5/2})$ and
$\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_{P,3,c}, 3) = \Theta(n^{8/3})$.

The paper's size parameter $d$ is renamed $r$, and $r > 0$ is added: for $r = 0$, $Q_{P,2,c}$ is
two points on a vertical line and $\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_{P,2,c}, 3) \le c n^2$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.19.

articles.title: Rational points of an embedded open planar set
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number and let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a nonempty open set. Let
$P' = P \times \{0\}^{m+1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m+3}$, and let $Q_{P'}$ be the set of points of
$P'$ all of whose coordinates are rational. Then $\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_{P'}, m + 3) = \Theta(n^{m+3})$
as the real number $n$ tends to infinity.

Nonemptiness is added: for $P = \emptyset$ the set $Q_{P'}$ is empty.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.7.

articles.title: Upper bound for continuous Turán numbers of stacked patterns
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$ and $t \ge 2$
be natural numbers and let $c > 0$. For $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ let
$Q_{P,t,c} = \{(x, ic) : x \in P,\ i \in \{1, \dots, t\}\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$. Then there
is a real constant $K$, depending only on $d$, $t$ and $c$, such that for every
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and every real $n > 0$,
$\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_{P,t,c}, d + 1) \le
K \left(\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d)^{1/t} \, n^{d + 1 - d/t} + n^d\right)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 5.16; `Q_{P,t,c}` as defined before it.

articles.title: Three-layer stacks of patterns with linear continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
Let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ contain three points with pairwise distinct $x$-coordinates, and
suppose that $\mathrm{opx}(n, P) = O(n)$ as the real number $n$ tends to infinity. Let $c > 0$
and $Q_{P,3,c} = \{(x, y, z) : (x, y) \in P,\ z \in \{c, 2c, 3c\}\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$. Then
$\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_{P,3,c}, 3) = \Theta(n^{8/3})$ as the real number $n$ tends to infinity.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.17, second sentence.

articles.title: Two-layer stacks of patterns with linear continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
Let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ have at least two points, and suppose that
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P) = O(n)$ as the real number $n$ tends to infinity. Let $c > 0$ and
$Q_{P,2,c} = \{(x, y, z) : (x, y) \in P,\ z \in \{c, 2c\}\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$. Then
$\mathrm{opx}(n, Q_{P,2,c}, 3) = \Theta(n^{5/2})$ as the real number $n$ tends to infinity.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 5.17, first sentence.

articles.title: Continuous Turán number in $\mathbb{R}^d$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a real number $n$
and a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, the continuous Turán number $\mathrm{opx}(n, P, d)$ is the
supremum of the $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measures $\mu_d(S)$ over all open sets
$S \subseteq [0, n]^d$ that do not contain $P$ in the sense of containment of point sets in
$\mathbb{R}^d$; it is $0$ when there is no such set.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 5 (definition of `opx(n, P, d)`).

articles.title: Continuous Turán number of a diagonal segment
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, n$ be real numbers with
$0 < a \le n$ and $0 < b \le n$, and let $P$ be the closed segment from $(0, 0)$ to $(a, b)$.
Then the continuous Turán number satisfies $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = (a + b)n - ab$.

The hypotheses $a \le n$ and $b \le n$ are missing from the paper, whose lower-bound construction
$(0, a) \times (0, n) \cup (0, n) \times (0, b) \subseteq [0, n]^2$ uses them: for
$0 < n < \max(a, b)$ no subset of $[0, n]^2$ contains $P$, so $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = n^2$
(for example $a = b = 2$ and $n = 1$, where $(a + b)n - ab = 0 \ne 1$).

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 4.2.

articles.title: Continuous Turán number of a dilated finite pattern
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be
finite, and let $c > 0$ and $d$ be real numbers such that any two consecutive distinct
$x$-coordinates of points of $P$ differ by at least $c$ and at most $d$, and likewise for
$y$-coordinates. Let $q > 1$ and $qP = \{qp : p \in P\}$. Then for every real $n > 0$,
$\mathrm{opx}(n, qP) \le (\lceil qd/c \rceil + 1)^2 \, \mathrm{opx}(m, P)$, where
$m = \lceil \lceil n/c \rceil / (\lceil qd/c \rceil + 1) \rceil \, c$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 2.12.

articles.title: Continuous Turán number of the empty pattern
articles.statement:
For every real number $n$,
$\mathrm{opx}(n, \emptyset) = 0$: every set contains the empty pattern, so no set avoids it.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (definition of `opx(n, P)`).

articles.title: Continuous Turán number of the equal-sign pattern
articles.statement:
Let $s > 0$ and $c > 0$ be real numbers
and let $P_{s,2,c} = [0, s] \times \{c, 2c\}$ be the equal-sign pattern, two horizontal segments of
length $s$ at heights $c$ and $2c$. Then, as the real number $n$ tends to infinity with $s$ and
$c$ fixed, $\operatorname{opx}(n, P_{s,2,c}) = \Theta(s^{1/2} n^{3/2})$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 4.7; `P_{s,t,c}` as defined before it.

articles.title: Upper bound for the continuous Turán number of a grid
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be finite sets of
real numbers, let $P = X \times Y$ be the grid they span and let $t = |X|$ be its number of
columns. Then $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = O(n^{2 - 1/t})$ as the natural number $n$ tends to
infinity, where for $t = 0$ (so that $P$ is empty) the exponent $2 - 1/t$ is read as $2$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 3.5.

articles.title: Continuous Turán number of a grid with three columns
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be finite sets of
real numbers with $|X| = 3$ and $|Y| \ge 3$, and let $P = X \times Y$ be the grid with $3$ columns
and $|Y|$ rows. Then $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = \Theta(n^{5/3})$ as the natural number $n$ tends
to infinity.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 3.7, second sentence.

articles.title: Continuous Turán number of a grid with two columns
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be finite sets of real
numbers with $|X| = 2$ and $|Y| \ge 2$, and let $P = X \times Y$ be the grid with $2$ columns and
$|Y|$ rows. Then $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = \Theta(n^{3/2})$ as the natural number $n$ tends to
infinity.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 3.7, first sentence.

articles.title: Continuous Turán number of a horizontal segment
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, c, n$ be real numbers with
$0 \le c \le n$, and let $P = [a, a + c] \times \{b\}$ be the closed horizontal segment of length
$c$ at height $b$. Then $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = cn$.

The hypothesis $n \ge c$ is missing from the paper, whose lower-bound construction
$(0, c) \times (0, n) \subseteq [0, n]^2$ uses it: for $0 < n < c$ no subset of $[0, n]^2$ contains
$P$, so $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = n^2 \ne cn$ (for example $c = 2$ and $n = 1$).

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 4.1.

articles.title: Linear bound for separated horizontal segments
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number and let
$a_i \le b_i$ and $y_i$ be real numbers for $i = 1, \dots, k$, such that the intervals
$[a_i, b_i]$ are pairwise disjoint and the heights $y_i$ are pairwise distinct, and let
$P = \bigcup_{i=1}^k [a_i, b_i] \times \{y_i\}$. Then the continuous Turán number satisfies
$\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = O(n)$ as the real number $n$ tends to infinity.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 4.10.

articles.title: Continuous Turán number of the graph of an increasing function
articles.statement:
Let $a > 0$ and $b$ be real
numbers and let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be strictly increasing on $[0, a]$ with
$(f(t) - f(s)) / (t - s) \le b$ for all $s < t$ in $[0, a]$. Then the graph
$P = \{(t, f(t)) : t \in [0, a]\}$ satisfies $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = \Theta(n)$ as the real
number $n$ tends to infinity.

The hypothesis $a > 0$ is needed: for $a = 0$ the set $P$ is a single point and
$\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Adding a point to the right of a pattern
articles.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ and let
$(x_0, y_0) \in P$ be such that every point of $P$ has $x$-coordinate at most $x_0$. Then
$\operatorname{opx}(n, P \cup \{(x_0 + c, y_0)\}) \le \operatorname{opx}(n, P) + cn$ for all real
numbers $c > 0$ and $n > 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 2.10.

articles.title: Upper bound for continuous Turán numbers of finite patterns
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite subset of
$\mathbb{R}^2$. Then the continuous Turán number $\mathrm{opx}(n, P)$ and the 0-1 matrix extremal
function $\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P)$ of $P$ on the $n \times n$ grid satisfy
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P) = O(\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P))$ as $n \to \infty$ through the natural numbers.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 3.3.

articles.title: Continuous Turán numbers versus 0-1 matrix extremal functions
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite subset
of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Then the continuous Turán number $\mathrm{opx}(n, P)$ and the 0-1 matrix
extremal function $\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P)$ of $P$ on the $n \times n$ grid satisfy
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P) = \Theta(\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P))$ as $n \to \infty$ through the natural numbers,
with constants depending on $P$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 3.1.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the continuous Turán number in the side length
articles.statement:
For every set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ and all real numbers $m \le n$, the continuous Turán numbers satisfy
$\operatorname{opx}(m, P) \le \operatorname{opx}(n, P)$.

The paper assumes $0 < m$. This is not needed, since $\operatorname{opx}(m, P) = 0$ for $m \le 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 2.4.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the continuous Turán number under containment
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a real number
and let $P, Q \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. If $Q$ contains $P$ in the sense of containment of planar
point sets, then $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) \le \operatorname{opx}(n, Q)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 2.3.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
For every real number $n$ and every set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (definition of `opx(n, P)`).

articles.title: Open patterns have quadratic continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
For every nonempty open set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) = \Theta(n^2)$ as the real number $n$ tends
to infinity.

The paper does not assume that $P$ is nonempty. The assumption is needed, since
$\operatorname{opx}(n, \emptyset) = 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 4.5.

articles.title: Linear bound for permutation-like point patterns
articles.statement:
There is a real constant $C$ such that
for every real $c > 0$ there is a real constant $K$ with the following property. Let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a finite set of $k$ points whose $x$-coordinates are pairwise
distinct and whose $y$-coordinates are pairwise distinct, such that any two consecutive
$x$-coordinates of points of $P$ differ by at most $c$, and so do any two consecutive
$y$-coordinates. Then $\operatorname{opx}(n, P) \le K \cdot 2^{Ck} \cdot n$ for every natural
number $n$.

The paper states the bound as $2^{O(k)} n$, with the implied constant depending on $c$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Corollary 3.4.

articles.title: Rational points of open patterns have quadratic continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
Let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a nonempty open set and let $Q_P$ be the set of points of $P$ both
of whose coordinates are rational. Then $\operatorname{opx}(n, Q_P) = \Theta(n^2)$ as the real
number $n$ tends to infinity.

The paper does not assume that $P$ is nonempty. The assumption is needed, since
$Q_\emptyset = \emptyset$ and $\operatorname{opx}(n, \emptyset) = 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 4.6.

articles.title: Rotation and reflection invariance of the continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
For every real
number $n$ and every set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, the value $\operatorname{opx}(n, P)$ does
not change when $P$ is replaced by its image under the rotation by $90^\circ$,
$(x, y) \mapsto (-y, x)$, under the reflection $(x, y) \mapsto (-x, y)$, or under the
reflection $(x, y) \mapsto (x, -y)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 2.1.

articles.title: Upper bound for stacked horizontal segments
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ be a natural number, let
$s, c > 0$ be real numbers, and let $P_{s,t,c} = [0, s] \times \{c, 2c, \dots, tc\}$ be the union
of the $t$ horizontal segments of length $s$ at heights $c, 2c, \dots, tc$. Then
$\operatorname{opx}(n, P_{s,t,c}) = O(s^{1/t} n^{2 - 1/t})$ as the real number $n$ tends to
infinity, with $s$, $t$ and $c$ fixed.

Since $s$ is fixed, the factor $s^{1/t}$ only changes the implied constant.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 4.9; `P_{s,t,c}` as defined before Theorem 4.7.

articles.title: Superadditivity of the continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
For every set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$
and all real numbers $m, n > 0$,
$\operatorname{opx}(m, P) + \operatorname{opx}(n, P) \le \operatorname{opx}(m + n, P)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 2.5.

articles.title: Translation invariance of the continuous Turán number
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a real number,
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ a set and $v \in \mathbb{R}^2$ a vector, and let
$P + v = \{p + v : p \in P\}$ be the translate of $P$ by $v$. Then
$\operatorname{opx}(n, P + v) = \operatorname{opx}(n, P)$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 2.2.

articles.title: Two-row patterns of growing width
articles.statement:
For each real $n$ let $Q_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$
be a set all of whose points have $y$-coordinate $0$ or $1$, whose least $x$-coordinate is $0$
and whose greatest $x$-coordinate is $s(n)$. Then the following are equivalent: for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, $\operatorname{opx}(n, Q_n) \ge n^{2 - \varepsilon}$ for all sufficiently large
real $n$; and for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $s(n) \ge n^{1 - \varepsilon}$ for all sufficiently
large real $n$.

In asymptotic notation: $\operatorname{opx}(n, Q_n) = \Omega(n^{2 - o(1)})$ if and only if
$s(n) = \Omega(n^{1 - o(1)})$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Proposition 6.4.

articles.title: Extending a pattern by a horizontal segment at its right edge
articles.statement:
Let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ and $(x_0, y_0) \in P$ with $x \le x_0$ for every $(x, y) \in P$, and let
$c \ge 0$ and $n > 0$ be real numbers. Then

$$\operatorname{opx}(n, P \cup ([x_0, x_0 + c] \times \{y_0\})) \le \operatorname{opx}(n, P) + cn.$$

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 2.9.

articles.title: Continuous Turán number in the plane
articles.statement:
For a real number $n$ and a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, the continuous Turán number $\operatorname{opx}(n, P)$ is the supremum
of the Lebesgue measures $\mu_2(S)$ over all open sets $S \subseteq [0, n]^2$ that do not contain
$P$ in the sense of point-set pattern containment; it is $0$ when there is no such set.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (definition of `opx(n, P)`).

articles.title: The saturation function is nonnegative
articles.statement:
For every real number $n$ and every set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, $\operatorname{osat}(n, P) \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 6 (definition of `osat(n, P)`).

articles.title: Saturation function and continuous Turán number of a single point
articles.statement:
For every real number
$n$ and every point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$, $\operatorname{osat}(n, \{p\}) = 0$ and
$\operatorname{opx}(n, \{p\}) = 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 6.5.

articles.title: Saturation function for continuous patterns
articles.statement:
For a real number $n$ and a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, call an open set $S \subseteq [0, n]^2$ saturating for $P$ if $S$
does not contain $P$ but every open set $S' \subseteq [0, n]^2$ properly containing $S$ contains
$P$ (containment in the sense of point-set pattern containment). The saturation function
$\operatorname{osat}(n, P)$ is the infimum of the Lebesgue measures $\mu_2(S)$ over all sets $S$
saturating for $P$, and is $0$ when no saturating set exists.

The paper leaves $\operatorname{osat}(n, P)$ undefined when no saturating set exists.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 6 (definition of `osat(n, P)`).

articles.title: The $d$-dimensional extremal function of the empty pattern vanishes
articles.statement:
For all natural
numbers $d$ and $n$, $\operatorname{ex}(n, M_\emptyset, d) = 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 5 (definitions of `ex(n, M, d)` and of `M_P`).

articles.title: The $d$-dimensional extremal function of a single point vanishes
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers
$d$ and $n$ and every point $p \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $\operatorname{ex}(n, M_{\{p\}}, d) = 0$, since a
single point is contained in every nonempty set of cells.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 5 (definitions of `ex(n, M, d)` and of `M_P`).

articles.title: Extremal function of a $d$-dimensional pattern
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $d$ and $n$ and a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, say that a set $A$ of cells of $\mathbb{N}^d$ contains $P$ when there
are maps $f_1, \dots, f_d$ to $\mathbb{N}$, each $f_i$ strictly increasing on the $i$-th
coordinates of the points of $P$, with $(f_1(p_1), \dots, f_d(p_d)) \in A$ for every $p \in P$.
Then $\operatorname{ex}(n, M_P, d)$ is the largest number of cells of a set of cells of the grid
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}^d$ that does not contain $P$, and is $0$ when every such set contains $P$.
For finite $P$ this is the $d$-dimensional 0-1 matrix extremal function of the matrix $M_P$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 5 (definitions of `ex(n, M, d)` and of `M_P`).

articles.title: The extremal function of the empty pattern vanishes
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
$\operatorname{ex}(n, M_\emptyset) = 0$, since every set of cells contains the empty pattern.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (definitions of `ex(n, M)` and of `M_P`).

articles.title: Lower bound for continuous Turán numbers of finite patterns
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite subset of
$\mathbb{R}^2$. For a natural number $n$, write $\mathrm{opx}(n, P)$ for the continuous Turán
number of $P$ (the supremum of the Lebesgue measures of the open subsets of $[0, n]^2$ that do not
contain $P$, or $0$ if there are none) and $\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P)$ for the 0-1 matrix extremal
function of $P$ on the $n \times n$ grid. Then $\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P) = O(\mathrm{opx}(n, P))$ as
$n \to \infty$ through the natural numbers; that is,
$\mathrm{opx}(n, P) = \Omega(\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P))$, with constants depending on $P$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Theorem 3.2.

articles.title: Trivial upper bound for the 0-1 matrix extremal function
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ a set, and let $\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P)$ be the largest number of cells of
the $n \times n$ grid $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}^2$ forming a set that does not contain $P$ ($0$ if
there is no such set). Then $\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P) \le n^2$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (definitions of `ex(n, M)` and of `M_P`).

articles.title: The extremal function of a single point vanishes
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every
point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$, the 0-1 matrix extremal function of the one-point pattern $\{p\}$ on
the $n \times n$ grid is zero: $\mathrm{ex}(n, M_{\{p\}}) = 0$. Indeed, a single point is contained
in every nonempty set of cells.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (definitions of `ex(n, M)` and of `M_P`).

articles.title: 0-1 matrix extremal function of a point pattern
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, $\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P)$ is the largest number of cells of the
$n \times n$ grid $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}^2$ forming a set that does not contain $P$ (cells contain
$P$ when there are strictly increasing maps from the $x$-coordinates of $P$ to columns and from the
$y$-coordinates of $P$ to rows that send every point of $P$ to a cell of the set), and $0$ if there
is no such set (as for $P = \emptyset$). For finite $P$ this is the 0-1 matrix extremal function
$\mathrm{ex}(n, M_P)$, the maximum number of ones in an $n \times n$ 0-1 matrix that does not
contain the 0-1 matrix $M_P$ of $P$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (definitions of `ex(n, M)` and of `M_P`).

articles.title: Every planar set contains the empty pattern
articles.statement:
Every set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ contains
the empty set $\emptyset$ in the sense of containment of planar point sets.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (definition of containment).

articles.title: Containment of planar point sets
articles.statement:
A set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ contains a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ when there are maps $f_X, f_Y : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that
$f_X(x_0) - f_X(x_1) \ge x_0 - x_1$ whenever $x_0 > x_1$ are $x$-coordinates of points of $P$,
$f_Y(y_0) - f_Y(y_1) \ge y_0 - y_1$ whenever $y_0 > y_1$ are $y$-coordinates of points of $P$,
and $(f_X(x), f_Y(y)) \in S$ for every $(x, y) \in P$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Section 1 (definition of containment).

articles.title: Sections of open sets avoiding a horizontal segment
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, c, n$ be real numbers with
$c \ge 0$, and let $S \subseteq [0, n]^2$ be an open set that does not contain the closed
horizontal segment $[a, a + c] \times \{b\}$ in the sense of containment of planar point sets.
Then for every $y \in [0, n]$ the horizontal section $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : (x, y) \in S\}$ has
one-dimensional Lebesgue measure at most $c$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 2.8.

articles.title: Lower bound on the volume of a staircase region
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a natural number and let
$c, n$ be real numbers with $c \ge 0$ and $ct \le n$. Let $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^t$ be the set of
points $y = (y_0, \dots, y_{t-1})$ such that $y_i < n - ic$ for every $i$, $y_{i+1} + c < y_i$ for
every $i < t - 1$, and $y_{t-1} > 0$ if $t \ge 1$. Then the $t$-dimensional Lebesgue measure of
$X$ is at least $(n/t - c)^t$, where $n/t$ is read as $0$ when $t = 0$.

## Sources

- Jesse Geneson, *Continuous Turán Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A1, Lemma 4.8, the explicit bound.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 651 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$ let $f_k(n)$ be the
least $m$ such that every set of $m$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ in general position (any at most
$k + 1$ of them affinely independent) contains $n$ points in convex position (none of them in the
convex hull of the others), with $f_k(n) = 0$ if there is no such $m$. It is not the case that for
every $k \ge 2$ there is a real $c > 0$ with $(1 + c)^n < f_k(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Pohoata and Zakharov proved $f_d(n) = 2^{o(n)}$ for every $d \ge 3$, so for $k = 3$ and every
$c > 0$ the bound $f_3(n) \le (1 + c)^n$ holds for all large $n$; erdosproblems.com/651 lists the
problem as disproved.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #651, https://www.erdosproblems.com/651 (status DISPROVED (LEAN)); resolution: C. Pohoata and D. Zakharov, Convex polytopes from fewer points, arXiv:2208.04878 (2022), abstract: ES_d(n) = 2^{o(n)} for all d ≥ 3, ES_d(n) being the least number such that any ES_d(n) points in general position in ℝ^d contain n points in convex position; erdosproblems.com/651: the answer is no, even for k = 3, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04878.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 651: exponential growth of convex position thresholds
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$k$ and $n$ let $f_k(n)$ be the least $m$ such that every set of $m$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ in
general position (any at most $k + 1$ of them affinely independent) contains $n$ points in convex
position (none of them in the convex hull of the others), with $f_k(n) = 0$ if there is no such
$m$. The claim is that for every $k \ge 2$ there is a real $c > 0$ with $(1 + c)^n < f_k(n)$ for
all sufficiently large $n$.

Erdős asked for a constant $c_k > 0$ with $f_k(n) > (1 + c_k)^n$; requiring this only for all
large $n$ makes the claim weaker and its refutation stronger.

articles.title: Convex position threshold
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, $f_k(n)$ is the least natural
