number $m$ such that every set of $m$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ in general position (any at most
$k + 1$ of them affinely independent) contains $n$ points in convex position (none of them in the
convex hull of the others). If there is no such $m$, then $f_k(n) = 0$.

For $k \ge 2$ such an $m$ exists by the Erdős-Szekeres theorem.

articles.title: Sets containing a convex $n$-gon
articles.statement:
A set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ contains a convex
$n$-gon if there is a set $S \subseteq P$ of exactly $n$ points that is convex independent: no
point of $S$ lies in the convex hull of the other points of $S$.

articles.title: Points in general position
articles.statement:
A set $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, finite or infinite, is in
_general position_ if no three distinct points of $X$ are collinear and no four distinct points
of $X$ lie on a common circle.

articles.title: Counterclockwise convex polygons
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an oriented two-dimensional Euclidean affine
space. Points $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1} \in P$ form a counterclockwise convex polygon if for all
indices $i < j < k$ the oriented angle $\measuredangle p_i p_j p_k$ at $p_j$ has sign $-1$, that
is, $p_i, p_j, p_k$ are not collinear and lie in counterclockwise order with respect to the
orientation of $P$. Every list of at most two points qualifies.

articles.title: Affinely independent triples are convex polygons
articles.statement:
If three points $A, B, C$ of an oriented
two-dimensional Euclidean affine space are affinely independent, then $A, B, C$ form a convex
polygon.

articles.title: Convex polygons
articles.statement:
Points $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$ of an oriented two-dimensional Euclidean
affine space form a convex polygon if one of the lists $p_0, p_1, \dots, p_{n-1}$ and
$p_0, p_{n-1}, p_{n-2}, \dots, p_1$ is a counterclockwise convex polygon: for any three of its
entries $q, r, s$, in the order in which they occur in that list, the oriented angle
$\measuredangle q r s$ at $r$ has sign $-1$. Thus for $n \ge 3$ the points are the vertices of a
strictly convex polygon, listed counterclockwise or clockwise starting from $p_0$; every list of
at most two points qualifies.

articles.title: Affinely independent families are in general position
articles.statement:
If a family $(p_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of
points of an affine space over a division ring $k$ is affinely independent over $k$, then it is in
general position through dimension $d$ for every $d \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: General position of projective points
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a division ring and $V$ a vector space
over $k$, with projective space $\mathbb{P}(V)$. A family $(p_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of points of
$\mathbb{P}(V)$ is in general position through dimension $d \in \mathbb{N}$ if for every finite set
$S \subseteq \iota$ of at most $d + 1$ indices, the subfamily $(p_i)_{i \in S}$ is projectively
independent.

articles.title: Projectively independent families are in general position
articles.statement:
If a family
$(p_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of points of the projective space $\mathbb{P}(V)$ of a vector space $V$ over a
division ring $k$ is projectively independent, then it is in general position through dimension $d$
for every $d \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: General position of affine points
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a division ring and $P$ an affine space over
$k$. A family $(p_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of points of $P$ is in general position through dimension
$d \in \mathbb{N}$ if for every finite set $S \subseteq \iota$ of at most $d + 1$ indices, the
subfamily $(p_i)_{i \in S}$ is affinely independent over $k$.

articles.title: Isosceles-free sets
articles.statement:
A set $A$ in a space with a distance function $d$ is isosceles-free if
there are no three distinct points $x, y, z \in A$ such that two of the distances $d(x, y)$,
$d(y, z)$, $d(z, x)$ are equal.

articles.title: Isosceles trapezoids
articles.statement:
Points $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{R}^2$ are the vertices, in
counterclockwise order, of an isosceles trapezoid if they are in strictly convex position and
listed counterclockwise (for any three of them $p, q, r$, in the order in which they occur in the
list $a, b, c, d$, the oriented angle $\measuredangle p q r$ at $q$ has sign $-1$), the line
through $a$ and $b$ is parallel to the line through $c$ and $d$ (the two bases), and the
diagonals have equal length: $\operatorname{dist}(a, c) = \operatorname{dist}(b, d)$.

One pair of parallel sides together with equal diagonals is the classical characterization of an
isosceles trapezoid; in particular it rules out non-rectangular parallelograms.

articles.title: Right-angled triangles
articles.statement:
Points $a, b, c$ of a Euclidean affine space are the vertices of a
right-angled triangle if they are pairwise distinct and the unoriented angle at one of the three
vertices equals $\pi / 2$: $\angle bac = \pi / 2$, $\angle abc = \pi / 2$ or
$\angle bca = \pi / 2$.

The distinctness hypothesis rules out degenerate triples, whose angles can coincide with
$\pi / 2$.

articles.title: Maximum number of distinct distance counts
articles.statement:
For a finite set $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$
and a point $x \in X$, let $R_X(x)$ be the number of distinct distances $\lvert y - x \rvert$
from $x$ to the points $y \in X$ other than $x$. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $g(n)$ is the maximum,
over all sets $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of exactly $n$ points, of the number of distinct values
among the numbers $R_X(x)$ with $x \in X$.

articles.title: General position in projective space is monotone in the dimension
articles.statement:
Let $d \le e$ be
natural numbers. If a family of points of the projective space $\mathbb{P}(V)$ of a vector space
$V$ over a division ring $k$ is in general position through dimension $e$, then it is in general
position through dimension $d$.

articles.title: General position in affine space is monotone in the dimension
articles.statement:
Let $d \le e$ be natural
numbers. If a family of points of an affine space over a division ring $k$ is in general position
through dimension $e$, then it is in general position through dimension $d$.

articles.title: Sets with no $n$ collinear points
articles.statement:
A set $S$ of points in a Euclidean affine space has no
$n$ collinear points if no subset of $S$ consisting of exactly $n$ points is collinear.

articles.title: Sets with no three collinear points
articles.statement:
A set $A$ of points in the plane is non-trilinear
if no three distinct points of $A$ lie on a common line.

articles.title: Oriented triangle area
articles.statement:
Let $\omega$ be the area form of the given orientation of the
Euclidean plane, so that $\omega(u, v)$ is the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the
vectors $u$ and $v$. For points $a$, $b$, $c$ of the plane, the oriented area of the triangle
with vertices $a$, $b$, $c$ is the real number $\omega(a - c, b - c) / 2$.

It changes sign when two vertices are swapped, and it is positive when $a$, $b$, $c$ are in
counterclockwise order and negative when they are in clockwise order.

articles.title: Relation holding triplewise on a set
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a ternary relation on a type $\alpha$ and let
$s \subseteq \alpha$. The relation $r$ holds triplewise on $s$ if $r(x, y, z)$ holds for all
pairwise distinct $x, y, z \in s$.

articles.title: Edge list of a cube
articles.statement:
For a real number $\ell$, the edge list of a cube of side $\ell$
consists of $12$ edges, each of length $\ell$ with dihedral angle $\pi / 2$.

articles.title: Dehn group
articles.statement:
The Dehn group is the tensor product
$\mathbb{R} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} (\mathbb{R} / 2\pi\mathbb{Z})$ of abelian groups; it is the target
of the Dehn invariant.

articles.title: Additivity of the Dehn invariant under concatenation
articles.statement:
For lists of edges $L_1$ and $L_2$,
the Dehn invariant of the concatenation of $L_1$ and $L_2$ is the sum of the Dehn invariants of
$L_1$ and $L_2$.

articles.title: The Dehn invariant splits off the first edge
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be an edge of length $\ell$ and
dihedral angle $\theta$, and let $L$ be a list of edges. Then the Dehn invariant of the list
obtained by putting $e$ in front of $L$ equals $\ell \otimes \theta$ plus the Dehn invariant of
$L$, where $\theta$ is taken modulo $2\pi$.

articles.title: The Dehn invariant of the cube is zero
articles.statement:
For every real number $\ell$, the edge list of a
cube of side $\ell$ (twelve edges of length $\ell$, each with dihedral angle $\pi / 2$) has Dehn
invariant $0$.

The reason is that $12 \cdot (\pi / 2) = 3 \cdot 2\pi$ vanishes in $\mathbb{R} / 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Conditionally, the cube and the regular tetrahedron have different Dehn invariants
articles.statement:
Suppose that $\arccos(1/3) / \pi$ is irrational. Then for all real numbers $\ell$ and $\ell'$ with
$\ell' \ne 0$, the edge list of a cube of side $\ell$ and the edge list of a regular tetrahedron
of side $\ell'$ have different Dehn invariants.

Since scissors-congruent polyhedra have equal Dehn invariants, under this hypothesis a cube and a
regular tetrahedron of equal volume are not scissors-congruent.

articles.title: Dehn invariant of the empty edge list
articles.statement: The empty list of edges has Dehn invariant $0$.

articles.title: Dehn invariant of a repeated edge
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and an edge of length $\ell$
and dihedral angle $\theta$, the Dehn invariant of the list consisting of $n$ copies of that edge
is $n \cdot (\ell \otimes \theta)$ in the Dehn group, where $\theta$ is taken modulo $2\pi$.

articles.title: Nonzero Dehn invariant of the regular tetrahedron, conditional on irrationality
articles.statement:
Suppose
that $\arccos(1/3) / \pi$ is irrational. Then for every nonzero real number $\ell$, the edge list
of a regular tetrahedron of side $\ell$ (six edges of length $\ell$, each with dihedral angle
$\arccos(1/3)$) has nonzero Dehn invariant.

articles.title: Dehn invariant
articles.statement:
The Dehn invariant of a list of edges is the sum, over the edges, of
$\ell \otimes \theta$ in the Dehn group, where $\ell$ is the length of the edge and $\theta$ its
dihedral angle taken modulo $2\pi$.

articles.title: Edge of a polyhedron
articles.statement:
An edge, as recorded for the Dehn invariant, is a pair of real
numbers: its length and its dihedral angle in radians. No positivity or range condition is
imposed on either.

articles.title: A $\mathbb{Q}$-linear functional separating $\alpha$ from $\pi$
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a real
number such that $\alpha / \pi$ is irrational. Then there is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(\pi) = 0$ and $f(\alpha) \neq 0$.

The idea of the proof: $\alpha$ lies outside the $\mathbb{Q}$-span of $\pi$, and a linear
functional on the quotient separates it.

articles.title: Dihedral angle of the regular tetrahedron
articles.statement:
The real number $\arccos(1/3)$, the dihedral
angle of a regular tetrahedron in radians.

articles.title: Edge list of the regular tetrahedron
articles.statement:
For a real number $\ell$, the edge list of a
regular tetrahedron with edge length $\ell$ is the list of $6$ edges, each of length $\ell$ and
dihedral angle $\arccos(1/3)$.

articles.title: Nonvanishing of an edge term in the Dehn group
articles.statement:
Let $\ell$ and $\alpha$ be real numbers
with $\ell \neq 0$ and $\alpha / \pi$ irrational. Then the pure tensor $\ell \otimes [\alpha]$ is
nonzero in the Dehn group $\mathbb{R} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} (\mathbb{R} / 2\pi\mathbb{Z})$, where
$[\alpha]$ is the class of $\alpha$ modulo $2\pi$.

The proof applies a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear functional that vanishes at $\pi$ but not at $\alpha$.

articles.title: A discrete subgroup is a lattice iff it has full rank
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional
real normed space and let $L \subseteq E$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule (an additive subgroup) that
is discrete in the subspace topology. Then the $\mathbb{Z}$-rank of $L$ equals $\dim_{\mathbb{R}} E$
if and only if $L$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-lattice in $E$, that is, $L$ spans $E$ over $\mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- ATLAS `NumberTheoryI`, Lemma 14.3 (full-rank clause only).

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 756 on rich distances
articles.statement:
For a finite set $A$ of points in the
Euclidean plane, call a distance $k$-rich for $A$ if at least $k$ unordered pairs of distinct points
of $A$ lie at that distance, and let $f(n)$ be the largest number of $(n+1)$-rich distances of a
set of $n$ points. This is the assertion that there is a constant $C$ with $n \le C f(n)$ for all
sufficiently large $n$; that for every $n$ there is a set of $n$ points with at least
$\lfloor n/4 \rfloor$ distances that are $(n+1)$-rich; and that for every $m \ge 1$ there is an
$N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ there is a set of $n$ points with at least
$\lfloor n/(2(m+1)) \rfloor$ distances that are $(n+m)$-rich.

articles.title: Bhowmick's theorem on rich distances
articles.statement:
For a finite set $A$ of points in the Euclidean plane,
call a distance $k$-rich for $A$ if at least $k$ unordered pairs of distinct points of $A$ lie at
that distance, and let $f(n)$ be the largest number of $(n+1)$-rich distances of a set of $n$
points. Then there is a constant $C$ with $n \le C f(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$; for every
$n$ there is a set of $n$ points with at least $\lfloor n/4 \rfloor$ distances that are
$(n+1)$-rich; and for every $m \ge 1$ there is an $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ there is a set
of $n$ points with at least $\lfloor n/(2(m+1)) \rfloor$ distances that are $(n+m)$-rich.

## Sources

- K. Bhowmick, A problem of Erdős about rich distances, arXiv:2407.01174 (2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01174; External Lean proof of Erdős Problem 756, https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos756.lean.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 652 is true
articles.statement:
For a finite set $X$ of points in the Euclidean plane and
$x \in X$, let $R_X(x)$ be the number of distinct distances from $x$ to the other points of
$X$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $\alpha_k$ be the infimum of the reals $c$ for which there is
$N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ some set $X$ of exactly $n$ points in the plane has at least
$k$ points $x$ with $R_X(x) < c\sqrt{n}$ (an empty set or a set unbounded below is given
infimum $0$). Then $\alpha_k \to \infty$ as $k \to \infty$.

Mathialagan proved that for $2 \le m \le n^{1/3}$, some point of an $m$-point set determines
$\Omega(\sqrt{mn})$ distances to an $n$-point set; with Elekes's circle-grid construction this
gives $\alpha_k = \Theta(\sqrt{k})$.

## Sources

- S. Mathialagan, On bipartite distinct distances in the plane, Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 28(4) (2021) P4.33, arXiv:1912.01883, https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01883.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 652
articles.statement:
For a finite set $X$ of points in the Euclidean plane and $x \in X$,
let $R_X(x)$ be the number of distinct distances from $x$ to the other points of $X$. For
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $\alpha_k$ be the infimum of the reals $c$ for which there is $N$ such
that for every $n \ge N$ some set $X$ of exactly $n$ points in the plane has at least $k$
points $x$ with $R_X(x) < c\sqrt{n}$ (an empty set or a set unbounded below is given infimum
$0$). The proposition is that $\alpha_k \to \infty$ as $k \to \infty$.

articles.title: Points with few distinct distances
articles.statement:
For a finite set $X$ of points in the Euclidean plane
and a real number $t$, the number of points $x \in X$ such that the number of distinct distances
from $x$ to the other points of $X$ is less than $t$.

articles.title: Multiplicity of a distance
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite set of points in a metric space and let
$d$ be a real number. The multiplicity of $d$ in $P$ is the number of unordered pairs
$\{p, q\}$ of distinct points of $P$ with $\operatorname{dist}(p, q) = d$.

articles.title: Distance set of a finite point set
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P$ of points in a metric space,
the distance set of $P$ is the finite set of real numbers $\operatorname{dist}(p, q)$ with $p$
and $q$ distinct points of $P$.

articles.title: Number of distinct distances from a point
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P$ of points in a metric
space and a point $x$ of the space, this is the number of distinct values
$\operatorname{dist}(y, x)$ with $y$ a point of $P$ other than $x$.

articles.title: Number of distinct distances
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P$ of points in a metric space, the number
of distinct distances of $P$ is the number of elements of its distance set, that is, the number
of distinct values $\operatorname{dist}(p, q)$ with $p$ and $q$ distinct points of $P$.

articles.title: The Erdős constant $\alpha_k$
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $\alpha_k$ is the infimum of the
set of real numbers that are admissible for $k$: the reals $c$ for which there is $N$ such
that for every $n \ge N$ some set $X$ of exactly $n$ points in the Euclidean plane contains
at least $k$ points $x$ such that the number of distinct distances from $x$ to the other points
of $X$ is less than $c\sqrt{n}$. If this set is empty or unbounded below, $\alpha_k = 0$.

articles.title: Erdős's unit distance conjecture is false
articles.statement:
There is a real number $\delta > 0$ such that for
every natural number $N$ there are an integer $n \ge N$ and a set $P$ of exactly $n$ points in the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with at least $n^{1+\delta}$ unordered pairs of points of $P$ at
distance exactly $1$.

Because $C / \log \log n \to 0$ for every constant $C$, this contradicts Erdős's conjecture that
$n$ points in the plane determine at most $n^{1 + C / \log \log n}$ unit distances for some
constant $C$ and all large $n$.

## Sources

- OpenAI, *Planar Point Sets with Many Unit Distances*, 2026. https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/74c24085-19b0-4534-9c90-465b8e29ad73/unit-distance-proof.pdf . Original conjecture: P. Erdős, *On sets of distances of n points*, Amer. Math. Monthly 53 (1946), 248-250. k-equidistant variant: P. Erdős, K. Falconer, *Some problems in combinatorial geometry*, 1997. Problem `erdos_unit_distance_conjecture_false` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 754: favourite distances in $\mathbb{R}^4$
articles.statement:
There is a real constant $C$ such
that for every nonempty finite set $A$ of points of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^4$ and every
natural number $f$, if for every $x \in A$ there is a real number $r > 0$ such that at least $f$
points of $A$ lie at distance $r$ from $x$, then $f \le |A|/2 + C$.

Swanepoel proved that for every finite $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^4$ with $|A| = n$ and every choice
of distances $r(x) > 0$, the number of pairs $(x, y)$ of points of $A$ with $|x - y| = r(x)$ is at
most $n^2/2 + O(n)$, which gives this bound.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #754, https://www.erdosproblems.com/754 (status PROVED (LEAN)); resolution: K. J. Swanepoel, Favourite distances in high dimensions, Thirty Essays on Geometric Graph Theory (2013), 499-519, abstract of arXiv:1108.4817: f_d(n) = max ∑_{x ∈ S} e_r(x, S) = (1 - 1/⌊d/2⌋) n² + Θ(n) for even d (n²/2 + O(n) for d = 4); erdosproblems.com/754: proved by Swanepoel (Avis, Erdős and Pach had n/2 + 2 ≤ f(n) ≤ (1 + o(1)) n/2), https://arxiv.org/abs/1108.4817.

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 754
articles.statement:
This is the statement that there is a real constant $C$
such that for every nonempty finite set $A$ of points of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^4$ and
every natural number $f$, if for every $x \in A$ there is a real number $r > 0$ such that at least
$f$ points of $A$ lie at distance $r$ from $x$, then $f \le |A|/2 + C$. Equivalently,
$f(n) \le n/2 + O(1)$, where $f(n)$ is the largest $f$ such that some set $A$ of $n \ge 1$ points of
$\mathbb{R}^4$ has, for every $x \in A$, at least $f$ points of $A$ at one common distance
$r(x) > 0$ from $x$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 659: few distances with every four points spanning three
articles.statement:
There is a real
constant $C$ such that for every sufficiently large natural number $n$ there is a set $P$ of $n$
points of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every $4$-element subset of $P$ determines
at least $3$ distinct distances and $P$ determines at most $C n / \sqrt{\log n}$ distinct
distances.

A suitable truncation of the lattice $\{(a, b\sqrt{2}) : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ has
$O(n / \sqrt{\log n})$ distinct distances (Moree and Osburn) and contains none of the six
four-point configurations that determine only two distances: five of them contain a square or an
equilateral triangle (Erdős–Fishburn, Lund–Sheffer), and the pentagon configuration is excluded by
Grayzel.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #659, https://www.erdosproblems.com/659 (status PROVED (LEAN)); resolution: B. Grayzel, Solution to a Problem of Erdős Concerning Distances and Points, arXiv:2601.09102 (2026); P. Moree and R. Osburn, Two-dimensional lattices with few distances, Enseign. Math. (2) 52 (2006), 361-380, abstract of arXiv:2601.09102: n-point sets taken from an m × m box of the lattice {(x, √2 y)} determine O(n / √(log n)) distinct distances (Bernays' theorem for u² + 2v²) and every 4 of their points determine at least 3 distances (Perucca's classification of the six two-distance 4-point configurations); erdosproblems.com/659 records the construction (Moree-Osburn, Lund-Sheffer) and the remaining pentagon case ruled out by Grayzel (using Gemini), 'thus giving a complete solution', https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09102.

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 659
articles.statement:
This is the statement that there is a real constant $C$
such that for every sufficiently large natural number $n$ there is a set $P$ of $n$ points of the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every $4$-element subset of $P$ determines at least $3$
distinct distances and $P$ determines at most $C n / \sqrt{\log n}$ distinct distances.

articles.title: Many points with few distinct distances
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $k$ and a real number
$c$, the property that some set $X$ of exactly $n$ points in the Euclidean plane contains at
least $k$ points $x$ such that the number of distinct distances from $x$ to the other points of
$X$ is less than $c\sqrt{n}$.

For $1 \le k \le n$ this says that, with the points of $X$ ordered by this number, the $k$-th
smallest value is less than $c\sqrt{n}$.

articles.title: Admissible constants in Erdős Problem 652
articles.statement:
A real number $c$ is admissible for
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ if there is $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ some set $X$ of exactly $n$
points in the Euclidean plane contains at least $k$ points $x$ such that the number of distinct
distances from $x$ to the other points of $X$ is less than $c\sqrt{n}$.

articles.title: Maximal number of rich distances
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, this is the largest, over all
sets $A$ of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane, of the number of rich distances of $A$ at level
$n + 1$, that is, of distances that occur for at least $n + 1$ unordered pairs of distinct points
of $A$.

articles.title: Minimum number of distinct distances
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a metric space and $n$ a natural number
such that $X$ contains a set of exactly $n$ points. The minimum number of distinct distances for
$n$ points in $X$ is the least number of distinct distances determined by a set of exactly $n$
points of $X$.

The hypothesis that some $n$-point set exists makes the minimum range over a nonempty
collection of sets.

articles.title: Number of pairs at a given distance
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P$ of points in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and a
real number $\delta$, this is the number of unordered pairs $\{p, q\}$ of distinct points
$p, q \in P$ with Euclidean distance $|p - q| = \delta$, computed as half the number of ordered
pairs $(p, q)$ of distinct points of $P$ at distance $\delta$ and taken as a real number.

articles.title: Euclidean plane for Erdős Problem 652
articles.statement:
The real Euclidean plane is the space
$\mathbb{R}^2$ of pairs of real numbers with the Euclidean inner product and norm.

articles.title: Rich distances
articles.statement:
For a finite set $A$ of points in the Euclidean plane and a natural number
$k$, the rich distances of $A$ at level $k$ are the distances $d$ between two distinct points of
$A$ such that at least $k$ unordered pairs of distinct points of $A$ are at distance $d$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 605 is true
articles.statement:
There is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$f(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ such that for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ there are a set $P$ of
$n$ distinct points on the unit sphere $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : \|x\| = 1\}$ and a real number
$\delta$ for which the number of unordered pairs of distinct points of $P$ at distance $\delta$
is at least $f(n) \cdot n$.

Erdős, Hickerson and Pach (Theorem 2(ii)) found an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that for every
$n$ there are $n$ points on the unit sphere each at distance $\sqrt{2}$ from at least
$c n^{1/3}$ others, hence at least $c n^{4/3} / 2$ pairs at distance $\sqrt{2}$;
erdosproblems.com/605 lists the problem as proved.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #605, https://www.erdosproblems.com/605 (status PROVED); resolution: P. Erdős, D. Hickerson and J. Pach, A problem of Leo Moser about repeated distances on the sphere, Amer. Math. Monthly (1989), 569-575, Theorem 2(ii): for every n there are n points on the unit sphere S² each at distance √2 from at least c₂ n^{1/3} others; Theorem 2(i): for every 0 < α < 2, n points each at distance α from at least c₁ log* n others, https://www.erdosproblems.com/605.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 605 (repeated distances on the sphere)
articles.statement:
The proposition that there is a
function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ such that for
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ there are a set $P$ of $n$ distinct points on the unit sphere
$\{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : \|x\| = 1\}$ and a real number $\delta$ for which the number of unordered
pairs of distinct points of $P$ at distance $\delta$ is at least $f(n) \cdot n$.

articles.title: Number of unit-distance pairs in a planar point set
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P$ of points in the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, the number of unit-distance pairs of $P$ is the number of unordered
pairs of points of $P$ at distance exactly $1$.

The distance is the Euclidean one, $\sqrt{(x_1 - y_1)^2 + (x_2 - y_2)^2}$ for $x = (x_1, x_2)$ and
$y = (y_1, y_2)$, not the largest coordinate difference used by the product metric on
$\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Trivial upper bound on unit distances
articles.statement:
For a finite set of $n$ points in a metric space,
the number of unit distances is at most $\binom{n}{2}$, the total number of unordered pairs of
distinct points.

articles.title: Number of unit distances
articles.statement:
For a finite set $S$ of points in a metric space, the number of
unit distances of $S$ is the number of unordered pairs $\{p, q\}$ of points of $S$ with
$\operatorname{dist}(p, q) = 1$, that is, the multiplicity of the distance $1$ in $S$.

articles.title: Unit distance count of a planar point set
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P$ of points in the Euclidean
plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, the unit distance count of $P$ is the number of unordered pairs of points of
$P$ at distance exactly $1$.

The distance is the Euclidean one, $\sqrt{(x_1 - y_1)^2 + (x_2 - y_2)^2}$ for $x = (x_1, x_2)$ and
$y = (y_1, y_2)$, not the largest coordinate difference used by the product metric on
$\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter unit distance bound
articles.statement:
There is a constant $C > 0$ such that every
finite set of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ has at most $C n^{4/3}$ unordered
pairs of points at distance exactly $1$.

## Sources

- J. Spencer, E. Szemerédi, W. T. Trotter Jr., *Unit distances in the Euclidean plane*, in Graph Theory and Combinatorics (Cambridge 1983), Academic Press, 1984. Short crossing-number proof: L. A. Székely, *Crossing numbers and hard Erdős problems in discrete geometry*, Combin. Probab. Comput. 6 (1997). Best constant: P. Ágoston, D. Pálvölgyi, *An improved constant factor for the unit distance problem*, Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. 59 (2022). Problem `unit_distance_upper_bound` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Equiangular systems of unit vectors
articles.statement:
For a real number $\alpha$ and a natural number $d$,
an equiangular system with inner product $\pm\alpha$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a set of unit vectors in
$d$-dimensional Euclidean space such that any two distinct vectors $x$ and $y$ in it satisfy
$|\langle x, y \rangle| = \alpha$.

## Sources

- Z. Jiang, J. Tidor, Y. Yao, S. Zhang, and Y. Zhao, `Equiangular lines with a fixed angle`, Annals of Math, 194 (3) 2021, third paragraph of the introduction.

articles.title: Maximum number of equiangular lines
articles.statement:
For a real number $\alpha$ and a natural number $d$,
$N_\alpha(d)$ is the supremum, taken in $\mathbb{N}$, of the cardinalities of the equiangular
systems of unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with inner product $\pm\alpha$. Here an infinite set
counts as having cardinality $0$, and a set of natural numbers that is not bounded above has
supremum $0$.

For $0 \le \alpha < 1$ these cardinalities are at most $\binom{d+1}{2}$ by Gerzon's bound, and a
system contains at most one of $x$ and $-x$, so $N_\alpha(d)$ is the maximum number of lines
through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with pairwise angle $\arccos \alpha$.

## Sources

- Z. Jiang, J. Tidor, Y. Yao, S. Zhang, and Y. Zhao, `Equiangular lines with a fixed angle`, Annals of Math, 194 (3) 2021, third paragraph of the introduction.

articles.title: Spectral radius order
articles.statement:
For a real number $\lambda$, the spectral radius order
$k(\lambda) \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ is the least natural number $k$ such that some simple
graph on $k$ vertices has an adjacency matrix with spectral radius $\max(\lambda, 0)$, and
$k(\lambda) = \infty$ if there is no such graph.

The source defines $k(\lambda)$ only for $\lambda > 0$, where $\max(\lambda, 0) = \lambda$.

## Sources

- Z. Jiang, J. Tidor, Y. Yao, S. Zhang, and Y. Zhao, `Equiangular lines with a fixed angle`, Annals of Math, 194 (3) 2021, Definition 1.1.

articles.title: Equiangular lines with a fixed angle
articles.statement:
Fix a real number $\alpha$ with $0 < \alpha < 1$, let
$\lambda = (1 - \alpha)/(2\alpha)$ and let $k = k(\lambda)$ be the spectral radius order of
$\lambda$. Let $N_\alpha(d)$ be the maximum number of equiangular lines in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with
common angle $\arccos \alpha$. Then:
(a) if $k < \infty$, then $N_\alpha(d) = \lfloor k(d - 1)/(k - 1) \rfloor$ for all sufficiently
large $d$;
(b) if $k = \infty$, then $N_\alpha(d) = d + o(d)$ as $d \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Z. Jiang, J. Tidor, Y. Yao, S. Zhang, and Y. Zhao, `Equiangular lines with a fixed angle`, Annals of Math, 194 (3) 2021. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_equiangular_lines_fixed_angle` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Number of equilateral triangles in a point set
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P$ of points in the
Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$, this is the number of three-element subsets of $P$ that are
equilateral triangles of some positive side length $s$, that is, whose three points are pairwise
at distance $s$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 755 holds (Clemen–Dumitrescu–Liu)
articles.statement:
Let $T_1(n)$ be the largest number of unit
equilateral triangles spanned by a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^6$, and let $T(n)$ be the
largest number of equilateral triangles of positive side length spanned by a set of $n$ points in
$\mathbb{R}^6$; a triangle spanned by a set is a three-element subset of it whose points are
pairwise at the same distance. Then there is a function $o : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$o(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ such that $T_1(n) \le (1/27 + o(n))\, n^3$ for all sufficiently
large $n$, and $T(n)$ is asymptotically equivalent to $n^3/27$ as $n \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Felix Christian Clemen, Adrian Dumitrescu, and Dingyuan Liu, The number of regular simplices in higher dimensions, arXiv:2507.19841 (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19841. Resolved true: Resolved externally by Clemen, Dumitrescu, and Liu. This repository records the statement, not an internal proof; a separate pinned Lean proof is cited in the registry.

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 755
articles.statement:
Let $T_1(n)$ be the largest number of unit equilateral
triangles spanned by a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^6$, and let $T(n)$ be the largest number
of equilateral triangles of positive side length spanned by a set of $n$ points in
$\mathbb{R}^6$; a triangle spanned by a set is a three-element subset of it whose points are
pairwise at the same distance. The statement asserts both of the following: there is a function
$o : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $o(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ such that
$T_1(n) \le (1/27 + o(n))\, n^3$ for all sufficiently large $n$; and $T(n)$ is asymptotically
equivalent to $n^3/27$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Equilateral triangle of any size
articles.statement:
A finite set $T$ of points in the Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^d$ is an equilateral triangle of any size when there is a real number $s > 0$ such
that $T$ is an equilateral triangle of side $s$: $T$ has exactly three elements and any two
distinct points of $T$ are at distance $s$.

articles.title: Equilateral triangle with given side
articles.statement:
For a real number $s$, a finite set $T$ of
points in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ is an equilateral triangle of side $s$ when $T$ has
exactly three elements and any two distinct points of $T$ are at distance $s$.

articles.title: Unit equilateral triangle
articles.statement:
A finite set $T$ of points in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$
is a unit equilateral triangle when it is an equilateral triangle of side $1$: $T$ has exactly
three elements and any two distinct points of $T$ are at distance $1$.

articles.title: Maximum number of equilateral triangles
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $d$ and $n$, $T(d, n)$ is the
supremum in $\mathbb{N}$, over all sets $P$ of exactly $n$ points in the Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^d$, of the number of equilateral triangles of positive side length spanned by $P$
(the three-element subsets of $P$ whose points are pairwise at the same positive distance). When
such sets exist this is the largest such number; when none exist (only for $d = 0$ and $n \ge 2$)
it is $0$.

articles.title: Maximum number of unit equilateral triangles
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $d$ and $n$, $T_1(d, n)$
is the supremum in $\mathbb{N}$, over all sets $P$ of exactly $n$ points in the Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^d$, of the number of unit equilateral triangles spanned by $P$ (the three-element
subsets of $P$ whose points are pairwise at distance $1$). When such sets exist this is the
largest such number; when none exist (only for $d = 0$ and $n \ge 2$) it is $0$.

articles.title: Number of unit equilateral triangles in a point set
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P$ of points in
the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$, this is the number of three-element subsets of $P$ that are
unit equilateral triangles, that is, whose three points are pairwise at distance $1$.

articles.title: Erdős–Anning theorem
articles.statement:
An infinite set of points in the plane with pairwise
integer distances is collinear.

## Sources

- N. H. Anning and P. Erdős, "Integral distances," Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 51 (1945), 598–600; P. Erdős, "Integral distances," Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 51 (1945), 996. Overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Anning_theorem

articles.title: Euler's polyhedron formula
articles.statement:
Let $V$, $E$ and $F$ be finite sets, let
$\iota : V \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be an injective map into Euclidean space, and let
$P = \operatorname{conv} \iota(V)$ be the convex hull of its image; assume $P$ has nonempty
interior $\operatorname{int} P$, and write $\partial P$ for its frontier. Each edge $e \in E$ has an
ordered pair of endpoints $(s(e), t(e)) \in V \times V$, with segment
$[e] = [\iota(s(e)), \iota(t(e))]$; each face $f \in F$ has a finite vertex set $V_f \subseteq V$,
with cell $C_f = \operatorname{conv} \iota(V_f)$. Say that the segment between vertices
$u, w \in V$ lies in the face $f$ when $u, w \in V_f$ and $[\iota(u), \iota(w)] \subseteq C_f$, and
that it lies in exactly two faces when it lies in two distinct faces $f_1, f_2$ and every face it
lies in is $f_1$ or $f_2$. Assume the following. For every edge $e$: $[e] \subseteq P$;
$s(e) \ne t(e)$; if $\iota(v) \in [e]$ for a vertex $v$, then $v = s(e)$ or $v = t(e)$; and the
segment between $s(e)$ and $t(e)$ lies in exactly two faces. Distinct edges $e_1, e_2$ never have
the same endpoints, in the same or in the reverse order, and every common point of $[e_1]$ and
$[e_2]$ is $\iota(v)$ for a vertex $v$ that is an endpoint of both. Every vertex is an endpoint of
some edge. For every face $f$: $C_f \subseteq P$; $V_f$ has at least $3$ elements;
$C_f \cap \operatorname{int} P = \emptyset$; the affine span of $C_f$ has dimension $2$; and every
$v \in V_f$ is an endpoint of two distinct edges whose segments are contained in $C_f$. For
distinct faces $f_1, f_2$, $V_{f_1} \not\subseteq V_{f_2}$, and every point of
$C_{f_1} \cap C_{f_2}$ is $\iota(v)$ for some vertex $v$ or lies on $[e]$ for some edge $e$. The
cells cover the frontier: $\partial P \subseteq \bigcup_{f \in F} C_f$. Finally, if $v_1 \ne v_2$
are vertices such that $[\iota(v_1), \iota(v_2)] \subseteq P$, this segment is disjoint from
$\operatorname{int} P$, it contains $\iota(v)$ only for $v \in \{v_1, v_2\}$, and it lies in
exactly two faces, then some edge has endpoints $(v_1, v_2)$ or $(v_2, v_1)$. Then
$|V| - |E| + |F| = 2$.

The vertex set may contain points that are not extreme points of $P$, such as subdivision
vertices on an edge or inside a face of the polyhedron, and the faces may subdivide a face of $P$
(for example by a diagonal); the statement concerns this cellulation, and $E$ and $F$ need not be
the edges and facets of $P$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_characteristic.

articles.title: Affine line
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field and $d$ a natural number. For $y, x \in F^d$, the
affine line with base point $y$ and direction $x$ is the set $\{y + a x : a \in F\} \subseteq F^d$.
When $x = 0$ this set is the single point $\{y\}$.

articles.title: Dot product
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field and $d$ a natural number. For $x, y \in F^d$, the
dot product is $x \cdot y = \sum_{i} x_i y_i \in F$, the sum running over the $d$ coordinates.

articles.title: Finite field Kakeya sets in dimension three have cubic size
articles.statement:
There is a real number $c > 0$
such that for every finite field $F$ and every Kakeya set $E \subseteq F^3$, that is, a set such
that for every $x \in F^3$ there is $y \in F^3$ with $\{y + a x : a \in F\} \subseteq E$, we have
$|E| \ge c\,|F|^3$.

Dvir proved by the polynomial method that every Kakeya set $K \subseteq F^n$ over a finite field
$F$ with $q$ elements has $|K| \ge C_n q^n$, with $C_n$ depending only on $n$ (Theorem 3, the
Alon–Tao form of his Theorem 1). For $n = 3$ this answers Tao's question, which asks for
$|E| \gtrsim |F|^{5/2 + \varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$, beyond Wolff's bound
$|F|^{5/2}$, with $\varepsilon = 1/2$.

## Sources

- AIM workshop Recent trends in additive combinatorics (2004), problem list collected by E. Croot and V. F. Lev, https://aimath.org/WWN/additivecomb/additivecomb.pdf, Problem 3.8 (T. Tao); resolution: Z. Dvir, On the size of Kakeya sets in finite fields, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 22 (2009), 1093-1097, arXiv:0803.2336, Theorem 3 (Section 1.1, the Alon-Tao improvement of Theorem 1): every Kakeya set K ⊂ Fⁿ satisfies |K| ≥ C_n qⁿ with C_n depending only on n; for n = 3 this is |K| ≫ q³, https://doi.org/10.1090/S0894-0347-08-00607-3.

articles.title: Statement of the finite field Kakeya bound in dimension three
articles.statement:
This is the statement that
there is a real number $c > 0$ such that for every finite field $F$ and every Kakeya set
$E \subseteq F^3$, that is, a set such that for every $x \in F^3$ there is $y \in F^3$ with
$\{y + a x : a \in F\} \subseteq E$, we have $|E| \ge c\,|F|^3$.

This is Dvir's form of Tao's question (AIM, Recent trends in additive combinatorics, Problem 3.8),
which asks for $|E| \gtrsim |F|^{5/2 + \varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$; the exponent $3$
gives $\varepsilon = 1/2$.

articles.title: Finite-field Fourier transform
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field, $d$ a natural number and $\chi$
an additive character of $F$ with values in $\mathbb{C}$. For $\mu : F^d \to \mathbb{R}$ and
$\xi \in F^d$, the Fourier transform of $\mu$ at $\xi$ is
$\hat{\mu}(\xi) = \sum_{x \in F^d} \chi(-\xi \cdot x)\, \mu(x) \in \mathbb{C}$, where
$\xi \cdot x$ is the dot product.

The definition allows any character; it is used with a nontrivial one.

articles.title: Fraser's Fourier decay theorem for finite-field Kakeya sets
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field
with $q$ elements, let $d \ge 2$ be a natural number, let $K \subseteq F^d$ be a Kakeya set and let
$\chi$ be a nontrivial additive character of $F$ with values in $\mathbb{C}$. Then, first, there is
a probability measure $\mu$ on $K$ whose Fourier transform $\hat{\mu}$ with respect to $\chi$
satisfies $|\hat{\mu}(\xi)| \le q^{-1}$ for every nonzero $\xi \in F^d$. Second, this bound is
sharp: for every real $\kappa$ with $0 < \kappa < 1$ there is a natural number $Q$ such that for
every finite field $F'$ with $q' \ge Q$ elements there is a Kakeya set $K' \subseteq (F')^d$ such
that every probability measure $\mu$ on $K'$ has a nonzero $\xi \in (F')^d$ at which its Fourier
transform $\hat{\mu}$ with respect to a fixed primitive additive character of $F'$ satisfies
$|\hat{\mu}(\xi)| \ge \kappa \, q'^{-1}$.

## Sources

- J.M. Fraser, 'Fourier analytic properties of Kakeya sets in finite fields', Bull. London Math. Soc. 58(5) (2026); DOI 10.1112/blms.70367; arXiv:2505.09464. Problem `fraser_kakeya_fourier_decay` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Kakeya set
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field and $d$ a natural number. A set $K \subseteq F^d$ is a
Kakeya set if for every $x \in F^d$ there is $y \in F^d$ such that the affine line
$\{y + a x : a \in F\}$ is contained in $K$; that is, $K$ contains a line in every direction.

articles.title: Probability measure supported on a set
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite field, $d$ a natural number
and $K \subseteq F^d$. A function $\mu : F^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is a probability measure on $K$ if
$\mu(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in F^d$, $\sum_{x \in F^d} \mu(x) = 1$, and $\mu(x) \ne 0$ implies
$x \in K$.

articles.title: Coordinate space
articles.statement:
For a type $F$ and a natural number $d$, $F^d$ denotes the set of
$d$-tuples $(x_1, \dots, x_d)$ of elements of $F$, that is, functions from a $d$-element index set
to $F$.

Here $F$ is a finite field, so $F^d$ is the $d$-dimensional vector space over $F$.

articles.title: Floor differences are bounded by a ceiling
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$, $b$ and $D$ with
$|a - b| \le D$, the integers $\lfloor a \rfloor$ and $\lfloor b \rfloor$ satisfy
$|\lfloor a \rfloor - \lfloor b \rfloor| \le \lceil D \rceil$.

articles.title: Counting integer cubes met by a dilated Lipschitz image
articles.statement:
Let $d$ and $n$ be natural
numbers, let $K \ge 0$, and let $f$ be a $K$-Lipschitz map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to
$\mathbb{R}^n$, both carrying the sup distance. For every real $t \ge 1$, the cardinality of the
integer cube set of $f$ at scale $t$, taken as a natural number, is at most
$\lceil t \rceil^d \, (2 \lceil K \sqrt{d} \rceil + 3)^n$.

The proof puts $T = \lceil t \rceil$, partitions the cube into $T^d$ cells with lower-corner
representatives, bounds every floor-coordinate offset from the representative by
$L = \lceil K \sqrt{d} \rceil$, and encodes each met integer cube injectively by its cell and an
offset in $\{0, \dots, 2L + 2\}^n$.

articles.title: Counting outer cubes by inner cubes and boundary charts
articles.statement:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,
let $f_1, \dots, f_m : [0,1]^d \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be maps whose ranges together cover the frontier
of $S$, and let $t$ be a real number. Let $O$ and $I$ be the outer and inner cube sets of $S$ at
scale $t$: the $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ for which some, respectively every, point $x$ of the half-open
unit cube $\prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$ has $x / t \in S$ (coordinatewise, with $x / 0 = 0$). Let $C_i$
be the integer cube set of $f_i$ at scale $t$: the $v$ whose half-open unit cube contains
$t f_i(y)$ for some $y \in [0,1]^d$. If $O$ and every $C_i$ are finite, then
$|O| \le |I| + \sum_{i=1}^m |C_i|$.

articles.title: Integer count of a dilate
articles.statement:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and $t > 0$. The number of
integer vectors $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ with $x / t \in S$ equals the lattice enumerator of $S$ at
$t$, the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ in the dilate $tS$; here an infinite set is counted
as $0$.

articles.title: Cubical measure sandwich
articles.statement:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be bounded, let $t > 0$, and let
$\mathrm{vol}(S)$ be the Lebesgue (outer) measure of $S$, which is finite. For
$v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ let $Q_v = \prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$. Let $I$ be the inner cube set of $S$ at
scale $t$, the $v$ with $Q_v \subseteq tS$, and $O$ the outer cube set, the $v$ with $Q_v$
meeting $tS$. Then $|I| \le \mathrm{vol}(S)\, t^n \le |O|$.

articles.title: Dilated Lipschitz images meet $O(t^d)$ integer cubes
articles.statement:
Let $d$ and $n$ be natural numbers,
let $K \ge 0$, and let $f$ be a $K$-Lipschitz map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$,
both carrying the sup distance. Then there is a real number $C > 0$ such that for every real
$t \ge 1$, the cardinality of the integer cube set of $f$ at scale $t$, taken as a natural number,
is at most $C t^d$.

The proof takes $C = 2^d M^n$ with $M = 2 \lceil K \sqrt{d} \rceil + 3$, which depends on $f$ only
through $K$, and on $n$ and $d$, but not on $t$; it uses $\lceil t \rceil \le 2t$ for $t \ge 1$.

articles.title: Dilated Lipschitz images meet finitely many integer cubes
articles.statement:
Let $d$ and $n$ be natural
numbers, let $K \ge 0$, and let $f$ be a $K$-Lipschitz map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to
$\mathbb{R}^n$, both carrying the sup distance. For every real $t \ge 1$, the integer cube set of
$f$ at scale $t$ is finite.

The image of $f$ is bounded, since each coordinate of $f(y)$ differs from the corresponding
coordinate of $f(0)$ by at most $K \sqrt{d}$, so every met cube index lies in an explicit
finite box.

articles.title: Finiteness of the lattice points in a positive dilate
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a
bounded set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $t > 0$, the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$
of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$ is
finite.

articles.title: Finiteness of the lattice points in a dilate
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a bounded set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and any real number $t$, the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of
the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$ is finite.

No positivity of $t$ is needed.

articles.title: Finiteness of the outer cube set
articles.statement:
If $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is bounded and $t > 0$,
then the outer cube set of $S$ at scale $t$, the set of $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ whose integer unit
cube $\prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$ meets $tS$, is finite.

articles.title: Finiteness of the lattice points in a translated positive dilate
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$d$, a bounded set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, a real number $t > 0$ and a vector
$x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the set $(tP + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the translated dilate $tP + x = \{tp + x : p \in P\}$ is finite.

articles.title: Finiteness of the lattice points in a translated dilate
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a
bounded set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, any real number $t$ and a vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$,
the set $(tP + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the
translated dilate $tP + x = \{tp + x : p \in P\}$ is finite.

articles.title: Lipschitz images of Lipschitz parametrizable sets
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be metric spaces,
let $d$ be a natural number and let $f : X \to Y$ be a Lipschitz map. If a set $B \subseteq X$ is
$d$-Lipschitz parametrizable, then its image $f(B) \subseteq Y$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable.

articles.title: Inner cube indices are outer cube indices
articles.statement:
For every set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and
every real $t$, the inner cube set of $S$ at scale $t$ is contained in the outer cube set of $S$
at scale $t$.

articles.title: Inner cube set
articles.statement:
For a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and a real number $t$, the inner cube
set of $S$ at scale $t$ is the set of $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ such that
$(x_1/t, \dots, x_n/t) \in S$ for every $x$ in the integer unit cube
$Q_v = \prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$. For $t > 0$ these are the $v$ with $Q_v \subseteq tS$; for $t = 0$
the division is read as $x_i/0 = 0$.

articles.title: Integer cube set
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let
$t$ be a real number. The integer cube set of $f$ at scale $t$ is the set of integer vectors
$v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ for which some point $y$ of the unit cube satisfies
$v_i \le t f(y)_i < v_i + 1$ for every coordinate $i$, that is, the set of integer vectors whose
half-open unit cube $\prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$ meets the dilate $t \cdot f([0, 1]^d)$.

articles.title: Integer unit cube
articles.statement:
For $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$, the integer unit cube at $v$ is the half-open
cube $Q_v = \prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, the set of $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with
$v_i \le x_i < v_i + 1$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Finite sets are Lipschitz parametrizable
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a metric space. Every finite set
$B \subseteq X$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable for every natural number $d$.

articles.title: Finsets are Lipschitz parametrizable
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a metric space and $d$ a natural number.
Every finite set $s$ of points of $X$, given as a finset, is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable.

articles.title: The empty set is Lipschitz parametrizable
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a metric space. For every natural
number $d$, the empty subset of $X$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable, via the empty family of
maps.

articles.title: Singletons are Lipschitz parametrizable
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a metric space. For every natural
number $d$ and every point $x \in X$, the set $\lbrace x \rbrace$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable,
via a single constant map.

articles.title: Lipschitz parametrizable sets
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a metric space and $d$ a natural number. A set
$B \subseteq X$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable if there are a natural number $n$ (possibly $0$)
and Lipschitz maps $f_1, \dots, f_n : [0, 1]^d \to X$ out of the closed unit cube
$[0, 1]^d \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $B$ equals the union of their images,
$B = f_1([0, 1]^d) \cup \dots \cup f_n([0, 1]^d)$.

articles.title: The lattice-point count of the empty set vanishes
articles.statement:
For every natural number $d$ and every
real number $t$, the lattice-point count of the empty set $\emptyset \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ at the
dilate $t$ is $0$.

articles.title: Lattice-point enumerator
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a bounded set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $t > 0$, the lattice-point enumerator $L_P(t)$ is
the number of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate
$tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$, that is, $L_P(t) = |(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$.

Since $P$ is bounded, the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ is finite, so $L_P(t)$ is its actual
number of elements.

## Sources

- Rocha-Neves, A Fourier-analytic Uniqueness Theorem for Lattice-point Enumerators, arXiv:2608.11078v1, lines 24-31.

articles.title: Lattice-point count of a real dilate
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $t$, this is the number of elements of the set
$(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate
$tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$, where an infinite set is assigned the value $0$.

For unbounded $P$ the set can be infinite, so the value $0$ is a convention and not a count;
the lattice-point enumerator for bounded $P$ and $t > 0$ is the faithful count.

articles.title: Lattice-point count of a dilate with boundary error
articles.statement:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be
bounded, and suppose its boundary $\partial S$ is $(n-1)$-Lipschitz parametrizable: it is the
union of the ranges of finitely many Lipschitz maps from the unit cube $[0,1]^{n-1}$, where
$n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$. Then there is a real constant $C$ such that for all
sufficiently large real $t$, the lattice enumerator $L_S(t)$, the number of points of
$\mathbb{Z}^n$ in $tS$, satisfies $|L_S(t) - \operatorname{vol}(S)\, t^n| \le C\, t^{n-1}$, where
$\operatorname{vol}$ is Lebesgue (outer) measure.

articles.title: Lattice-point error bound from boundary charts
articles.statement:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be
bounded, let $f_1, \dots, f_m$ be maps from the unit cube $[0,1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose
ranges cover the boundary $\partial S$, and let $t > 0$. For each $i$, let $N_i(t)$ be the number
of $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ such that $t f_i(y)$ lies in the half-open cube $\prod_j [v_j, v_j + 1)$
for some $y \in [0,1]^d$, and assume each of these sets of $v$ is finite. Then the lattice
enumerator $L_S(t)$, the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ in $tS$, satisfies
$|L_S(t) - \operatorname{vol}(S)\, t^n| \le N_1(t) + \dots + N_m(t)$, where $\operatorname{vol}$
is Lebesgue (outer) measure.

articles.title: Lattice points in a positive dilate
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $t > 0$, this is the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of
points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$.

No boundedness of $P$ is assumed.

articles.title: Lattice points in a dilate
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$
and a real number $t$, this is the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$.

The source only uses this set for $t > 0$.

articles.title: Membership in the inner cube set
articles.statement:
For $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and
$v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$, $v$ belongs to the inner cube set of $S$ at scale $t$ if and only if
$(x_1/t, \dots, x_n/t) \in S$ for every $x$ in the integer unit cube at $v$.

articles.title: Membership in the integer cube set
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to
$\mathbb{R}^n$, let $t$ be a real number and let $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$. Then $v$ belongs to the
integer cube set of $f$ at scale $t$ if and only if some point $y$ of the unit cube satisfies
$v_i \le t f(y)_i < v_i + 1$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Membership in an integer unit cube
articles.statement:
For $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $x$
lies in the integer unit cube at $v$ if and only if $v_i \le x_i < v_i + 1$ for every
coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Membership in the outer cube set
articles.statement:
For $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and
$v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$, $v$ belongs to the outer cube set of $S$ at scale $t$ if and only if
$(x_1/t, \dots, x_n/t) \in S$ for some $x$ in the integer unit cube at $v$.

articles.title: Membership in the standard lattice
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a vector
$x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ lies in the standard lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the integer span of the standard
basis vectors of $\mathbb{R}^d$, exactly when every coordinate $x_i$ of $x$ is an integer.

articles.title: Outer cube set
articles.statement:
For a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and a real number $t$, the outer cube
set of $S$ at scale $t$ is the set of $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ such that
$(x_1/t, \dots, x_n/t) \in S$ for some $x$ in the integer unit cube
$Q_v = \prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$. For $t > 0$ these are the $v$ with $Q_v$ meeting $tS$; for $t = 0$
the division is read as $x_i/0 = 0$.

articles.title: Boundary cubes meet the dilated frontier charts
articles.statement:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, let
$f_1, \dots, f_m : [0,1]^d \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be maps whose ranges together cover the frontier of
$S$, and let $t$ be a real number. For $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ write $Q_v$ for the half-open unit
cube $\prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$. If $v$ lies in the outer cube set of $S$ at scale $t$ (some
$x \in Q_v$ has $x / t \in S$, coordinatewise, with $x / 0 = 0$) but not in the inner cube set
(not every $x \in Q_v$ has $x / t \in S$), then $v$ lies in the integer cube set of some $f_i$ at
scale $t$: there is $y \in [0,1]^d$ with $t f_i(y) \in Q_v$.

articles.title: Integer points of a dilate
articles.statement:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and $t > 0$. Viewing an
integer vector as a real vector gives a bijection from the set of $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ with
$x / t \in S$ onto the lattice point set $tS \cap \mathbb{Z}^n$.

articles.title: Dilated Lipschitz maps vary by at most $K$ on cells of size $1/T$
articles.statement:
Let $K \ge 0$, let $f$
be a $K$-Lipschitz map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$, both carrying the sup
distance, and let $t$ and $T$ be real numbers with $0 < t \le T$. If $y$ and $y'$ are points of
the unit cube at distance at most $1/T$, then $|t f(y)_i - t f(y')_i| \le K$ for every coordinate
$i$.

articles.title: The standard integer lattice
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the standard integer lattice
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ is the $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule of $\mathbb{R}^d$ (the real-valued functions on
$\{0, \dots, d-1\}$) spanned by the standard basis vectors $e_0, \dots, e_{d-1}$.

articles.title: The translated lattice-point count of the empty set is zero
articles.statement:
For every $d \in \mathbb{N}$,
every real $t$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the translated lattice-point count
$|((t \cdot \emptyset) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$ is $0$.

articles.title: Translated lattice-point enumerator of a bounded set
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded set, let $t > 0$ be real and let $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$. The
translated lattice-point enumerator is $F_{t,P}(x) = |((t \cdot P) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$, the
number of points of the standard integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $t \cdot P$
translated by $x$.

## Sources

- Rocha-Neves, arXiv:2608.11078v1, lines 62-67.

articles.title: Translated lattice-point count for arbitrary sets
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, a real $t$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the translated lattice-point
count is the number of elements of the translated lattice-point set
$((t \cdot P) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$, taken to be $0$ when this set is infinite.

articles.title: Translated lattice-point set at a positive dilation
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, a real $t > 0$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, this is the set
$((t \cdot P) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the standard integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$
in the dilate $t \cdot P$ translated by $x$. No boundedness of $P$ is assumed.

articles.title: Translated lattice-point set
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, a
real $t$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the translated lattice-point set is
$((t \cdot P) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$, the set of points of the standard integer lattice
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $t \cdot P$ translated by $x$.

The dilation comes first: in general this set differs from $(t \cdot (P + x)) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$.

## Sources

- Rocha-Neves, arXiv:2608.11078v1, lines 62-67.

articles.title: The origin lies in the unit cube
articles.statement:
For every natural number $d$, the origin of
$\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in the closed unit cube $[0, 1]^d$.

articles.title: The unit cube
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, the closed unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ is the set of
points $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $0 \le x_i \le 1$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: The origin is a lattice point
articles.statement:
For every $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the origin of $\mathbb{R}^d$
lies in the standard integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$.

articles.title: Monsky's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a finite set of subsets of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every member of $T$ is the convex hull of three points $a, b, c$ of the
plane (not necessarily distinct), the union of the members of $T$ is the closed unit square
$[0,1]^2$, any two distinct members of $T$ have disjoint interiors, and all members of $T$ have
the same Lebesgue measure. Then the number of members of $T$ is even.

Proof: A 2-adic valuation on ℝ gives a three-colouring of the plane, and a Sperner-type parity
count supplies a rainbow triangle whose area valuation rules out an odd number of pieces.

## Sources

- Paul Monsky, "On Dividing A Square Into Triangles," *The American Mathematical Monthly* 77(2) (1970), 161–164, DOI 10.1080/00029890.1970.11992441.

articles.title: The ambidextrous optimal area is at most the optimal area
articles.statement:
The supremum, in $[0, \infty]$,
of the Lebesgue areas of all ambidextrous sofas is at most the supremum of the Lebesgue areas of
all sofas. This holds because every ambidextrous sofa is a sofa.

articles.title: Optimal area of ambidextrous sofas
articles.statement:
The ambidextrous optimal area is the supremum, taken
in $[0, \infty]$, of the Lebesgue areas of all ambidextrous sofas $K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$.

articles.title: Baek upper bound for the ambidextrous sofa
articles.statement:
The supremum of the areas of
ambidextrous sofas, taken in $[0, \infty]$, is at most $22195/10000 = 2.2195$.

## Sources

- catalogue upper row, Baek (2024) naive bound from C41a, exact decimal endpoint `22195 / 10000`.

articles.title: Passing the mirrored corridor
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ can pass the mirrored
corridor if there are continuous maps $u$ from $[0, 1]$ to the unit circle
$\{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w| = 1\}$ and $c$ from $[0, 1]$ to $\mathbb{C}$ such that, writing
$K_t = \{u(t) z + c(t) : z \in K\}$ for the position of $K$ at time $t$, $K_0$ lies in the
entrance arm of the mirrored corridor, $K_1$ lies in the exit arm of the mirrored corridor, and
$K_t$ lies in the mirrored corridor for every $t \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Passing the Z corridor for all large separations
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ can pass
the Z corridor if there is a real number $D$ such that, for every real $d \ge D$, $K$ can pass
the Z corridor with corner separation $d$; that is, $K$ passes whenever the corners are
sufficiently separated.

Unlike the mirrored corridor, this is not implied by an ordinary passage: time reversal plus a
rigid motion transports an ordinary passage to the mirrored corridor, but a Z passage couples
both turns in one motion.

articles.title: Passing the Z corridor at a given separation
articles.statement:
For a real number $d$, a set
$K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ can pass the Z corridor with corner separation $d$ if there are
continuous maps $u$ from $[0, 1]$ to the unit circle $\{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w| = 1\}$ and $c$
from $[0, 1]$ to $\mathbb{C}$ such that, writing $K_t = \{u(t) z + c(t) : z \in K\}$ for the
position of $K$ at time $t$, $K_0$ lies in the entrance arm of the Z corridor, $K_1$ lies in the
exit arm of the Z corridor with corner separation $d$, and $K_t$ lies in the Z corridor with
corner separation $d$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$.

Such a passage is a single motion that turns once in each direction.

articles.title: Passing the corridor
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ can pass the corridor if there are
continuous maps $u$ from $[0, 1]$ to the unit circle $\{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w| = 1\}$ and $c$
from $[0, 1]$ to $\mathbb{C}$ such that, writing $K_t = \{u(t) z + c(t) : z \in K\}$ for the
position of $K$ at time $t$, $K_0$ lies in the entrance arm, $K_1$ lies in the exit arm, and
$K_t$ lies in the corridor for every $t \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Mirrored corridor
articles.statement:
The mirrored corridor is the set of points $z \in \mathbb{C}$ with
$\operatorname{Re} z \ge -1$ and $0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1$ (the horizontal arm,
extending to the right) together with the points $z$ with $-1 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 0$
and $\operatorname{Im} z \ge 0$ (the vertical arm, extending upward). It is the reflection of
the corridor in the imaginary axis, so passing it requires the opposite turn.

articles.title: Z-shaped corridor
articles.statement:
For a real number $d$, the Z-shaped corridor with corner separation
$d$ is the set of points $z \in \mathbb{C}$ lying in at least one of three pieces: the lower
horizontal arm, where $\operatorname{Re} z \le 1$ and $0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1$; the
middle channel, where $0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1$ and $0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 2 + d$;
and the upper horizontal arm, where $\operatorname{Re} z \ge 0$ and
$1 + d \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 2 + d$.

The middle channel is bounded: it does not contain the upward ray above the upper arm. For
$d = 1$ the two corner squares are separated by one full corridor width. Passing the corridor
requires one turn in each direction inside a single passage.

articles.title: Corridor
articles.statement:
The corridor is the L-shaped set of points $z \in \mathbb{C}$ with
$\operatorname{Re} z \le 1$ and $0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1$ (the horizontal arm, extending
to the left) together with the points $z$ with $0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1$ and
$\operatorname{Im} z \ge 0$ (the vertical arm, extending upward): two perpendicular
semi-infinite arms of width one.

articles.title: Entrance arm of the mirrored corridor
articles.statement:
The entrance arm of the mirrored corridor is the
set of points $z \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\operatorname{Re} z \ge 0$ and
$0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1$: the part of its horizontal arm beyond the corner square
$-1 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 0$, $0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1$.

articles.title: Entrance arm of the Z corridor
articles.statement:
The entrance region of the Z corridor is the closed
half-strip $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} z \le 0,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$,
the part of its horizontal entrance arm to the left of the middle channel.

articles.title: Entrance of the corridor
articles.statement:
The entrance region of the unit right-angle corridor is
the closed half-strip
$\{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} z \le 0,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$,
the part of its horizontal arm to the left of the corner square.

articles.title: Exit of the mirrored corridor
articles.statement:
The exit region of the mirrored unit corridor is the
closed half-strip
$\{z \in \mathbb{C} : -1 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 0,\ \operatorname{Im} z \ge 1\}$,
the part of its vertical arm above its corner square.

articles.title: Exit arm of the Z corridor
articles.statement:
For a real number $d$ (the corner separation), the exit region
of the Z corridor with separation $d$ is the closed half-strip
$\{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} z \ge 1,\ 1 + d \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 2 + d\}$,
the part of its horizontal exit arm to the right of the middle channel.

articles.title: Exit of the corridor
articles.statement:
The exit region of the unit right-angle corridor is the closed
half-strip $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ \operatorname{Im} z \ge 1\}$,
the part of its vertical arm above the corner square.

articles.title: Gerver's lower bound for the moving sofa constant
articles.statement:
The moving sofa constant, the
supremum of the areas of connected Lebesgue-measurable planar shapes that a continuous rigid motion
can carry through the right-angled corridor of width $1$, is at least $2.2195$.

## Sources

- catalogue line 22, printed Gerver lower target, not an exact area formula.

articles.title: Gibbs lower bound for the ambidextrous sofa
articles.statement:
The supremum of the areas of
ambidextrous sofas, taken in $[0, \infty]$, is at least $164495/100000 = 1.64495$.

## Sources

- catalogue lower row, Gibbs (2014) numerical construction, exact decimal endpoint `164495 / 100000`.

articles.title: Hammersley's lower bound for the moving sofa constant
articles.statement:
The moving sofa constant, the
supremum of the areas of connected Lebesgue-measurable planar shapes that a continuous rigid motion
can carry through the right-angled corridor of width $1$, is at least $\pi/2 + 2/\pi$.

## Sources

- catalogue line 21, Hammersley (1968). Construction not retained.

articles.title: Hammersley's upper bound for the moving sofa constant
articles.statement:
The moving sofa constant, the
supremum of the areas of connected Lebesgue-measurable planar shapes that a continuous rigid motion
can carry through the right-angled corridor of width $1$, is at most $2\sqrt{2}$.

## Sources

- catalogue line 13, attributed to Hammersley (1968). Primary not retained.

articles.title: Hammersley upper bound for the ambidextrous sofa
articles.statement:
The supremum of the areas of
ambidextrous sofas, taken in $[0, \infty]$, is at most $2\sqrt{2}$.

## Sources

- catalogue upper row, Hammersley (1968), adapted from C41a.

articles.title: Ambidextrous sofa shapes
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is an ambidextrous sofa when it is
a sofa and there is a real number $D$ such that, for every corner separation $d \ge D$, a single
motion places $K$ inside the entrance arm of the Z corridor with separation $d$ at time $0$, inside
its exit arm at time $1$, and inside that corridor at every time; such a passage turns once in
each direction.

(Two independent passages, one through each mirrored L corridor, would not suffice: an ordinary
passage transports to the mirrored corridor by time reversal plus a rigid motion, so that
formulation would collapse to the ordinary sofa condition.)

articles.title: Sofa shapes
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a sofa when it is Lebesgue measurable,
nonempty and connected, and can be moved through the unit right-angle corridor: there is a motion
(a rotation by a unit complex number and a translation, both varying continuously with time
$t \in [0, 1]$) that places $K$ inside the corridor's entrance region at time $0$, inside its exit
region at time $1$, and inside the corridor at every time $t$.

articles.title: Kallus–Romik upper bound for the moving sofa constant
articles.statement:
The moving sofa constant, the
supremum of the areas of connected Lebesgue-measurable planar shapes that a continuous rigid motion
can carry through the right-angled corridor of width $1$, is at most $2.37$.

## Sources

- catalogue line 14, Kallus-Romik (2018). Numerical certificate not retained.

articles.title: Motions preserve distance
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a motion, $t \in [0, 1]$ a time, and write $m_t(z)$
for the position of a point $z \in \mathbb{C}$ under $m$ at time $t$. Then
$|m_t(z) - m_t(w)| = |z - w|$ for all $z, w \in \mathbb{C}$.

articles.title: Planar rigid motion
articles.statement:
A motion consists of a continuous map $t \mapsto u_t$ from $[0, 1]$
to the unit circle $\{u \in \mathbb{C} : |u| = 1\}$ (the rotation) and a continuous map
$t \mapsto c_t$ from $[0, 1]$ to $\mathbb{C}$ (the translation).

articles.title: The ambidextrous sofa constant is at least one
articles.statement:
The supremum of the Lebesgue areas of all
ambidextrous sofas, taken in $[0, \infty]$, is at least $1$.

The unit square $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ is an ambidextrous sofa of area $1$.

articles.title: The optimal sofa area is at least one
articles.statement:
The optimal sofa area, that is, the supremum
in $[0, \infty]$ of the Lebesgue areas of all sofas, is at least $1$.

The unit square, a sofa of area $1$, witnesses the bound.

articles.title: Optimal sofa area
articles.statement:
Let the corridor be
$L = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\} \cup
\{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z\}$, with entrance
$E = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} z \le 0,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$ and exit
$X = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 1 \le \operatorname{Im} z\}$. A sofa
is a nonempty connected Lebesgue-measurable set $K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ for which there are
continuous maps $u : [0, 1] \to \{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w| = 1\}$ and $c : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$
such that, writing $K_t = \{u(t)\,z + c(t) : z \in K\}$, we have $K_0 \subseteq E$,
$K_1 \subseteq X$ and $K_t \subseteq L$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$. The optimal sofa area is the
supremum, taken in $[0, \infty]$, of the Lebesgue measures of all sofas.

Because the supremum is taken in $[0, \infty]$, neither its finiteness nor its attainment is
assumed.

articles.title: Position under a rigid motion
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a motion with rotation $u(t)$ in the unit circle
and translation $c(t) \in \mathbb{C}$ at each time $t \in [0, 1]$. The position at time $t$ of a
point $z \in \mathbb{C}$ is $u(t)\,z + c(t)$.

articles.title: Romik lower bound for the ambidextrous sofa
articles.statement:
The supremum of the areas of
ambidextrous sofas, taken in $[0, \infty]$, is at least
$164495521/100000000 = 1.64495521$.

## Sources

- catalogue lower row, Romik (2016), exact decimal endpoint `164495521 / 100000000`.

articles.title: The unit square has area one
articles.statement:
The unit square
$\{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$ has
Lebesgue measure $1$.

articles.title: The unit square passes the mirrored corridor
articles.statement:
Let the mirrored corridor be
$L' = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : -1 \le \operatorname{Re} z,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\} \cup
\{z \in \mathbb{C} : -1 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 0,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z\}$, with entrance
$E' = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$ and exit
$X' = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : -1 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 0,\ 1 \le \operatorname{Im} z\}$. For the
unit square
$Q = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$
there are continuous maps $u : [0, 1] \to \{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w| = 1\}$ and
$c : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ such that, writing $Q_t = \{u(t)\,z + c(t) : z \in Q\}$, we have
$Q_0 \subseteq E'$, $Q_1 \subseteq X'$ and $Q_t \subseteq L'$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$.

articles.title: Z-corridor passage of the unit square for large separations
articles.statement:
There is a real $D$ such
that for every $d \ge D$ the unit square passes the Z corridor with corner separation $d$.

articles.title: Z-corridor passage of the unit square at separation one
articles.statement:
The unit square passes the Z
corridor with corner separation $1$.

articles.title: Z-corridor passage of the unit square
articles.statement:
For every real $d \ge 0$, the unit square passes
the Z corridor with corner separation $d$.

articles.title: The unit square passes the corridor
articles.statement:
Let the corridor be
$L = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\} \cup
\{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z\}$, with entrance
$E = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} z \le 0,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$ and exit
$X = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 1 \le \operatorname{Im} z\}$. For the
unit square
$Q = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$
there are continuous maps $u : [0, 1] \to \{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w| = 1\}$ and
$c : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ such that, writing $Q_t = \{u(t)\,z + c(t) : z \in Q\}$, we have
$Q_0 \subseteq E$, $Q_1 \subseteq X$ and $Q_t \subseteq L$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$.

A pure translation, first to the right and then upward, suffices.

articles.title: The unit square is connected
articles.statement:
The unit square
$\{z \in \mathbb{C} : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$ is a
nonempty connected subset of $\mathbb{C}$.

articles.title: The unit square is an ambidextrous sofa
articles.statement:
The unit square $[0,1] \times [0,1]$ in the
complex plane is an ambidextrous sofa.

articles.title: The unit square is a sofa
articles.statement:
The unit square $[0,1] \times [0,1]$ in the complex plane is a
sofa: it is null-measurable for Lebesgue measure, connected, and there are continuous maps
$u \colon [0,1] \to \{w \in \mathbb{C} : |w| = 1\}$ and $v \colon [0,1] \to \mathbb{C}$ such that
the motion $z \mapsto u(t) z + v(t)$ carries the square into the entrance
$\{z : \operatorname{Re} z \le 0,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\}$ at $t = 0$, into the exit
$\{z : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 1 \le \operatorname{Im} z\}$ at $t = 1$, and into the
unit right-angle corridor
$\{z : \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1\} \cup
\{z : 0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1,\ 0 \le \operatorname{Im} z\}$ at every time $t \in [0,1]$.

articles.title: The unit square is Borel measurable
articles.statement:
The unit square $[0,1] \times [0,1]$ is a measurable
set for the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of the complex plane.

articles.title: The square's translation through the mirrored corner
articles.statement:
The motion with no rotation that
sends a point $z$ at time $t \in [0,1]$ to $z + \tau(t)$, where $\tau(t) = -2t$ for $t \le 1/2$ and
$\tau(t) = -1 + (2t - 1)i$ for $t \ge 1/2$: it moves a shape one unit to the left during the first
half of the time interval and then one unit upward.

articles.title: The square's translation through the Z corridor at separation one
articles.statement:
The square's
translation through the Z corridor at separation $d = 1$: the motion with no rotation that sends a
point $z$ at time $t \in [0,1]$ to $z + \tau(t)$, where $\tau(t) = 3t - 1$ for $t \le 1/3$,
$\tau(t) = 2(3t - 1)i$ for $1/3 \le t \le 2/3$, and $\tau(t) = (3t - 2) + 2i$ for $t \ge 2/3$.

articles.title: The square's translation through the Z corridor
articles.statement:
For a real number $d$, the motion with no
rotation that sends a point $z$ at time $t \in [0,1]$ to $z + \tau(t)$, where $\tau(t) = 3t - 1$ for
$t \le 1/3$, $\tau(t) = (1 + d)(3t - 1)i$ for $1/3 \le t \le 2/3$, and
$\tau(t) = (3t - 2) + (1 + d)i$ for $t \ge 2/3$: it translates a shape by $1$, then by $(1 + d)i$,
