then by $1$, each segment taking a third of the time interval.

articles.title: The square's translation through the corner
articles.statement:
The motion with no rotation that sends a
point $z$ at time $t \in [0,1]$ to $z + \tau(t)$, where $\tau(t) = 2t - 1$ for $t \le 1/2$ and
$\tau(t) = (2t - 1)i$ for $t \ge 1/2$: it moves a shape one unit to the right during the first
half of the time interval and then one unit upward.

articles.title: Unit square
articles.statement:
The unit square is the set of complex numbers $z$ with
$0 \le \operatorname{Re} z \le 1$ and $0 \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 1$, that is, the square
$[0,1] \times [0,1]$ in the complex plane.

articles.title: Stem–circle intersections of two lollipops
articles.statement:
For a point $c = (a, b) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, a
radius $r > 0$ and an angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, the lollipop with center $c$, radius $r$ and
stem direction $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ consists of the circle
$\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2\}$ and the stem
$\{c + s(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) : s \ge r\}$, the part of the ray from $c$ in that direction
outside the open disc. For all $c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{R}^2$, $r_1, r_2 > 0$ and
$\theta_1, \theta_2 \in \mathbb{R}$, consider the lollipops with centers $c_i$, radii $r_i$ and
stem directions $(\cos\theta_i, \sin\theta_i)$. If the number of points where the stem of the
first meets the circle of the second plus the number of points where the stem of the second meets
the circle of the first is $3$ or $4$, then $\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2) < 0$.

## Sources

- David O. H. Cutler, Jonas Karlsson and Neil J. A. Sloane, *Cutting a Pancake with an Exotic Knife*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.5, Lemma 3 (`jis-2026-26.4.5-lem-3`), with the definition in the subsection *The lollipop or qoppa*.

articles.title: Four-point intersections of constrained T's
articles.statement:
For a point $c \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and an angle
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, the constrained long-legged T $\bar T(c, \theta)$ is the union of the
crossbar, the line $\{c + s(-\sin\theta, \cos\theta) : s \in \mathbb{R}\}$, and the stem, the ray
$\{c + s(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) : s \ge 0\}$. For all $c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and
$\theta_1, \theta_2 \in \mathbb{R}$, if $\bar T(c_1, \theta_1) \cap \bar T(c_2, \theta_2)$ has
exactly four points, then $\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2) < 0$, that is, the two stem directions make
an angle greater than $\pi/2$.

## Sources

- David O. H. Cutler, Jonas Karlsson and Neil J. A. Sloane, *Cutting a Pancake with an Exotic Knife*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.5, Lemma 2 (`jis-2026-26.4.5-lem-2`), with the definition in the subsection *The constrained long-legged T̄*.

articles.title: Maximum region count for long-legged A's
articles.statement:
For a tip $c \in \mathbb{R}^2$, nonzero vectors
$u_1, u_2 \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and reals $a, b > 0$, the long-legged A is the union of the rays
$\{c + s u_1 : s \ge 0\}$ and $\{c + s u_2 : s \ge 0\}$ and the crossbar segment
$[c + a u_1, c + b u_2]$. For every natural number $n$, the largest number of regions into which
the union of $n$ long-legged A's can divide the plane is $(9n^2 - 5n + 2)/2$.

## Sources

- David O. H. Cutler, Jonas Karlsson and Neil J. A. Sloane, *Cutting a Pancake with an Exotic Knife*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.5, Theorem 1 (`jis-2026-26.4.5-thm-1`), with the definition in the section *The long-legged A*.

articles.title: Maximum region count for three-armed V's
articles.statement:
A long-legged three-armed V is the union of
three rays $\{c + s u_j : s \ge 0\}$, $j = 1, 2, 3$, from a common tip $c \in \mathbb{R}^2$, with
nonzero direction vectors $u_1, u_2, u_3 \in \mathbb{R}^2$ in arbitrary directions. For every
natural number $n$, the largest number of regions into which the union of $n$ long-legged
three-armed V's can divide the plane is $(9n^2 - 5n + 2)/2$.

## Sources

- David O. H. Cutler, Jonas Karlsson and Neil J. A. Sloane, *Cutting a Pancake with an Exotic Knife*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.5, Theorem 1 (`jis-2026-26.4.5-thm-1`), with the definition in the section *The k-armed V*.

articles.title: Maximum region count for 3-chains
articles.statement:
For points $p, q \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and nonzero vectors
$u, v \in \mathbb{R}^2$, the 3-chain is the union of the ray $\{p + s u : s \ge 0\}$, the segment
$[p, q]$ and the ray $\{q + s v : s \ge 0\}$; the directions are arbitrary and the 3-chain may
intersect itself. For every natural number $n$, the largest number of regions into which the
union of $n$ 3-chains can divide the plane is $(9n^2 - 5n + 2)/2$.

## Sources

- David O. H. Cutler, Jonas Karlsson and Neil J. A. Sloane, *Cutting a Pancake with an Exotic Knife*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.5, Theorem 1 (`jis-2026-26.4.5-thm-1`), with the definition in the section *The k-chain*.

articles.title: No cuts, one region
articles.statement:
The empty set of cuts divides the plane into exactly one region.

## Sources

- David O. H. Cutler, Jonas Karlsson and Neil J. A. Sloane, *Cutting a Pancake with an Exotic Knife*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.5, Section 1 (`n = 0`).

articles.title: Number of regions cut out of the plane
articles.statement:
For a set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of cuts, the
number of regions into which $K$ divides the plane is the number of connected components of the
complement $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus K$, or $0$ if there are infinitely many components.

## Sources

- David O. H. Cutler, Jonas Karlsson and Neil J. A. Sloane, *Cutting a Pancake with an Exotic Knife*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.5, Section 1.

articles.title: Cyclically adjacent indices
articles.statement:
Two indices $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ are adjacent when
$j \equiv i + 1 \pmod n$ or $i \equiv j + 1 \pmod n$.

articles.title: Enclosed area
articles.statement:
The area enclosed by a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ is the Lebesgue
measure, as a real number, of the region enclosed by $S$ (the points $x \notin S$ whose connected
component in $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus S$ is bounded); it is taken to be $0$ when that measure is
infinite.

articles.title: Number of boundary lattice points
articles.statement:
For integer points
$v_0, \dots, v_{n-1} \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, the number of lattice points $z \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ that lie
on the boundary (the union of the edges) of the lattice polygon on $v$.

articles.title: Region enclosed by a planar set
articles.statement:
For a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, the region enclosed
by $S$ is the set of points $x \notin S$ whose connected component in the complement
$\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus S$ is bounded. For a simple closed curve $S$ this is the Jordan interior.

articles.title: Number of interior lattice points
articles.statement:
For integer points
$v_0, \dots, v_{n-1} \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, the number of lattice points $z \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ that lie
in the region enclosed by the boundary of the lattice polygon on $v$, that is, the points off the
boundary whose connected component in its complement is bounded.

articles.title: Simple polygon
articles.statement:
A polygon in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with vertices $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$ (indices
taken mod $n$) and edges the segments $e_i = [p_i, p_{i+1}]$ is simple when consecutive vertices
are distinct ($p_i \ne p_{i+1}$ for all $i$), any two edges $e_i$ and $e_j$ with $i \ne j$,
$j \not\equiv i + 1$ and $i \not\equiv j + 1 \pmod n$ are disjoint, and every two consecutive
edges meet only in their common vertex: $e_i \cap e_{i+1} = \{p_{i+1}\}$ for all $i$.

articles.title: Lattice polygon
articles.statement:
Given integer points $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1} \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, the lattice
polygon on $v$ is the polygon in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $n$ vertices whose $i$-th vertex is $v_i$,
viewed as a point of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

articles.title: Pick's theorem for convex lattice polygons
articles.statement:
Let $V \subset \mathbb{Z}^2$ be a finite
set of lattice points, let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be the convex hull of $V$, and suppose that
$P$ has nonempty interior. Let $I$ be the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ in the interior of
$P$ and $B$ the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ on the boundary of $P$. Then the area
(two-dimensional Lebesgue measure) of $P$ equals $I + B/2 - 1$.

Proof: The triangle case counts lattice points in a half-open fundamental
parallelogram. A crossing diagonal then cuts larger polygons into two smaller
full-dimensional lattice polygons, allowing strong induction on the vertex set.

## Sources

- Eugen J. Ionascu, "A Parametrization of Equilateral Triangles Having Integer Coordinates", Journal of Integer Sequences 10 (2007), Article 07.6.7, standard formula `Area = #b / 2 + #i - 1`, lines 87–100, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL10/Ionascu/ionascu2.tex>; Kevin A. Broughan, "The gcd-sum function", Journal of Integer Sequences 4 (2001), Article 01.2.2, trapezium application, lines 699–715 (the prose there prints "+1" but the paper's own derived formula uses the minus-one form), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL4/BROUGHAN/gcdsum.tex>; Gil Alon and Pete L. Clark, "On the Number of Representations of an Integer by a Linear Form", Journal of Integer Sequences 8 (2005), Article 05.5.2, generalized lattice version `A(P) = δ * (h + b / 2 - 1)`, lines 633–638 (this article is the `δ = 1` standard-lattice case), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL8/Clark/clark80.tex>.

articles.title: Pick's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ and let $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1} \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ be integer
points such that the lattice polygon $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$ is
simple. Then the area of the region enclosed by the boundary of $P$ equals $I + B/2 - 1$, where
$I$ is the number of lattice points in that region and $B$ is the number of lattice points on the
boundary of $P$.

## Sources

- G. Pick, *Geometrisches zur Zahlenlehre* (1899). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §154. Problem `pick` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Lattice points in the plane
articles.statement:
The map $\mathbb{Z}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ sending a lattice
point $(a, b)$ to the point $(a, b)$ of the real plane.

articles.title: Pick's theorem for lattice triangles with a vertex at the origin
articles.statement:
Let
$u, v \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ with $u_0 v_1 - u_1 v_0 \neq 0$, and let $T \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be
the convex hull of $0$, $u$ and $v$. Let $I$ be the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ in the
interior of $T$ and $B$ the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ on the boundary of $T$. Then
the area (two-dimensional Lebesgue measure) of $T$ equals $I + B/2 - 1$.

articles.title: Convex polytope
articles.statement:
A convex polytope in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is given by its vertex set: a finite
nonempty set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ that equals the set of extreme points of its convex hull
$\operatorname{conv}(V)$. The polytope itself is the convex set $\operatorname{conv}(V)$.

articles.title: Dimension of a convex polytope
articles.statement:
The dimension of a convex polytope
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is its affine dimension: the dimension of the real vector space
spanned by the differences $x - y$ of points $x, y \in P$.

articles.title: Ambient Euclidean space of the Platonic classification
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the real
Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$: $n$-tuples of reals with the standard inner product and norm.

articles.title: Affine dimension of a set
articles.statement:
For a subset $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, its affine dimension is
the dimension of the real vector space spanned by the differences $x - y$ with $x, y \in F$.
The empty set and every single point get dimension $0$.

articles.title: Flag of a convex polytope
articles.statement:
A flag of a convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a
sequence $F_0, F_1, \dots, F_{n-1}$ of faces of $P$ such that each $F_k$ has affine dimension $k$
and $F_i \subsetneq F_j$ whenever $i < j$.

The definition applies to every $P$; it is used for full-dimensional $P$.

articles.title: Face of a convex polytope
articles.statement:
A face of a convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a
nonempty set of the form $\{x \in P : \ell(y) \le \ell(x) \text{ for all } y \in P\}$ for some
linear functional $\ell$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, the set of points where $\ell$ attains its
maximum over $P$. Taking $\ell = 0$ shows that $P$ itself is a face.

articles.title: Full-dimensional convex polytope
articles.statement:
A convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
full-dimensional if its dimension equals $n$.

articles.title: Regular convex polytope
articles.statement:
A convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is regular
(Platonic) if it is full-dimensional and for any two flags $(F_0, \dots, F_{n-1})$ and
$(G_0, \dots, G_{n-1})$ of $P$ there is an affine isometry $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with
$\varphi(P) = P$ and $\varphi(F_k) = G_k$ for every $k < n$.

articles.title: Symmetry of a convex polytope
articles.statement:
An affine isometry $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a
symmetry of a convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ if $\varphi(P) = P$.

articles.title: Rigid motions
articles.statement:
The rigid motions of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are the affine isometric bijections
$\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: Classification of the Platonic polytopes
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$ let $p_d \in
\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ be the number of regular convex polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ up to
similarity. Then $p_2 = \infty$, $p_3 = 5$, $p_4 = 6$, and $p_d = 3$ for every $d \ge 5$.

## Sources

- Euclid, Elements, Book XIII (~300 BC, p_3 = 5); L. Schläfli, Theorie der vielfachen Kontinuität (1852, posthumous publication; p_4 = 6, p_d = 3 for d ≥ 5). Listed as §42 in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `platonic_classification` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Number of Platonic polytopes
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, $p_d \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$
is the number of similarity classes of regular convex polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^d$, with
$p_d = \infty$ when there are infinitely many classes.

articles.title: Classification of the Platonic solids
articles.statement:
Let $V, E, F, p, q$ be natural numbers with
$V, E, F > 0$ and $p, q \ge 3$, and let $l > 0$ and $d > 0$ be real numbers. Let
$x_0, \dots, x_{V-1}$ be points of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^3$, let $K$ be their convex
hull and let $\partial K$ be its topological boundary. Let each edge $e < E$ be an ordered pair
$(a_e, b_e)$ of point indices, with segment $[x_{a_e}, x_{b_e}]$, and let each face $f < F$ be a
list $\phi_f(0), \dots, \phi_f(p-1)$ of point indices, read cyclically: positions are taken
modulo $p$, the sides of $f$ are the pairs $(\phi_f(i), \phi_f(i+1))$, and the filled face is
the convex hull of $x_{\phi_f(0)}, \dots, x_{\phi_f(p-1)}$. An edge $e$ lies on side $i$ of $f$
when $(a_e, b_e)$ equals $(\phi_f(i), \phi_f(i+1))$ or $(\phi_f(i+1), \phi_f(i))$. Assume:
$K$ is convex and contains every $x_i$; no $x_i$ lies in the convex hull of the $x_j$ with
$j \ne i$; the differences $x_i - x_j$ span a space of dimension $3$; every edge segment has
length $l$; for every face $f$ and position $i$,
$\operatorname{dist}(x_{\phi_f(i)}, x_{\phi_f(i+1)}) = l$ and
$\operatorname{dist}(x_{\phi_f(i-1)}, x_{\phi_f(i+1)}) = d$; the indices
$\phi_f(0), \dots, \phi_f(p-1)$ of each face are distinct; no vertex $x_{\phi_f(k)}$ of a face
lies in the convex hull of the other vertices of that face; two sides $(i_1, i_1+1)$ and
$(i_2, i_2+1)$ of a face whose four endpoint positions are all different have disjoint
segments; some edge lies on each side of every face, and every edge lies on a side of some face;
every edge lies on a side of exactly two faces; every edge segment and every filled face is
contained in $K$; the differences of the vertices of each face span a space of dimension at
most $2$; for every face $f$ there are a nonzero vector $n$ and a real $c$ with
$\langle n, x \rangle \le c$ for all $x \in K$ and $\langle n, x_{\phi_f(i)} \rangle = c$ for
every position $i$; two edges $e_1, e_2$ with $(a_{e_1}, b_{e_1})$ equal to
$(a_{e_2}, b_{e_2})$ or $(b_{e_2}, a_{e_2})$ are equal; two faces with the same set of indices
are equal; every $x_i$, every edge segment and every filled face is contained in $\partial K$;
every point of $\partial K$ lies in some filled face; every point index occurs in exactly $q$
faces; and $2E = pF$, $2E = qV$ and $V - E + F = 2$. Then $(p, q, V, E, F)$ is one of
$(3, 3, 4, 6, 4)$ (tetrahedron), $(4, 3, 8, 12, 6)$ (cube), $(3, 4, 6, 12, 8)$ (octahedron),
$(5, 3, 20, 30, 12)$ (dodecahedron) or $(3, 5, 12, 30, 20)$ (icosahedron).

Conversely, each of these five tuples $(p, q, V, E, F)$ is realized: there are points, edges,
faces and reals $l, d > 0$ satisfying all the conditions above, except that the points, edge
segments and filled faces are required to lie in $\partial K$ but not separately in $K$.

Euler's relation $V - E + F = 2$ and the incidence counts $2E = pF$, $2E = qV$ are hypotheses,
and the classification is up to the tuple $(p, q, V, E, F)$, not up to congruence. Together they
give $1/p + 1/q > 1/2$, which leaves the five tuples; explicit coordinates realize each one.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platonic_solid.

articles.title: Regular polytopes
articles.statement:
For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the set of regular (Platonic) convex
polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^d$: the convex polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that are full-dimensional and
whose symmetry group acts transitively on their flags.

articles.title: Similarity of regular polytopes
articles.statement:
For regular convex polytopes $P$ and $Q$ in
$\mathbb{R}^d$, $P$ is related to $Q$ when they are similar as convex polytopes, that is, when
there are a real number $a > 0$ and an affine isometry $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that the
underlying set of $Q$ is $\{a\,\varphi(x) : x \in P\}$.

articles.title: Similar polytopes
articles.statement:
Two convex polytopes $P$ and $Q$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are **similar** when
there are a real number $a > 0$ and an affine isometry $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that the
underlying set of $Q$ is $\{a\,\varphi(x) : x \in P\}$.

articles.title: Underlying set of a convex polytope
articles.statement:
The underlying set of a convex polytope $P$ in
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is the convex hull of its vertex set.

articles.title: Szemerédi–Trotter bound on line-compatible sequences
articles.statement:
There is a real constant $C$ such that
for every natural number $n$, the number of line-compatible sequences for $n$, that is, of
distinct multisets of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the distinct lines $\ell$ through two
distinct points of an $n$-point set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, each line counted once, is at
most $e^{C \sqrt{n}}$. This answers Erdős Problem 733.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #733, https://www.erdosproblems.com/733 (status PROVED); resolution: E. Szemerédi and W. T. Trotter, Extremal problems in discrete geometry, Combinatorica 3 (1983), 381-392, erdosproblems.com/733: 'This is true, and was proved by Szemerédi and Trotter', https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02579194.

articles.title: Subexponential count of line-compatible sequences (statement)
articles.statement:
The proposition that
there is a real constant $C$ such that for every natural number $n$, the number $f(n)$ of
line-compatible sequences for $n$ is at most $e^{C \sqrt{n}}$; that is, there are at most
$\exp(O(\sqrt{n}))$ line-compatible sequences. This is Erdős Problem 733.

articles.title: Number of line-compatible sequences
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $f(n)$ is the number of
distinct multisets that arise as the line sizes of some $n$-point set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$,
that is, as the multiset of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the distinct lines $\ell$ through
two distinct points of $P$, each line counted once. These multisets are the line-compatible
sequences for $n$; there are finitely many, since each has at most $n^2$ entries, all at most
$n$.

articles.title: Szemerédi–Trotter bound for line-incidence sets (Erdős Problem 607)
articles.statement:
For a finite set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, let $A(P)$ be the set of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the lines
$\ell$ through at least two distinct points of $P$, and let $F(n)$ be the number of distinct sets
$A(P)$ over all $n$-point sets $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. There is a real constant $C$ such that
$F(n) \le e^{C\sqrt{n}}$ for every natural number $n$.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #607, https://www.erdosproblems.com/607 (status PROVED); resolution: E. Szemerédi and W. T. Trotter, Extremal problems in discrete geometry, Combinatorica 3 (1983), 381-392, erdosproblems.com/607: proved by Szemerédi and Trotter [SzTr83], https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02579194.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 607: subexponentially many line-incidence sets
articles.statement:
For a finite set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, let $A(P)$ be the set of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the lines
$\ell$ through at least two distinct points of $P$, and let $F(n)$ be the number of distinct sets
$A(P)$ over all $n$-point sets $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. This is the statement that there is a
real constant $C$ such that $F(n) \le e^{C\sqrt{n}}$ for every natural number $n$, that is,
$F(n) \le \exp(O(\sqrt{n}))$.

articles.title: Number of line-incidence sets
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, let $A(P)$ be
the set of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the lines $\ell$ through at least two distinct points
of $P$. For a natural number $n$, $F(n)$ is the number of distinct sets $A(P)$ over all $n$-point
sets $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. Every such $A(P)$ is a subset of $\{0, \dots, n\}$.

articles.title: Line-incidence set of a finite planar point set
articles.statement:
For a finite set
$P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, $A(P)$ is the set of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the lines $\ell$
determined by $P$, that is, the lines through at least two distinct points of $P$.

articles.title: Line sizes of a planar point set
articles.statement:
For a finite set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, this is
the multiset of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$, where $\ell$ ranges over the lines determined by
$P$, that is, the distinct lines through two distinct points of $P$, each counted once.

articles.title: Affine hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^d$
articles.statement:
An affine subspace $A$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is an affine
hyperplane when there are a nonzero linear functional $\ell \colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ and
a real number $c$ such that $A = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \ell(x) = c\}$.

## Sources

- `OWR-1183-011`.

articles.title: Spanning point sets have injective point-to-hyperplane matchings
articles.statement:
For every $d \ge 1$ and
every set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ whose affine span is all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\mathcal{H}$
be the set of affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that equal the affine span of some subset of
$P$. Then there is an injective map $f \colon P \to \mathcal{H}$ with $p \in f(p)$ for every
$p \in P$.

This answers the question of `OWR-1183-011` affirmatively. It follows from Farley's Theorem 11:
every geometric lattice of finite rank greater than $1$, of any cardinality, has an injective
map sending each atom to a coatom containing it; apply it to the lattice of affine flats
spanned by subsets of $P$.

## Sources

- J. D. Farley, A question of Björner from 1981: infinite geometric lattices of finite rank have matchings, Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 82 (2022) 228-235, arXiv:2004.11972, https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.11972.

articles.title: Injective point-to-hyperplane matching question
articles.statement:
The statement that for every $d \ge 1$
and every set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ whose affine span is all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, writing
$\mathcal{H}$ for the set of affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that equal the affine span of
some subset of $P$, there is an injective map $f \colon P \to \mathcal{H}$ with $p \in f(p)$ for
every $p \in P$.

## Sources

- the question of `OWR-1183-011`.

articles.title: Hyperplanes spanned by a point set
articles.statement:
For a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, the hyperplanes
spanned by $P$ are the affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that equal the affine span of some
subset of $P$.

## Sources

- `OWR-1183-011`.

articles.title: Chung–Graham lower bound for the Steiner ratio
articles.statement:
The Steiner ratio constant, the infimum
over finite sets $V$ of at least two points in the Euclidean plane of the length of a Steiner
minimal tree for $V$ divided by the length of a minimum spanning tree of $V$, is at least $0.824$.

## Sources

- Chung and Graham (1985), via the catalogue's best unconditional published lower bound `0.824` before the conditional 2026 computer-assisted rows.

articles.title: Length of an edge
articles.statement:
For points $x$ and $y$ of the Euclidean plane, the length of the
unordered pair $\{x, y\}$ is the Euclidean distance between $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Gilbert–Pollak conjecture
articles.statement:
The Steiner ratio of the Euclidean plane, that is, the
infimum of the ratio of the Steiner minimal tree length to the minimum spanning tree length
over all finite sets of at least two points in the plane, equals $\sqrt{3}/2$.

The vertices of an equilateral triangle have ratio exactly $\sqrt{3}/2$, so the conjecture
says that no finite set of at least two points in the plane has a smaller ratio.

articles.title: Gilbert–Pollak upper bound for the Steiner ratio
articles.statement:
The Steiner ratio constant, the infimum
over finite sets $V$ of at least two points in the Euclidean plane of the length of a Steiner
minimal tree for $V$ divided by the length of a minimum spanning tree of $V$, is at most
$\sqrt{3}/2$.

## Sources

- Gilbert and Pollak, *Steiner minimal trees* (1968): the equilateral triangle gives the upper bound `√3 / 2`.

articles.title: Minimum spanning tree length
articles.statement:
For a finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, the
minimum spanning tree length of $V$ is the infimum of the total lengths of the trees with
vertex set $V$. For nonempty $V$ this set of lengths is finite and nonempty, so the infimum
is a minimum; for empty $V$ the value is $0$ by convention.

articles.title: The Euclidean plane of the Steiner ratio problem
articles.statement:
The space $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the
Euclidean distance, in which the point sets of the Steiner ratio problem lie.

articles.title: Lengths of spanning trees
articles.statement:
For a finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, this is
the set of real numbers $\ell$ such that some tree with vertex set $V$ has total length $\ell$,
the total length being the sum of the Euclidean lengths of its edges.

articles.title: The Steiner length is at most the minimum spanning tree length
articles.statement:
For every nonempty
finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, the Steiner minimal tree length of $V$ is at
most the minimum spanning tree length of $V$: allowing Steiner points never increases the
optimal length.

articles.title: Steiner minimal tree length
articles.statement:
For a finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, the
Steiner length of $V$ is the infimum of the total lengths of the trees whose vertex set is a
finite set of points of the plane containing $V$. This set of lengths is nonempty and bounded
below by $0$, so the infimum exists.

articles.title: The Steiner ratio of the Euclidean plane
articles.statement:
The Steiner ratio constant is the infimum,
over all finite sets $V$ of at least two points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, of the
ratio of the Steiner minimal tree length of $V$ to the minimum spanning tree length of $V$.

articles.title: Lengths of Steiner trees
articles.statement:
For a finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, this is
the set of real numbers $\ell$ such that, for some finite set $W$ of points of the plane
containing $V$, some tree with vertex set $W$ has total length $\ell$. The points of $W$
outside $V$ are the Steiner points.

articles.title: Total length of a graph on points of the plane
articles.statement:
For a finite set $V$ of points in the
Euclidean plane and a simple graph $G$ with vertex set $V$, the total length of $G$ is the sum,
over all edges $\{x, y\}$ of $G$, of the Euclidean distance between $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Squaring the square with distinct squares
articles.statement:
There are an integer $n > 1$ and real numbers
$x_i$, $y_i$ and $s_i > 0$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, with the $s_i$ pairwise distinct, such that
the union of the closed squares $[x_i, x_i + s_i] \times [y_i, y_i + s_i]$ is the unit square
$[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ and any two of these squares with different indices have disjoint
interiors.

## Sources

- S. Ruziewicz, Problem 59 of the Scottish Book, asking whether a square can be decomposed into a finite number of squares all different from one another; the answer is affirmative. The first published solution is R. Sprague's 1939 squaring of the square with distinct squares; see the commentary in R. D. Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book, 2nd ed. (Birkhäuser, 2015), and the 2026 survey "90+ years of the Scottish Book" (arXiv:2603.27867).

articles.title: Sylvester–Gallai theorem
articles.statement:
Every finite non-collinear subset of the real Euclidean plane determines an ordinary line: two
points of the set such that no third point of the set is collinear with them.

## Sources

- J. J. Sylvester, Mathematical Question 11851, Educational Times 59 (1893) 98; L. M. Kelly, A resolution of the Sylvester–Gallai problem, Discrete Comput. Geom. 1 (1986) 101–104 standard real-plane version.

articles.title: Core identity behind Casey's theorem in cyclic order
articles.statement:
In the Euclidean plane, write
$d(p, q)$ for the distance between points $p$ and $q$. Let $O, c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4$ be points and
$R, r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$ real numbers with $r_i < R$ and $d(c_i, O) + r_i = R$ for each $i$.
Suppose $c_i - O = d(c_i, O)(\cos\theta_i, \sin\theta_i)$ for real numbers
$\theta_1 < \theta_2 < \theta_3 < \theta_4 < \theta_1 + 2\pi$. For each pair $(i, j)$ among
$(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 1), (1, 3), (2, 4)$ let $t_{ij} > 0$ satisfy
$t_{ij}^2 = d(c_i, c_j)^2 - (r_i - r_j)^2$. Then $t_{12} t_{34} + t_{23} t_{41} = t_{13} t_{24}$.

Compared with Casey's theorem for four circles in arbitrary cyclic order, neither $R$ nor the
$r_i$ need be positive and the circles need not be pairwise disjoint.

articles.title: Casey's theorem for four circles in arbitrary cyclic order
articles.statement:
In the Euclidean plane, write
$d(p, q)$ for the distance between points $p$ and $q$. Let $O$ be a point and $R > 0$, and let
$c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4$ be points and $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$ real numbers with $0 < r_i < R$ and
$d(c_i, O) + r_i = R$ for each $i$, so that the circle with center $c_i$ and radius $r_i$ is
internally tangent to the circle with center $O$ and radius $R$. Suppose any two of the four
inner circles are disjoint, that is $r_i + r_j < d(c_i, c_j)$ for $i \ne j$, and that
$c_i - O = d(c_i, O)(\cos\theta_i, \sin\theta_i)$ for real numbers
$\theta_1 < \theta_2 < \theta_3 < \theta_4 < \theta_1 + 2\pi$. For each pair $(i, j)$ among
$(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 1), (1, 3), (2, 4)$ let $t_{ij} > 0$ satisfy
$t_{ij}^2 = d(c_i, c_j)^2 - (r_i - r_j)^2$, so that $t_{ij}$ is the length of an outer common
tangent. Then $t_{12} t_{34} + t_{23} t_{41} = t_{13} t_{24}$.

Unlike the version of Casey's theorem that requires each consecutive pair of centers to make a
positive oriented angle at $O$, a gap between consecutive directions may be at least $\pi$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey%27s_theorem

articles.title: Casey's theorem
articles.statement:
In the Euclidean plane, let a circle have center $O$ and radius $R > 0$,
and let four circles have centers $c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4$ and radii $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$ with
$0 < r_i < R$ and $|c_i O| + r_i = R$ for each $i$, so that each is internally tangent to the
outer circle. Assume that the four circles lie outside each other, $r_i + r_j < |c_i c_j|$ for
all $i \ne j$, and that they appear counterclockwise around $O$ with every consecutive angular
gap less than $\pi$: writing $u \times v = u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1$ for vectors $u = (u_1, u_2)$ and
$v = (v_1, v_2)$ of the plane, $(c_i - O) \times (c_j - O) > 0$ for
$(i, j) = (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 1)$. For the pairs $ij = 12, 23, 34, 41, 13, 24$ let
$t_{ij} > 0$ satisfy $t_{ij}^2 = |c_i c_j|^2 - (r_i - r_j)^2$, the length of an exterior common
tangent of the circles $i$ and $j$. Then $t_{12} t_{34} + t_{23} t_{41} = t_{13} t_{24}$.

Configurations with a consecutive angular gap of at least $\pi$ are not covered here; they are
covered by the cyclic-order form of Casey's theorem.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Descartes' circle theorem
articles.statement:
Let four circles in the Euclidean plane have centers $c_i$ and
radii $r_i > 0$ for $i = 1, 2, 3, 4$, let $d$ be the Euclidean distance, and let
$k_1, k_2, k_3, k_4$ be real numbers. Suppose that either
(a) any two of the circles are externally tangent, $d(c_i, c_j) = r_i + r_j$ for $i \ne j$, and
$k_i = 1/r_i$ for every $i$; or
(b) for some index $e$, each other circle is internally tangent to circle $e$, that is,
$d(c_e, c_j) = r_e - r_j$ for $j \ne e$; any two circles other than circle $e$ are externally
tangent, $d(c_i, c_j) = r_i + r_j$ for distinct $i, j \ne e$; and $k_e = -1/r_e$ and
$k_j = 1/r_j$ for $j \ne e$.
Then $(k_1 + k_2 + k_3 + k_4)^2 = 2(k_1^2 + k_2^2 + k_3^2 + k_4^2)$.

Proof: Following the Cayley-Menger/Gram-determinant argument in Lagarias, Mallows, and Wilks,
*Beyond the Descartes circle theorem*, Section 3, and Wikipedia's proof sketch, introduce signed
radii, expand the planar Gram determinant in coordinates, and clear denominators.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descartes%27_theorem.

articles.title: Lens curvature recurrence
articles.statement:
For real numbers $K$ and $A$, a real sequence
$(b_n)_{n \ge 0}$ satisfies the lens curvature recurrence with parameters $K$ and $A$ when
$1 + K \neq 0$ and, for every $n \ge 0$,

$$b_{n+2} = \frac{6 - 2K}{1 + K}\, b_{n+1} - b_n + \frac{-8A}{1 + K}.$$

This is the second-order nonhomogeneous recurrence of the source for the curvatures of a chain
of circles in a symmetric lens, where $A$ is the common curvature of the two lens circles.

articles.title: Right-angle vertex of the lune triangle
articles.statement:
The point $A = (0, 0)$, the origin of the
coordinate plane; it is the right-angle vertex of the triangle in Hippocrates' theorem on
lunes.

articles.title: Horizontal leg endpoint of the lune triangle
articles.statement:
For a real number $a$, the point
$B = (a, 0)$ on the $x$-axis of the coordinate plane; it is the endpoint of the horizontal leg of
the right triangle in Hippocrates' theorem on lunes.

articles.title: Vertical leg endpoint of the lune triangle
articles.statement:
For a real number $b$, the point
$C = (0, b)$ on the $y$-axis of the coordinate plane; it is the endpoint of the vertical leg of
the right triangle in Hippocrates' theorem on lunes.

articles.title: Closed half-disk on a diameter
articles.statement:
Given points $p$ and $q$ of the coordinate plane and a
property $S$ of real numbers, this is the set of points $x$ such that the squared Euclidean
distance from $x$ to the midpoint of $p$ and $q$ is at most one quarter of the squared Euclidean
distance from $p$ to $q$ (so $x$ lies in the closed disk with diameter $pq$), and $S$ holds of
the planar determinant $\det(q - p, x - p)$. For $p \ne q$, taking $S(t)$ to be $t \ge 0$
(respectively $t \le 0$) selects the closed half of that disk to the left (respectively right)
of the directed line from $p$ to $q$.

articles.title: Planar determinant for Hippocrates' lunes
articles.statement:
For vectors $u = (u_1, u_2)$ and
$v = (v_1, v_2)$ of the coordinate plane, $\det(u, v) = u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1$, the signed area of
the parallelogram spanned by $u$ and $v$.

articles.title: Squared Euclidean distance in the plane
articles.statement:
For points $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and
$q = (q_1, q_2)$ of the coordinate plane, the squared Euclidean distance between them is
$(p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$.

This uses the Euclidean distance, not the sup metric of the product
$\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Hippocrates' theorem on lunes
articles.statement:
Let $a, b > 0$ and consider the right triangle with
vertices $A = (0, 0)$, $B = (a, 0)$ and $C = (0, b)$. The Lebesgue measure of the lune on the
horizontal leg plus the Lebesgue measure of the lune on the vertical leg equals the Lebesgue
measure of the triangle, that is, of the convex hull of $A$, $B$ and $C$.

## Sources

- Hippocrates of Chios (c. 440 BC). Knill, §166. Problem `hippocrates_lunes` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Lune on the horizontal leg
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$ and $b$, let $A = (0, 0)$,
$B = (a, 0)$ and $C = (0, b)$. The lune on the horizontal leg is the set of points
$x = (x_1, x_2)$ of the closed disk with diameter $AB$ satisfying $a x_2 \le 0$ that do not
lie in the half-disk on the hypotenuse, the set of points of the closed disk with diameter $BC$
satisfying $b x_1 + a x_2 \le ab$. For $a, b > 0$ this is the set of points of the closed lower
half-disk on the leg $AB$ that lie outside the closed disk with diameter $BC$.

articles.title: Half-disk on the hypotenuse
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$ and $b$, let $B = (a, 0)$ and
$C = (0, b)$. The half-disk on the hypotenuse is the set of points $x = (x_1, x_2)$ of the
closed disk with diameter $BC$ satisfying $\det(C - B, x - B) \ge 0$, that is,
$b x_1 + a x_2 \le ab$. For $a, b > 0$ this is the half of the disk on the side of the line
$BC$ containing the right-angle vertex $(0, 0)$.

articles.title: Midpoint of two points in the plane
articles.statement:
For points $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and
$q = (q_1, q_2)$ of the coordinate plane, their midpoint is
$\left(\frac{p_1 + q_1}{2}, \frac{p_2 + q_2}{2}\right)$.

articles.title: Coordinate plane for Hippocrates' lunes
articles.statement:
The coordinate plane is the set
$\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ of ordered pairs $(x, y)$ of real numbers.

articles.title: Right triangle with legs on the axes
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$ and $b$, the right triangle
$T(a, b)$ is the convex hull in the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ of the three points $(0, 0)$, $(a, 0)$
and $(0, b)$.

articles.title: Displacement vector between two points of the plane
articles.statement:
For points $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and
$q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, the displacement vector from $p$ to $q$ is
$(q_1 - p_1, q_2 - p_2)$.

articles.title: Hippocrates lune on the vertical leg
articles.statement:
For real numbers $a$ and $b$, the vertical lune is
the set of points $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $x^2 + (y - b/2)^2 \le b^2/4$ and $bx \le 0$
that do not satisfy both $(x - a/2)^2 + (y - b/2)^2 \le (a^2 + b^2)/4$ and $bx + ay \le ab$.

For $a, b > 0$ this is the closed half-disk on the segment from $(0, 0)$ to $(0, b)$, on the side
away from $(a, 0)$, minus the closed half-disk on the hypotenuse from $(a, 0)$ to $(0, b)$, on
the side of the origin.

articles.title: Lattice step of the billiard unfolding in a rectangle
articles.statement:
For a natural number $j$, let
$\varepsilon_j = 1$ if $j$ is odd and $\varepsilon_j = 0$ if $j$ is even. Let $a, b > 0$ be real
numbers with $a n = b m$ for some positive integers $m, n$. Then there are a real number $t > 0$
and natural numbers $k > 0$, $l > 0$ and $N$ such that $t = k a = l b$, $N + 2 = k + l$, $k$ and
$l$ are coprime, and the point $(\varepsilon_k a, \varepsilon_l b)$ is one of $(a, 0)$, $(0, b)$,
$(a, b)$.

In the billiard argument for the $a \times b$ rectangle, the unfolded diagonal from the
corner $(0, 0)$ first meets a corner of the tiling at $(t, t)$ (coprimality is the first-hit
condition), $N$ counts the reflections, and folding back yields the corner
$(\varepsilon_k a, \varepsilon_l b)$. This lemma covers only that lattice step; it does not
formalize the reflected trajectory and does not prove Problem 147.

## Sources

- H. Auerbach and S. Mazur, Problem 147 of the Scottish Book; the typescript labels the entry Theorem (Problem Mazur). Elementary unfolding argument for polygonal billiards, see e.g. S. Tabachnikov, Geometry and Billiards.

articles.title: Bialy–Tabachnikov: $k_{602}$ is invariant
articles.statement:
The elliptic billiard invariant $k_{602}$
conjecture holds. Write $|XY|$ for the distance between points $X$ and $Y$. For every natural
number $N$, all points $O, f_1, f_2$ of the Euclidean plane and all reals $a, a_c$ with
$O = \frac{1}{2}(f_1 + f_2)$, $|f_1 f_2| < a$, $|f_1 f_2| < a_c$ and $a_c < a$, there is a real
number $C$ with the following property. Let $P_0, P_1, P_2, \dots$ be points of the plane such
that $|P_i f_1| + |P_i f_2| = a$ and $P_{i+N} = P_i$ for every $i$, and such that for every
$i < N$ the points $P_i$ and $P_{i+1}$ are distinct and the line $P_i P_{i+1}$ contains exactly
one point $X$ with $|X f_1| + |X f_2| = a_c$. For $i < N$ let $Q_{1,i}$ and $Q_{2,i}$ be any
points of the line $P_i P_{i+1}$ closest to $f_1$ and to $f_2$ respectively. Then
$\prod_{i\lt N} |f_1 Q_{1,i}| \cdot \prod_{i\lt N} |f_2 Q_{2,i}| = C$.

Bialy and Tabachnikov (Lemma 4.2) show that for each side tangent to the confocal caustic with
semi-minor axis $b$ the two focal distances multiply to $b^2$, so the common value is $b^{2N}$.

## Sources

- M. Bialy, S. Tabachnikov, Dan Reznik's identities and more, European Journal of Mathematics (2020), arXiv:2001.08469, https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08469.

articles.title: Elliptic billiard invariant $k_{602}$
articles.statement:
Write $|XY|$ for the distance between points $X$
and $Y$ of the Euclidean plane. For every natural number $N$, all points $O, f_1, f_2$ of the
plane and all reals $a, a_c$ with $O = \frac{1}{2}(f_1 + f_2)$, $|f_1 f_2| < a$,
$|f_1 f_2| < a_c$ and $a_c < a$, there is a real number $C$ with the following property. Let
$P_0, P_1, P_2, \dots$ be points of the plane such that $|P_i f_1| + |P_i f_2| = a$ and
$P_{i+N} = P_i$ for every $i$, and such that for every $i < N$ the points $P_i$ and $P_{i+1}$
are distinct and the line $P_i P_{i+1}$ contains exactly one point $X$ with
$|X f_1| + |X f_2| = a_c$. For $i < N$ let $Q_{1,i}$ and $Q_{2,i}$ be points of the line
$P_i P_{i+1}$ closest to $f_1$ and to $f_2$ respectively. Then

$$\prod_{i\lt N} |f_1 Q_{1,i}| \cdot \prod_{i\lt N} |f_2 Q_{2,i}| = C.$$

In words: the vertices lie on the ellipse with foci $f_1, f_2$ and major axis $a$, every side
is tangent to the confocal caustic with major axis $a_c$, and $Q_{j,i}$ is the foot of the
perpendicular from $f_j$ to the $i$-th side.

## Sources

- [AMR-050-0031] Reznik, Garcia and Koiller, Eighty New Invariants of N-Periodics in the Elliptic Billiard (2021), Table row $k_{602}$, arXiv:2004.12497.

articles.title: Miquel's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be non-collinear points of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$, and let $D$, $E$, $F$ be points on the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ respectively with
$D \ne B$, $D \ne C$, $E \ne C$, $E \ne A$, $F \ne A$ and $F \ne B$. If $A$, $E$, $F$ lie on the
circle with center $O_1$ and radius $r_1$, $B$, $F$, $D$ lie on the circle with center $O_2$ and
radius $r_2$, and $C$, $D$, $E$ lie on the circle with center $O_3$ and radius $r_3$, then these
three circles have a common point.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miquel%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Monge's three-circle theorem, algebraic form
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a real vector space, let
$c_1, c_2, c_3 \in V$, and let $r_1, r_2, r_3$ be pairwise distinct real numbers. Then the three
points $(r_1 - r_2)^{-1}(r_1 c_2 - r_2 c_1)$, $(r_2 - r_3)^{-1}(r_2 c_3 - r_3 c_2)$ and
$(r_1 - r_3)^{-1}(r_1 c_3 - r_3 c_1)$ of $V$ are collinear.

For positive $r_i$, read as the radii of circles centered at the $c_i$, these points are the
external homothety centers of the pairs of circles. If $r_i$ and $r_j$ have opposite signs, the
point $(r_i - r_j)^{-1}(r_i c_j - r_j c_i)$ is instead the internal homothety center of the
circles of radii $|r_i|$ and $|r_j|$ centered at $c_i$ and $c_j$; for example $r_1 = -1$ and
$r_2 = 2$ give $\frac{1}{3}(c_2 + 2 c_1)$.

articles.title: Monge's three-circle theorem
articles.statement:
Let $c_1, c_2, c_3$ be points of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $r_1, r_2, r_3$ be pairwise distinct positive real numbers such that the
closed disks of radius $r_i$ centered at $c_i$ are pairwise disjoint. Then the external homothety
centers $(r_1 - r_2)^{-1}(r_1 c_2 - r_2 c_1)$, $(r_2 - r_3)^{-1}(r_2 c_3 - r_3 c_2)$ and
$(r_1 - r_3)^{-1}(r_1 c_3 - r_3 c_1)$ of the three pairs of circles are collinear.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monge%27s_theorem. The source's hypothesis is that no circle lies inside another; the pairwise disjointness of the closed disks (`hd12`, `hd23`, `hd13`) is stronger. Omitted source case: the source also treats two circles of equal radius, whose external tangents are parallel and meet at a point at infinity. The distinct-radii hypotheses `h12`, `h23`, `h13` exclude it, and the affine formula for the centers cannot express it. It follows from `monge_three_circles_general`; the positivity hypotheses `hr₁`, `hr₂`, `hr₃` and the disjointness hypotheses are unused and keep the `Wanted` statement's shape.

articles.title: Collinear projective points
articles.statement:
Writing $\cdot$ and $\times$ for the dot and cross products
on $\mathbb{R}^3$, three vectors $p, q, r \in \mathbb{R}^3$ represent collinear points of the
real projective plane when their triple product vanishes: $p \cdot (q \times r) = 0$.

articles.title: Meet of two lines
articles.statement:
Writing $\times$ for the cross product on $\mathbb{R}^3$, the meet of
the line through $a$ and $b$ with the line through $c$ and $d$, for $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{R}^3$,
is the vector $(a \times b) \times (c \times d)$.

When $a \times b$ and $c \times d$ are nonzero and not proportional, this vector represents the
intersection point of the two projective lines.

articles.title: Points on a conic
articles.statement:
For a real $3 \times 3$ matrix $M$, a vector $v \in \mathbb{R}^3$ lies on
the conic $x^\top M x = 0$ when $v^\top M v = 0$.

articles.title: Pascal's theorem in an affine plane
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic different from
$2$ and let $P$ be an affine plane over $k$, that is, an affine space whose space of translations
$V$ is a $k$-vector space of dimension $2$. Fix a point $O \in P$ and a nondegenerate symmetric
bilinear form $\beta$ on $V \times k$, and call the set of points $x \in P$ with
$\beta((x - O, 1), (x - O, 1)) = 0$ the conic. Let $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_5$ be six distinct points
of the conic such that, for each of the three pairs of opposite sides $(v_0 v_1, v_3 v_4)$,
$(v_1 v_2, v_4 v_5)$ and $(v_2 v_3, v_5 v_0)$ of the hexagon $v_0 v_1 v_2 v_3 v_4 v_5$, the four
endpoints are not collinear, so that the two lines are distinct. If $q_1$ lies on the lines
$v_0 v_1$ and $v_3 v_4$, $q_2$ lies on the lines $v_1 v_2$ and $v_4 v_5$, and $q_3$ lies on the
lines $v_2 v_3$ and $v_5 v_0$, then $q_1$, $q_2$, $q_3$ are collinear.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Pascal's theorem for real projective conics
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a real symmetric $3 \times 3$
matrix with $\det M \ne 0$, and let $a_1, a_2, a_3, b_1, b_2, b_3 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ be nonzero
vectors on the conic $x^\top M x = 0$, no two of which represent the same projective point.
Writing $\cdot$ and $\times$ for the dot and cross products on $\mathbb{R}^3$, let
$p = (a_1 \times b_2) \times (a_2 \times b_1)$, $q = (a_1 \times b_3) \times (a_3 \times b_1)$ and
$r = (a_2 \times b_3) \times (a_3 \times b_2)$ be the meets of the opposite sides of the hexagon
$a_1 b_2 a_3 b_1 a_2 b_3$. Then $p$, $q$ and $r$ are collinear: $p \cdot (q \times r) = 0$.

## Sources

- B. Pascal, *Essay pour les coniques* (1640). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §146. Problem `pascal` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Same projective point
articles.statement:
Two vectors $v, w \in \mathbb{R}^3$ represent the same point of the
real projective plane when $w = c v$ for some real number $c \ne 0$.

articles.title: Pizza theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ be a natural number, let $D$ be the open disk of radius
$R > 0$ centered at a point $c$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, let $p$ be a point of $D$, and let $\theta_0$
be a real number. Put $\alpha = \pi / (2n)$ and, for $k = 0, 1, \dots, 4n - 1$, let $S_k$ be the
set of points of $D$ of the form $p + r(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ with $r \ge 0$ and
$\theta_0 + k\alpha \le \theta < \theta_0 + (k + 1)\alpha$. Then the sum of the Lebesgue measures
of the $S_k$ with $k$ even equals the sum of the Lebesgue measures of the $S_k$ with $k$ odd.

The $4n$ sectors $S_k$ are the slices cut from the disk by $2n$ lines through $p$ at equal
angles, so alternately shading the slices gives equal shaded and unshaded areas.

## Sources

- *Pizza theorem*, Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pizza_theorem.

articles.title: Impossibility of angle trisection
articles.statement:
Let "constructible" be any property of real numbers such
that a real number $x$ is constructible exactly when there are $n \ge 0$ and subfields
$K_0 \subseteq K_1 \subseteq \dots \subseteq K_n$ of $\mathbb{R}$ with $K_0 = \mathbb{Q}$ (the
smallest subfield of $\mathbb{R}$), $x \in K_n$, and, for each $i < n$, some $b \in K_{i+1}$ with
$b^2 \in K_i$ such that every element of $K_{i+1}$ equals $u + bv$ for some $u, v \in K_i$. Let
an angle $\theta$ be constructible exactly when $\cos \theta$ is constructible. Then the polynomial
$8X^3 - 6X - 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, $\cos(\pi/9)$ is a root of it, $\cos(\pi/9)$ is
not constructible, and it is not true that $\theta / 3$ is a constructible angle for every
constructible angle $\theta$.

In particular the $60^\circ$ angle, whose cosine $1/2$ is constructible, cannot be trisected: by
the triple-angle formula, $\cos 20^\circ = \cos(\pi/9)$ is a root of $8X^3 - 6X - 1$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_trisection.

articles.title: Tarski's Euclidean axiom
articles.statement:
For a model $M$ of Tarski's absolute plane geometry with
betweenness relation $B$, where $B(a, b, c)$ means that $b$ lies between $a$ and $c$ (allowing
$b = a$ or $b = c$), the Euclidean axiom A10 holds in $M$ when for all points $a, b, c, d, t$ of
$M$ with $B(a, d, t)$, $B(b, d, c)$ and $a \ne d$ there are points $x$ and $y$ of $M$ with
$B(a, b, x)$, $B(a, c, y)$ and $B(x, t, y)$.

In the presence of the other axioms of absolute geometry, this axiom is equivalent to Euclid's
parallel postulate.

articles.title: Independence of the parallel postulate
articles.statement:
Tarski's Euclidean axiom A10 is independent of
Tarski's axioms of absolute plane geometry: there is a model of absolute plane geometry in which
the Euclidean axiom holds, and there is a model of absolute plane geometry in which it fails.

## Sources

- Independence of Euclid's parallel postulate; the hyperbolic-plane models are due to E. Beltrami (1868) and F. Klein (1871). Tarski's axiomatization: W. Schwabhäuser, W. Szmielew, A. Tarski, Metamathematische Methoden in der Geometrie, Springer (1983). Formalized in HOL Light by John Harrison and in Isabelle by Tim Makarios (T.J.M. Makarios, A Mechanical Verification of the Independence of Tarski's Euclidean Axiom, MSc thesis, Victoria University of Wellington, 2012; Isabelle/AFP entry Tarskis_Geometry). Problem `parallel_postulate_independent` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Tarski's absolute plane geometry
Beckman–Quarles theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ and let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a map of
$n$-dimensional real Euclidean space such that $\lVert f(x) - f(y) \rVert = 1$ whenever
$\lVert x - y \rVert = 1$. Then $f$ is an isometry, that is,
$\lVert f(x) - f(y) \rVert = \lVert x - y \rVert$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

Surjectivity of $f$ is neither assumed nor concluded.

## Sources

- F. S. Beckman and D. A. Quarles Jr., On isometries of Euclidean spaces, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 4 (1953) 810–815 original theorem; standard formulation for `ℝ^n, n ≥ 2`.

articles.title: Glide reflection
articles.statement:
An isometry $f$ of the Euclidean plane is a glide reflection if the
determinant of its linear part is $-1$ and there are a line $L$ and a nonzero vector $v$
parallel to $L$ such that $f(x) = x + v$ for every point $x$ of $L$.

articles.title: Reflection
articles.statement:
An isometry $f$ of the Euclidean plane is a reflection if there is a line
$L$ such that $f(x) = x$ for every point $x$ of $L$, and the determinant of the linear part
of $f$ is $-1$.

articles.title: Rotation
articles.statement:
An isometry $f$ of the Euclidean plane is a rotation if it fixes some point
$p$, the determinant of its linear part is $1$, and $f$ is not a translation.

articles.title: Translation
articles.statement:
An isometry $f$ of the Euclidean plane is a translation if there is a
vector $v$ such that $f(x) = x + v$ for every point $x$.

articles.title: Linear determinant of a plane isometry
articles.statement:
The linear determinant of an isometry $f$ of
the Euclidean plane is the determinant of the linear part of $f$.

articles.title: Classification of plane isometries
articles.statement:
Every isometry of the Euclidean
plane is a translation, a rotation, a reflection, or a glide reflection.

articles.title: The Euclidean plane
articles.statement:
The Euclidean plane is the real vector space $\mathbb{R}^2$ with
its standard inner product $\langle x, y \rangle = x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2$.

articles.title: Orientation-preserving affine equivalence
articles.statement:
Two subgroups $G_1$ and $G_2$ of the group of
affine isometries of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ are orientation-preserving affinely
equivalent if there is an affine bijection $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ whose linear part has
positive determinant such that $\{\varphi g \varphi^{-1} : g \in G_1\} = G_2$ as sets of affine
maps of $\mathbb{R}^d$.

articles.title: Number of orientation-preserving affine classes of crystallographic groups
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $d$, this is the number, in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, of classes of $d$-dimensional
crystallographic groups under orientation-preserving affine equivalence. Here a crystallographic
group is a subgroup $G$ of the group of affine isometries of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that is discrete (for
every point $x$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ only finitely many $g \in G$ satisfy
$\operatorname{dist}(g x, x) \le \varepsilon$) and contains translations by $d$ linearly
independent vectors.

articles.title: Number of orientation-preserving affine classes of orientation-preserving crystallographic groups
articles.statement:
**Number of orientation-preserving affine classes of orientation-preserving crystallographic
groups.** For a natural number $d$, this is the number, in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, of classes
under orientation-preserving affine equivalence of those $d$-dimensional crystallographic groups
all of whose elements are orientation-preserving isometries. Here a crystallographic group is a
subgroup $G$ of the group of affine isometries of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that is discrete (for every
point $x$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ only finitely many $g \in G$ satisfy
$\operatorname{dist}(g x, x) \le \varepsilon$) and contains translations by $d$ linearly
independent vectors.

articles.title: Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ for the space-group problem
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, this
is the $d$-dimensional real Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ with its standard inner product.

articles.title: Euclidean space for wallpaper groups
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, the $d$-dimensional real
Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ with its standard inner product.

articles.title: Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, $E(d)$ is the $d$-dimensional
Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$, with coordinates indexed by $0, 1, \dots, d - 1$ and the standard
inner product.

articles.title: Orientation-preserving isometry
articles.statement:
An affine isometry of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$
is orientation-preserving if its linear part has positive determinant.

articles.title: The 230 space groups
articles.statement:
In dimension $3$ there are exactly $230$ classes of crystallographic
groups under orientation-preserving affine equivalence, exactly $219$ classes of crystallographic
groups under affine equivalence (conjugation by an arbitrary affine bijection of $\mathbb{R}^3$),
and exactly $65$ classes under orientation-preserving affine equivalence of crystallographic
groups all of whose elements are orientation-preserving isometries.

## Sources

- E. Fedorov, 'Симметрія правильныхъ системъ фигуръ' (Symmetry of regular systems of figures), Trans. Min. Soc. St. Petersburg 28 (1891) 1–146; A. Schoenflies, *Krystallsysteme und Krystallstructur*, Teubner 1891, independently. Listed as §94 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `space_groups_230` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: There are exactly 17 wallpaper groups
articles.statement:
Call a group $G$ of isometries of the Euclidean
plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ crystallographic if it is discrete, meaning that for every point $x$ and
every $\varepsilon > 0$ only finitely many $g \in G$ satisfy
$\operatorname{dist}(g x, x) \le \varepsilon$, and it contains translations by two linearly
independent vectors. Call two such groups $G_1$ and $G_2$ affinely equivalent if some invertible
affine map $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfies $\{\varphi g \varphi^{-1} : g \in G_1\} = G_2$.
Up to affine equivalence there are exactly $17$ crystallographic groups of the plane.

## Sources

- G. Pólya, 'Über die Analogie der Kristallsymmetrie in der Ebene', Z. Kristallogr. 60 (1924) 278–282; P. Niggli, 'Die Flächensymmetrien homogener Diskontinuen', Z. Kristallogr. 60 (1924) 283–298. Listed as §94 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `wallpaper_groups_17` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Carrier of the translation lattice subgroup
articles.statement:
For every group $G$ of affine isometries of
the Euclidean plane, the underlying set of the translation lattice subgroup of $G$ is the
translation lattice of $G$.

articles.title: Conjugating a translation by a plane isometry
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an affine isometry of the
Euclidean plane with linear part $A$, let $v$ be a vector, and write $\tau_w$ for translation by
a vector $w$. Then $g \circ \tau_v \circ g^{-1} = \tau_{A v}$.

articles.title: Classification of discrete additive subgroups of the plane
articles.statement:
Every
discrete additive subgroup `G` of `ℝ²` is trivial, cyclic (generated by a
single nonzero vector), or a rank-two lattice (generated by two
`ℝ`-linearly independent vectors).

articles.title: The Euclidean plane for discrete isometry groups
articles.statement:
$E_2$ is the Euclidean plane:
the real vector space $\mathbb{R}^2$ of pairs of real numbers with the standard Euclidean inner
product and norm.

articles.title: Separation criterion for groups of plane isometries
articles.statement:
A group $G$ of affine isometries of
the Euclidean plane satisfies the separation criterion if there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that
every element $f \ne \mathrm{id}$ of $G$ whose linear part is the identity satisfies
$\|f(0)\| \ge \varepsilon$, and every element $f$ of $G$ whose linear part $A$ is not the
identity satisfies $\|A - I\| \ge \varepsilon$, where $I$ is the identity map and the norm is
the operator norm.

Its linear-part condition measures operator-norm separation from the identity, rather than the
numerical rotation angle.

articles.title: Linear part of a plane isometry
articles.statement:
The linear part of an affine isometry $f$ of the
Euclidean plane is the linear isometry $A$ of the plane such that $f(x + v) = f(x) + A v$ for
every point $x$ and every vector $v$.

articles.title: Isometry group of the Euclidean plane
articles.statement:
$M_2$ is the group, under composition, of affine
isometries of the Euclidean plane onto itself.

articles.title: Membership in the translation lattice subgroup
articles.statement:
For every group $G$ of affine isometries
of the Euclidean plane and every vector $v$ of the plane, $v$ belongs to the translation lattice
subgroup of $G$ if and only if $v$ belongs to the translation lattice of $G$.

articles.title: The point group preserves the translation lattice
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group of affine
isometries of the Euclidean plane. If $A$ belongs to the point group of $G$, that is, $A$ is the
linear part of some element of $G$, and $v$ belongs to the translation lattice of $G$, then $A v$
belongs to the translation lattice of $G$.

articles.title: Point group of a group of plane isometries
articles.statement:
The point group of a group $G$ of affine
isometries of the Euclidean plane is the set of linear parts of the elements of $G$.

articles.title: Translations are determined by their vectors
articles.statement:
For vectors $v$ and $w$ of the Euclidean
plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, if translation by $v$ and translation by $w$ are the same affine isometry,
then $v = w$. Equivalently, the translation homomorphism $v \mapsto (x \mapsto v + x)$ from the
additive group of the plane to the group of affine isometries of the plane is injective.

articles.title: Translation homomorphism
articles.statement:
The group homomorphism from the additive group of the Euclidean
plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ (written multiplicatively) to the group of affine isometries of the plane that
sends a vector $v$ to translation by $v$, the isometry $x \mapsto v + x$.

articles.title: Classification of translation lattices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group of affine isometries of the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, and suppose there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every
non-identity translation in $G$ moves the origin by at least $\varepsilon$, and every element of
$G$ whose linear part $A$ is not the identity satisfies $\|A - I\| \ge \varepsilon$ in operator
norm. Let $L$ be the translation lattice of $G$, the additive subgroup of vectors $v$ such that
translation by $v$ lies in $G$. Then either $L = \{0\}$, or $L = \mathbb{Z}\alpha$ for some nonzero
vector $\alpha$, or $L = \mathbb{Z}a + \mathbb{Z}b$ for some $\mathbb{R}$-linearly independent
vectors $a$ and $b$.

articles.title: The translation lattice of a discrete isometry group is discrete
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group of
affine isometries of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, and suppose there is $\varepsilon > 0$
such that every non-identity translation in $G$ moves the origin by at least $\varepsilon$, and
every element of $G$ whose linear part $A$ is not the identity satisfies
$\|A - I\| \ge \varepsilon$ in operator norm. Then the translation lattice of $G$, the additive
subgroup of vectors $v$ such that translation by $v$ lies in $G$, is discrete in the subspace
topology of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

articles.title: Translation lattice as an additive subgroup
articles.statement:
For a group $G$ of affine isometries of the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, the additive subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of the vectors
$v$ such that translation by $v$ belongs to $G$; it is the preimage of $G$ under the translation
homomorphism $v \mapsto (x \mapsto v + x)$.

articles.title: Translation lattice
articles.statement:
The translation lattice of a subgroup $G$ of the group $M_2$ of
affine isometries of the Euclidean plane $E_2$ is the set of vectors $v \in E_2$ such that the
translation $x \mapsto v + x$ belongs to $G$.

articles.title: Isometries of Euclidean space are affine
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, every
isometry $f$ of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is affine: there is a linear map
$A : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$, the linear part of $f$, such that $f(x) = A x + f(0)$
for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: Isometries of Euclidean space fixing the origin are linear
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n$, if $f$ is an isometry of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $f(0) = 0$, then
$f$ is $\mathbb{R}$-linear: $f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)$ and $f(c x) = c f(x)$ for all
$x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Brahmagupta's formula
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q, R, S$ be points of the Euclidean plane with side
lengths $|PQ| = a$, $|QR| = b$, $|RS| = c$, $|SP| = d$ and diagonal $|PR| = e$, and let
$s = (a + b + c + d)/2$. Suppose that some point $O$ is equidistant from $P, Q, R, S$ (so the
quadrilateral $PQRS$ is cyclic) and that some point $T$ satisfies $|PT| + |TR| = |PR|$ and
$|QT| + |TS| = |QS|$ with $|PT|, |TR|, |QT|, |TS| > 0$ (so $T$ lies strictly inside both
diagonals and $PQRS$ is convex). Let $p = (a + b + e)/2$ and $q = (c + d + e)/2$, and let $A$ be
the sum of the Heron areas of the triangles $PQR$ and $RSP$:

$$A = \sqrt{p(p - a)(p - b)(p - e)} + \sqrt{q(q - c)(q - d)(q - e)}.$$

Then $A = \sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahmagupta%27s_formula

articles.title: Euler's quadrilateral theorem
articles.statement:
For any four points $A, B, C, D$ of the Euclidean plane,
write $XY$ for the distance between points $X$ and $Y$, and let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of
$AC$ and $BD$. Then

$$AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + DA^2 = AC^2 + BD^2 + 4 MN^2.$$

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_quadrilateral_theorem

articles.title: Finsler–Hadwiger theorem for distinct squares
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, C, D, E, F, G$ be points of
the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $B \ne E$, and let $\rho(x, y) = (-y, x)$ be the
counterclockwise rotation by $90^\circ$. Suppose that $ABCD$ and $AEFG$ are squares sharing the
vertex $A$, in the sense that $D - A = \rho(B - A)$, $C = B + D - A$, $G - A = \rho(E - A)$ and
$F = E + G - A$. Let $O_1 = (A + C)/2$ and $O_2 = (A + F)/2$ be their centers, and let
$P = (B + G)/2$ and $Q = (D + E)/2$. Then $\|P - Q\| = \|O_1 - O_2\|$, the vectors $P - Q$ and
$O_1 - O_2$ are orthogonal, $O_1 + O_2 = P + Q$ and $O_1 \ne O_2$; so the segments $O_1O_2$ and
$PQ$ are nonzero, equal, perpendicular and share their midpoint, and $O_1 P O_2 Q$ is a square.

The points $B$ and $E$ may equal $A$: if, say, $E = A$, then $AEFG$ is the single point $A$
and $O_1 P O_2 Q$ is a quarter of $ABCD$.

articles.title: Finsler–Hadwiger theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, C, D, E, F, G$ be points of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$ with $B \ne A$ and $E \ne A$, and let $\rho(x, y) = (-y, x)$ be the
counterclockwise rotation by $90^\circ$. Suppose that $ABCD$ and $AEFG$ are squares sharing the
vertex $A$, in the sense that $D - A = \rho(B - A)$, $C = B + D - A$, $G - A = \rho(E - A)$ and
$F = E + G - A$. Let $O_1 = (A + C)/2$ and $O_2 = (A + F)/2$ be their centers, and let
$P = (B + G)/2$ and $Q = (D + E)/2$. Then $\|P - Q\| = \|O_1 - O_2\|$, the vectors $P - Q$ and
$O_1 - O_2$ are orthogonal, and $O_1 + O_2 = P + Q$; that is, the segments $O_1O_2$ and $PQ$
have equal length, are perpendicular and share their midpoint.

The hypotheses $B \ne A$ and $E \ne A$ are not used. When $B = E$ both segments are zero; with
$B \ne E$ one also gets $O_1 \ne O_2$, so that $O_1 P O_2 Q$ is a square as in the source.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finsler%E2%80%93Hadwiger_theorem.

articles.title: Japanese theorem for concyclic quadrilaterals
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, C, D$ be pairwise distinct
points of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ lying on a circle of positive radius, such that the
diagonals $AC$ and $BD$, as closed segments, intersect; so $ABCD$ is a convex cyclic
quadrilateral. Let $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4 > 0$, and suppose that for each of the triangles $ABC$,
$CDA$, $BCD$ and $DAB$ there is a closed disc of radius $r_1$, $r_2$, $r_3$ and $r_4$
respectively that is contained in the closed triangle and whose boundary circle meets each of
the three closed sides of the triangle; so $r_1, r_2$ are the inradii of the triangles $ABC$,
$CDA$ of one triangulation and $r_3, r_4$ those of the triangles $BCD$, $DAB$ of the other.
Then $r_1 + r_2 = r_3 + r_4$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_theorem_for_concyclic_quadrilaterals.

articles.title: Van Aubel's theorem with squares on the right
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ be any four
points of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, and let $\rho(x, y) = (y, -x)$ be the clockwise
rotation by $90^\circ$. On each directed side $A \to B$, $B \to C$, $C \to D$, $D \to A$
erect the square lying to its right; its centre is the side midpoint plus half the side vector
rotated by $\rho$:
$O_{AB} = \tfrac12(A + B) + \tfrac12\rho(B - A)$,
$O_{BC} = \tfrac12(B + C) + \tfrac12\rho(C - B)$,
$O_{CD} = \tfrac12(C + D) + \tfrac12\rho(D - C)$ and
$O_{DA} = \tfrac12(D + A) + \tfrac12\rho(A - D)$.
Then $\lVert O_{AB} - O_{CD} \rVert = \lVert O_{BC} - O_{DA} \rVert$ and
$\langle O_{AB} - O_{CD}, O_{BC} - O_{DA} \rangle = 0$: the segments joining the centres of
opposite squares have equal length and are perpendicular.

When $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are listed counterclockwise these are the outward squares; together
with Van Aubel's theorem for squares on the left this covers the outward construction for both
orientations.

articles.title: Van Aubel's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ be any four points of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$, and let $\rho(x, y) = (-y, x)$ be the counterclockwise rotation by $90^\circ$.
On each directed side $A \to B$, $B \to C$, $C \to D$, $D \to A$ erect the square lying to its
left; its centre is the side midpoint plus half the side vector rotated by $\rho$:
$O_{AB} = \tfrac12(A + B) + \tfrac12\rho(B - A)$,
$O_{BC} = \tfrac12(B + C) + \tfrac12\rho(C - B)$,
$O_{CD} = \tfrac12(C + D) + \tfrac12\rho(D - C)$ and
$O_{DA} = \tfrac12(D + A) + \tfrac12\rho(A - D)$.
Then $\lVert O_{AB} - O_{CD} \rVert = \lVert O_{BC} - O_{DA} \rVert$ and
$\langle O_{AB} - O_{CD}, O_{BC} - O_{DA} \rangle = 0$: the segments joining the centres of
opposite squares have equal length and are perpendicular.

No orientation hypothesis is needed. When the vertices are listed clockwise these are the
outward squares; when they are listed counterclockwise they are the inward squares, and the
outward version is Van Aubel's theorem with squares on the right.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Aubel%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Varignon's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ be any four points of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$, degenerate and self-crossing configurations included, and let $P$, $Q$, $R$,
$S$ be the midpoints of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$, that is $2P = A + B$, $2Q = B + C$,
$2R = C + D$ and $2S = D + A$. Write $[XYZ]$ for the oriented area of the triangle $XYZ$,
positive when $X$, $Y$, $Z$ are listed counterclockwise. Then $P + R = Q + S$, so the diagonals
of $PQRS$ bisect each other and $PQRS$ is a possibly degenerate parallelogram, and

$$2([PQR] + [PRS]) = [ABC] + [ACD],$$

that is, the signed area of $PQRS$ is half the signed area of $ABCD$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varignon%27s_theorem. `A B C D` are arbitrary points in the Euclidean plane, including degenerate or self-crossing configurations. `P Q R S` are the midpoints of sides AB, BC, CD, DA (`2 • P = A + B`, etc.). Conclusion: `P + R = Q + S` (the diagonals of PQRS bisect each other, i.e. PQRS is a parallelogram via parallel opposite sides / bisecting diagonals), and twice the signed area of PQRS, expressed through `EuclideanGeometry.orientedTriangleArea`, equals the signed area of ABCD.

articles.title: De Gua's theorem with Heron's formula
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, c > 0$ and let $p_0 = (a, 0, 0)$,
$p_1 = (0, b, 0)$, $p_2 = (0, 0, c)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, so that the tetrahedron with vertices
$0, p_0, p_1, p_2$ has a right angle between any two of the edges at $0$, with legs of lengths
$a$, $b$, $c$. Let $d_{01} = d(p_0, p_1)$, $d_{12} = d(p_1, p_2)$ and $d_{20} = d(p_2, p_0)$ be the
Euclidean distances, let $s = (d_{01} + d_{12} + d_{20})/2$, and let
$A = \sqrt{s(s - d_{01})(s - d_{12})(s - d_{20})}$, the area of the face $p_0 p_1 p_2$ by Heron's
formula. Then $A^2 = (ab/2)^2 + (bc/2)^2 + (ca/2)^2$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Gua%27s_theorem

articles.title: De Gua's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $u, v, w \in \mathbb{R}^3$ be pairwise orthogonal vectors, so that
the tetrahedron with vertices $0, u, v, w$ has a right angle between any two of the edges at $0$.
Write $|x|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\langle x, y \rangle$ for the inner product. Let
$A_{uv}, A_{uw}, A_{vw}, A$ be real numbers with $A_{uv} = |u||v|/2$, $A_{uw} = |u||w|/2$,
$A_{vw} = |v||w|/2$ (the areas of the three right-angled faces) and
$(2A)^2 = |u - v|^2 |u - w|^2 - \langle u - v, u - w \rangle^2$, so that $A$ is, up to sign, the
area of the face with vertices $u, v, w$. Then $A^2 = A_{uv}^2 + A_{uw}^2 + A_{vw}^2$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Gua%27s_theorem

articles.title: Spherical law of cosines, general form
articles.statement:
Write $x \cdot y = \sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i y_i$ for the
dot product and $\lVert x \rVert = \sqrt{x \cdot x}$ for the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^3$. Let
$u, v, w \in \mathbb{R}^3$ be unit vectors and let $a, b, c, C$ be real numbers with $0 < a < \pi$
and $0 < b < \pi$. Suppose that $v \cdot w = \cos a$, $u \cdot w = \cos b$, $u \cdot v = \cos c$
and

$$
\cos C = \frac{u \cdot v - (u \cdot w)(v \cdot w)}
{\lVert u - (u \cdot w)\, w \rVert \, \lVert v - (v \cdot w)\, w \rVert}.
$$

Then $\cos c = \cos a \cos b + \sin a \sin b \cos C$.

Only $a$ and $b$ need to lie in $(0, \pi)$: $c$ and $C$ enter only through their cosines. The
quotient above is the cosine of the angle at $w$ between the great-circle arcs from $w$ to $u$
and from $w$ to $v$.

articles.title: Spherical law of cosines
articles.statement:
Write $x \cdot y = \sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i y_i$ for the dot product
and $\lVert x \rVert = \sqrt{x \cdot x}$ for the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^3$. Let
$u, v, w \in \mathbb{R}^3$ be unit vectors and let $a, b, c, C$ be real numbers, each strictly
between $0$ and $\pi$. Suppose that $v \cdot w = \cos a$, $u \cdot w = \cos b$,
$u \cdot v = \cos c$ and

$$
\cos C = \frac{u \cdot v - (u \cdot w)(v \cdot w)}
{\lVert u - (u \cdot w)\, w \rVert \, \lVert v - (v \cdot w)\, w \rVert}.
$$

Then $\cos c = \cos a \cos b + \sin a \sin b \cos C$.

Geometrically, $u$, $v$, $w$ are the vertices of a spherical triangle on the unit sphere, $a$,
$b$, $c$ are the lengths of the sides opposite $u$, $v$, $w$, and $C$ is the angle at $w$,
opposite the side $c$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_law_of_cosines. It follows from `spherical_law_of_cosines_general`; the hypotheses `hc` and `hC` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Converse of the angle bisector theorem without distinctness hypotheses
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$,
$D$ be points of a Euclidean affine space (a metric affine space over a real inner product space)
with $A$, $B$, $C$ affinely independent, so that $ABC$ is a nondegenerate triangle. If $D$ lies on
the closed segment $BC$ and $BD / DC = AB / AC$, then $\angle BAD = \angle DAC$ (unoriented
angles), that is, $D$ lies on the internal bisector of the angle at $A$.

The hypotheses $A \ne B$, $A \ne C$ and $A \ne D$ of the usual statement are not needed: they
follow from the others.

articles.title: Converse of the angle bisector theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ be points of a Euclidean
affine space (a metric affine space over a real inner product space) with $A$, $B$, $C$ affinely
independent, so that $ABC$ is a nondegenerate triangle, and with $A \ne B$, $A \ne C$ and
$A \ne D$. If $D$ lies on the closed segment $BC$ and $BD / DC = AB / AC$, then
$\angle BAD = \angle DAC$ (unoriented angles), that is, $D$ lies on the internal bisector of the
angle at $A$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_bisector_theorem. It follows from `angle_bisector_converse_general`; the hypotheses `hAB`, `hAC` and `hAD` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Angle bisector theorem without distinctness hypotheses
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ be points of
a Euclidean affine space (a metric affine space over a real inner product space) with $A$, $B$, $C$
affinely independent, so that $ABC$ is a nondegenerate triangle. If $D$ lies strictly between $B$
and $C$ and $\angle BAD = \angle DAC$ (unoriented angles), then $BD / DC = AB / AC$.

The hypotheses $A \ne B$, $A \ne C$ and $A \ne D$ of the usual statement are not needed: they
follow from the others.

articles.title: Angle bisector theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ be points of a Euclidean affine space (a
metric affine space over a real inner product space) with $A$, $B$, $C$ affinely independent, so
that $ABC$ is a nondegenerate triangle, and with $A \ne B$, $A \ne C$ and $A \ne D$. If $D$ lies
strictly between $B$ and $C$ and $\angle BAD = \angle DAC$ (unoriented angles), then
$BD / DC = AB / AC$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_bisector_theorem. It follows from `angle_bisector_theorem_general`; the hypotheses `hAB`, `hAC` and `hAD` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Carnot's theorem (inradius and circumradius), general form
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, C$ be non-collinear
points of a Euclidean affine plane lying on the circle with center $O$ and radius $R > 0$. Take
unit vectors $n_a$, $n_b$, $n_c$ normal to the sides and pointing toward the opposite vertices:
$n_a \perp C - B$ with $\langle A - B, n_a \rangle > 0$, $n_b \perp A - C$ with
$\langle B - C, n_b \rangle > 0$, and $n_c \perp B - A$ with $\langle C - A, n_c \rangle > 0$.
Let $x = \langle O - B, n_a \rangle$, $y = \langle O - C, n_b \rangle$ and
$z = \langle O - A, n_c \rangle$ be the signed distances from $O$ to the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$.
If a point $I$ and a real number $r$ satisfy
$\langle I - B, n_a \rangle = \langle I - C, n_b \rangle = \langle I - A, n_c \rangle = r$
(so $I$ is the incenter and $r$ the inradius), then $x + y + z = R + r$.

This form does not assume $r > 0$ or that $O$ lies in the affine span of $A, B, C$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnot%27s_theorem_(inradius,_circumradius). Statement ID: carnot-inradius-s1.

articles.title: Carnot's theorem (inradius and circumradius)
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, C$ be non-collinear points of a
Euclidean affine plane lying on the circle with center $O$ and radius $R > 0$, and suppose $O$
lies in the affine span of $A, B, C$. Take unit vectors $n_a$, $n_b$, $n_c$ normal to the sides
and pointing toward the opposite vertices: $n_a \perp C - B$ with $\langle A - B, n_a \rangle > 0$,
$n_b \perp A - C$ with $\langle B - C, n_b \rangle > 0$, and $n_c \perp B - A$ with
