$\langle C - A, n_c \rangle > 0$. Let $x = \langle O - B, n_a \rangle$,
$y = \langle O - C, n_b \rangle$ and $z = \langle O - A, n_c \rangle$ be the signed distances
from $O$ to the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$. If a point $I$ and a real number $r > 0$ satisfy
$\langle I - B, n_a \rangle = \langle I - C, n_b \rangle = \langle I - A, n_c \rangle = r$
(so $I$ is the incenter and $r$ the inradius), then $x + y + z = R + r$.

The hypotheses $r > 0$ and that $O$ lies in the affine span of $A, B, C$ are not used; the
general form of the theorem drops them.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnot%27s_theorem_(inradius,_circumradius). Statement ID: carnot-inradius-s1.

articles.title: Conway circle theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be affinely independent points of the Euclidean
plane, and write $a = d(B, C)$, $b = d(A, C)$, $c = d(A, B)$ for the side lengths, where $d$ is
the Euclidean distance. Extend each side beyond each of its endpoints by the length of the side
opposite that endpoint; this gives the six points

$$A + \tfrac{a}{c}(A - B),\quad B + \tfrac{b}{c}(B - A),\quad B + \tfrac{b}{a}(B - C),$$



$$C + \tfrac{c}{a}(C - B),\quad C + \tfrac{c}{b}(C - A),\quad A + \tfrac{a}{b}(A - C).$$

Then there are a point $O$ and a real number $r$ such that all six points are at distance $r$
from $O$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conway_circle_theorem

articles.title: Erdős–Mordell inequality
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be affinely independent points of the Euclidean
plane and $P$ a point in the interior of the triangle $ABC$. Let $M$, $N$, $L$ be points on the
lines $BC$, $AB$, $CA$ such that $PM \perp BC$, $PN \perp AB$ and $PL \perp CA$. Then, writing
$XY$ for the distance between points $X$ and $Y$, we have $PA + PB + PC \ge 2(PM + PN + PL)$.

## Sources

- Paul Erdős, L. J. Mordell, and David F. Barrow, Problem 3740, American Mathematical Monthly 44 (1937), 252–254, https://doi.org/10.2307/2300713.

articles.title: Statement of the Erdős–Mordell inequality
articles.statement:
Writing $XY$ for the distance between points
$X$ and $Y$, this is the assertion that for all affinely independent points $A$, $B$, $C$ of the
Euclidean plane, every point $P$ in the interior of the triangle $ABC$, and all points $M$, $N$,
$L$ on the lines $BC$, $AB$, $CA$ such that the lines $PM$, $PN$, $PL$ are perpendicular to $BC$,
$AB$, $CA$ respectively, we have $PA + PB + PC \ge 2(PM + PN + PL)$.

articles.title: Euler's theorem on the circumcenter–incenter distance
articles.statement:
Let $P_0, P_1, P_2$ be affinely
independent points of the Euclidean plane, $d$ the Euclidean distance and $\langle x, y \rangle$
the inner product. Let $O$ be a point and $R \ge 0$ with $d(O, P_i) = R$ for each $i$, so that
$O$ is the circumcenter and $R$ the circumradius. Let $I = w_0 P_0 + w_1 P_1 + w_2 P_2$ with
$w_0, w_1, w_2 > 0$ and $w_0 + w_1 + w_2 = 1$, and let $r \ge 0$. Suppose there are points $F_0$
on the line $P_0 P_1$, $F_1$ on the line $P_1 P_2$ and $F_2$ on the line $P_2 P_0$ with
$d(I, F_k) = r$ for each $k$ and
$\langle F_0 - I, P_1 - P_0 \rangle = \langle F_1 - I, P_2 - P_1 \rangle =
\langle F_2 - I, P_0 - P_2 \rangle = 0$, so that $I$ is an interior point at distance $r$ from
all three side lines, that is, the incenter, and $r$ is the inradius. Then
$d(O, I)^2 = R(R - 2r)$ and $R \ge 2r$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_theorem_in_geometry

articles.title: Feuerbach's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a triangle in a two-dimensional Euclidean affine space,
with incircle $\omega$, nine-point circle $N$, and excircle $\omega_i$ opposite its $i$-th vertex
for each $i$. If $T$ is not equilateral, then there is a point $F$ at which $\omega$ is internally
tangent to $N$ (that is, $F$ lies on both circles and the center of $\omega$ lies on the segment
from the center of $N$ to $F$), and $F$ is the only common point of $\omega$ and $N$. For every
triangle $T$ and every $i$, the nine-point circle $N$ is externally tangent to $\omega_i$.

## Sources

- K. W. Feuerbach, 1822; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feuerbach_point

articles.title: Hinge theorem in inner product spaces
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a real inner product space and let
$A, B, C, D, E, F \in V$. If $\|B - A\| = \|E - D\|$, $\|C - A\| = \|F - D\|$ and
$\langle B - A, C - A \rangle < \langle E - D, F - D \rangle$, then $\|F - E\| < \|C - B\|$.

Proof: Expand both squared opposite sides by the law of cosines and compare them.

## Sources

- Euclid's *Elements*, Book I, Proposition 24.

articles.title: Hinge theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, C$ and $D, E, F$ be two triples of pairwise distinct points of
the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ forming nondegenerate triangles: $C - A$ is not a real
multiple of $B - A$, and $F - D$ is not a real multiple of $E - D$. Write $XY$ for the distance
between points $X$ and $Y$. If $AB = DE$, $AC = DF$ and
$\langle B - A, C - A \rangle < \langle E - D, F - D \rangle$, that is, the angle at $A$ is
larger than the angle at $D$, then $EF < BC$.

Proof: The vector law of cosines compares the squared opposite sides, following Euclid's
*Elements*, Book I, Proposition 24.

## Sources

- Euclid's Elements, Book I, Proposition 24 (https://mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/elements/bookI/propI24.html); see also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinge_theorem.

articles.title: Intercept theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, C, D, E$ be points of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$,
and write $XY$ for the distance between points $X$ and $Y$. Suppose that $C - A$ is not a real
multiple of $B - A$; that $AD + DB = AB$ with $AD > 0$ and $DB > 0$, so $D$ lies strictly
between $A$ and $B$; that $AE + EC = AC$ with $AE > 0$ and $EC > 0$, so $E$ lies strictly
between $A$ and $C$; and that $E - D = r(C - B)$ for some real $r \ne 0$, so $DE$ is parallel
to $BC$. Then $AD / DB = AE / EC$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercept_theorem.

articles.title: Marden's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, c$ be complex numbers such that $(b - a)/(c - a)$ has
nonzero imaginary part, so that they are the vertices of a nondegenerate triangle, and let
$p(z) = (z - a)(z - b)(z - c)$. Then there are complex numbers $f_1, f_2$ and a real number $L$
such that the roots of $p'$, counted with multiplicity, are exactly $f_1$ and $f_2$, and such
that the function $\sigma(z) = |z - f_1| + |z - f_2|$ satisfies
$\sigma((a + b)/2) = \sigma((b + c)/2) = \sigma((c + a)/2) = L$ and, for every real $t \ne 0$,
$\sigma((a + b)/2 + t(b - a)) > L$, $\sigma((b + c)/2 + t(c - b)) > L$ and
$\sigma((c + a)/2 + t(a - c)) > L$.

Thus the ellipse $\sigma(z) = L$ with foci $f_1$ and $f_2$ (a circle when $f_1 = f_2$) passes
through the midpoints of the three sides and touches each side line only at its midpoint: it is
the Steiner inellipse, and its foci are the roots of $p'$.

Proof: The statement is Marden's theorem (M. Marden, *Geometry of Polynomials*, 2nd ed.,
Math. Surveys No. 3, AMS, 1966; D. Kalman, *An Elementary Proof of Marden's Theorem*,
Amer. Math. Monthly 115(4) (2008), 330-338, <https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.2008.11920532>).
Following [Wikipedia, *Marden's theorem*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marden%27s_theorem),
we use Vieta's relations, the midpoint identity for the derivative, and the ellipse reflection
property expressed by a strict triangle inequality.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marden%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Menelaus's theorem, general form
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be points of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$ with $A \ne B$ and $C$ not on the line $AB$. Let $D$, $E$, $F$ be points and
let $\alpha, \alpha', \beta, \beta', \gamma, \gamma'$ be real numbers with
$F - A = \alpha (B - A)$, $B - F = \alpha' (B - A)$, $D - B = \beta (C - B)$,
$C - D = \beta' (C - B)$, $E - C = \gamma (A - C)$, $A - E = \gamma' (A - C)$, and
$\alpha', \beta', \gamma' \ne 0$. Then $F$ lies on the line through $D$ and $E$ if and only if
$\frac{\alpha}{\alpha'} \cdot \frac{\beta}{\beta'} \cdot \frac{\gamma}{\gamma'} = -1$.

The numbers $\alpha, \alpha', \beta, \beta', \gamma, \gamma'$ are the signed ratios $AF/AB$,
$FB/AB$, $BD/BC$, $DC/BC$, $CE/CA$, $EA/CA$, so the product is the classical signed ratio
product $\frac{AF}{FB} \cdot \frac{BD}{DC} \cdot \frac{CE}{EA}$.

articles.title: Menelaus's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be pairwise distinct points of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$ with $C$ not on the line $AB$. Let $D$, $E$, $F$ be points on the lines $BC$, $CA$
and $AB$ respectively, with $D \ne B$, $D \ne C$, $E \ne C$, $E \ne A$, $F \ne A$ and $F \ne B$.
Let $\alpha, \alpha', \beta, \beta', \gamma, \gamma'$ be real numbers with
$F - A = \alpha (B - A)$, $B - F = \alpha' (B - A)$, $D - B = \beta (C - B)$,
$C - D = \beta' (C - B)$, $E - C = \gamma (A - C)$, $A - E = \gamma' (A - C)$, and
$\alpha', \beta', \gamma' \ne 0$. Then $F$ lies on the line through $D$ and $E$ if and only if
$\frac{\alpha}{\alpha'} \cdot \frac{\beta}{\beta'} \cdot \frac{\gamma}{\gamma'} = -1$.

The numbers $\alpha, \alpha', \beta, \beta', \gamma, \gamma'$ are the signed ratios $AF/AB$,
$FB/AB$, $BD/BC$, $DC/BC$, $CE/CA$, $EA/CA$, so the product is the classical signed ratio
product $\frac{AF}{FB} \cdot \frac{BD}{DC} \cdot \frac{CE}{EA}$. The incidence hypotheses,
$B \ne C$, $A \ne C$ and the conditions that $D$, $E$, $F$ avoid the vertices follow from the
other hypotheses or are not needed; they keep the shape of the classical statement.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menelaus%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Equilateral triple of points
articles.statement:
Three points $P$, $Q$, $R$ of the Euclidean plane form an
equilateral triple when, writing $d$ for the Euclidean distance, $d(P, Q) = d(Q, R)$ and
$d(Q, R) = d(R, P)$. Coincident points are allowed, so $P = Q = R$ qualifies.

articles.title: Morley configuration
articles.statement:
Points $A$, $B$, $C$, $P$, $Q$, $R$ of the Euclidean plane form a
Morley configuration when $A$, $B$, $C$ are not collinear, each of $P$, $Q$, $R$ lies in the
closed triangle $ABC$, and, writing $\angle XYZ \in [0, \pi]$ for the unoriented angle at $Y$,
$0 < \angle CAR = \angle RAP = \angle PAB$ and $3 \angle PAB = \angle CAB$;
$0 < \angle ABP = \angle PBQ = \angle QBC$ and $3 \angle QBC = \angle ABC$;
$0 < \angle BCQ = \angle QCR = \angle RCA$ and $3 \angle RCA = \angle BCA$.
Thus $P$, $Q$, $R$ are the intersections of adjacent angle trisectors of the triangle $ABC$.

articles.title: Point in a closed triangle
articles.statement:
A point $X$ of the Euclidean plane lies in the triangle with
vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ when $X$ belongs to the convex hull of $\{A, B, C\}$, the closed triangle
$ABC$ (a segment or a point when $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear).

articles.title: Morley's trisector theorem
articles.statement:
If points $A$, $B$, $C$, $P$, $Q$, $R$ of the Euclidean plane
form a Morley configuration, so that $ABC$ is a nondegenerate triangle and $P$, $Q$, $R$ are the
intersections of its adjacent angle trisectors, then $P$, $Q$, $R$ form an equilateral triple:
writing $d$ for the Euclidean distance, $d(P, Q) = d(Q, R)$ and $d(Q, R) = d(R, P)$.

## Sources

- F. Morley (c. 1899). Knill, §162. Problem `morley_theorem` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Euclidean plane for Morley's theorem
articles.statement:
The Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with its
standard Euclidean distance.

articles.title: Napoleon's theorem, general form
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $A_2$, $B_2$, $C_2$ be points of the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $|BA_2| = |CA_2| = |BC|$, $|CB_2| = |AB_2| = |CA|$ and
$|AC_2| = |BC_2| = |AB|$, such that $A_2$ and $A$ lie strictly on opposite sides of the line
$BC$, $B_2$ and $B$ lie strictly on opposite sides of the line $CA$, and $C_2$ and $C$ lie
strictly on opposite sides of the line $AB$. Let $G_1 = \frac{1}{3}(B + C + A_2)$,
$G_2 = \frac{1}{3}(C + A + B_2)$ and $G_3 = \frac{1}{3}(A + B + C_2)$. Then
$|G_1G_2| = |G_2G_3| = |G_3G_1| > 0$.

Thus the centroids $G_1$, $G_2$, $G_3$ of the equilateral triangles erected outward on the sides
of $ABC$ form a nondegenerate equilateral triangle; the hypotheses force $A$, $B$, $C$ to be
non-collinear. Opposite sides are expressed by signed areas, for instance
$((C - B) \times (A - B)) \, ((C - B) \times (A_2 - B)) < 0$, where
$(x, y) \times (x', y') = x y' - y x'$.

articles.title: Napoleon's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be pairwise distinct, non-collinear points of the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, and let $A_2$, $B_2$, $C_2$ be points with
$|BA_2| = |CA_2| = |BC|$, $|CB_2| = |AB_2| = |CA|$ and $|AC_2| = |BC_2| = |AB|$, such that $A_2$
and $A$ lie strictly on opposite sides of the line $BC$, $B_2$ and $B$ lie strictly on opposite
sides of the line $CA$, and $C_2$ and $C$ lie strictly on opposite sides of the line $AB$. Let
$G_1 = \frac{1}{3}(B + C + A_2)$, $G_2 = \frac{1}{3}(C + A + B_2)$ and
$G_3 = \frac{1}{3}(A + B + C_2)$. Then $|G_1G_2| = |G_2G_3| = |G_3G_1|$.

That is, the centroids of the equilateral triangles erected outward on the sides of $ABC$ are
pairwise equidistant. Non-collinearity is stated as $(B - A) \times (C - A) \ne 0$ and opposite
sides by signed areas, for instance $((C - B) \times (A - B)) \, ((C - B) \times (A_2 - B)) < 0$,
where $(x, y) \times (x', y') = x y' - y x'$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon%27s_theorem (statement id `napoleon-s1`; raw: "Outer equilateral-triangle centers on any triangle form an equilateral triangle."). It follows from `napoleon_theorem_general`, which also shows the common distance is positive; the hypotheses `A ≠ B`, `B ≠ C`, `C ≠ A` and nondegeneracy are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Pompeiu's theorem
articles.statement:
Write $XY$ for the Euclidean distance between points $X$ and $Y$ of the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be points of the plane with $AB = BC = CA$ and
$AB > 0$, so that $ABC$ is an equilateral triangle, and let $P$ be any point of the plane. Then
$PA \le PB + PC$, $PB \le PC + PA$ and $PC \le PA + PB$; that is, $PA$, $PB$, $PC$ are the side
lengths of a (possibly degenerate) triangle.

articles.title: Pompeiu's theorem for a point other than a vertex
articles.statement:
Write $XY$ for the Euclidean distance
between points $X$ and $Y$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be points of
the plane with $AB = BC = CA$ and $AB > 0$, so that $ABC$ is an equilateral triangle, and let $P$
be a point of the plane with $P \ne A$, $P \ne B$ and $P \ne C$. Then $PA \le PB + PC$,
$PB \le PC + PA$ and $PC \le PA + PB$; that is, $PA$, $PB$, $PC$ are the side lengths of a
(possibly degenerate) triangle.

The hypothesis that $P$ is not a vertex is not needed: the conclusion holds for every point $P$
of the plane.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeiu%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Routh's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, C$ be points of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose
triangle (the convex hull of $\{A, B, C\}$) has nonzero area, and let $x, y, z$ be positive
reals with $xyz \ne 1$. Let $D = \frac{x}{x+1} B + \frac{1}{x+1} C$,
$E = \frac{1}{y+1} A + \frac{y}{y+1} C$ and $F = \frac{z}{z+1} A + \frac{1}{z+1} B$, the
points of the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ with $DC/DB = x$, $EA/EC = y$ and $FB/FA = z$. If $P$
lies on the segments $BE$ and $CF$, $Q$ lies on the segments $CF$ and $AD$, and $R$ lies on
the segments $AD$ and $BE$, then the area of the triangle $PQR$ (the convex hull of
$\{P, Q, R\}$) is

$$\frac{(xyz - 1)^2}{(xy + y + 1)(yz + z + 1)(zx + x + 1)}$$

times the area of $ABC$. Areas are Lebesgue measures.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Routh%27s_theorem

articles.title: Van Schooten's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $P$ and $O$ be points of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $r > 0$. Suppose that $AB = BC = CA$, that $A$, $B$, $C$ and $P$ lie
on the circle of radius $r$ about $O$, and that $CP > AP$ and $CP > BP$. Then
$PA + PB = PC$.

No hypothesis that $P$ differs from $A$, $B$ or $C$ is needed.

articles.title: Van Schooten's theorem with distinctness hypotheses
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $P$ and $O$ be
points of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $r > 0$. Suppose that $AB = BC = CA$,
that $A$, $B$, $C$ and $P$ lie on the circle of radius $r$ about $O$, that $P \ne A$,
$P \ne B$ and $P \ne C$, and that $CP > AP$ and $CP > BP$. Then $PA + PB = PC$.

In the source, $P$ is a point on the arc $AB$ of the circumcircle not containing $C$; here that
condition is expressed by $CP > AP$ and $CP > BP$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Schooten%27s_theorem. It follows from `vanSchooten_general`; the hypotheses `P ≠ A`, `P ≠ B` and `P ≠ C` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Viviani's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be points of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with
$AB = BC = CA$, and let $P$ be a point of the interior of the convex hull of
$\lbrace A, B, C \rbrace$. Then the sum of the distances from $P$ to the lines $AB$, $BC$ and
$CA$ equals the distance from $A$ to the line $BC$, the altitude of the triangle.

No positivity hypothesis on the side length is needed: since $P$ is an interior point, the
points $A$, $B$, $C$ are affinely independent, so the triangle is nondegenerate.

Proof: Following the barycentric-coordinate area decomposition in Wikipedia, "Viviani's theorem"
(Proof section), we express the three distances as barycentric weights times a common height.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viviani%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Viviani's theorem with a positive side length
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be points of the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $AB = BC = CA$ and $AB > 0$, and let $P$ be a point of the
interior of the convex hull of $\lbrace A, B, C \rbrace$. Then the sum of the distances from
$P$ to the lines $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ equals the distance from $A$ to the line $BC$, the
altitude of the triangle.

The hypothesis $AB > 0$ is not needed: Viviani's theorem gives the same conclusion without it.

articles.title: Negative answer to the cocompact asymptotic-metrics question
articles.statement:
The conjecture is false: there
exist a group $\Gamma$, a complete metric space $(M, d_1)$ on which $\Gamma$ acts, and a cocompact
asymptotically equivalent length-space pair on $M$ with second metric $d_2$, such that for every
real number $C$ there are points $x, y \in M$ with $|d_1(x, y) - d_2(x, y)| > C$.

Counterexample of Le Donne, Nalon, Nicolussi Golo and Ryoo (arXiv:2503.00560, 2025), Example 4.2:
on the Engel group, a left-invariant Riemannian metric and its canonical asymptotic
sub-Riemannian metric are complete, left-invariant (transitive, hence cocompact), asymptotic,
yet their difference is unbounded.

## Sources

- E. Le Donne, L. Nalon, S. Nicolussi Golo, S.-Y. Ryoo, Asymptotics of Riemannian Lie groups with nilpotency step 2, arXiv preprint (2025), arXiv:2503.00560, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00560.

articles.title: Bounded-difference conjecture for cocompact asymptotically equivalent metrics
articles.statement:
The statement
that for every group $\Gamma$, every complete metric space $(M, d_1)$ on which $\Gamma$ acts, and
every cocompact asymptotically equivalent length-space pair on $M$ with second metric $d_2$, there
is a real number $C$ such that $|d_1(x, y) - d_2(x, y)| \le C$ for all $x, y \in M$.

## Sources

- open question of [OWR-1319-022] (Geometric Group Theory, Hyperbolic Dynamics and Symplectic Geometry (2007), Oberwolfach Reports, DOI 10.4171/owr/2006/33, pp. 1991--2058).

articles.title: Cocompact asymptotically equivalent length-space pair
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a group acting on a
complete metric space $(M, d_1)$. A cocompact asymptotically equivalent length-space pair on $M$
is a function $d_2 \colon M \times M \to \mathbb{R}$ with the following properties. It is a
metric: $d_2(x, y) \ge 0$, $d_2(x, y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$, $d_2(x, y) = d_2(y, x)$ and
$d_2(x, z) \le d_2(x, y) + d_2(y, z)$. It is complete: every sequence that is Cauchy for $d_2$
converges for $d_2$ to some point of $M$. Both $d_1$ and $d_2$ have approximate midpoints: for
$i = 1, 2$, all $x, y \in M$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $z \in M$ with
$\max(d_i(x, z), d_i(z, y)) \le d_i(x, y)/2 + \varepsilon$. The action is by isometries of both:
$d_i(g x, g y) = d_i(x, y)$ for all $g \in \Gamma$, $x, y \in M$ and $i = 1, 2$. The action is
cocompact: some compact set $K \subseteq M$ (compact for $d_1$) contains a point $g x$ of the orbit
of every $x \in M$. The two metrics induce the same topology: for every $x \in M$ and every
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $d_2(x, y) < \varepsilon$ whenever
$d_1(x, y) < \delta$, and there is $\delta > 0$ with $d_1(x, y) < \varepsilon$ whenever
$d_2(x, y) < \delta$. Finally, $d_1$ and $d_2$ are asymptotically equivalent: for every
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real number $R$ such that
$|d_1(x, y) / d_2(x, y) - 1| < \varepsilon$ for all $x, y \in M$ with $d_1(x, y) \ge R$.

For complete metric spaces the approximate-midpoint property is equivalent to being a length
space.

articles.title: Isometry invariance of the CAT(0) four-point condition
articles.statement:
If $X$ and $Y$ are metric spaces
and there is an isometric bijection from $X$ onto $Y$, then $X$ satisfies the CAT(0) four-point
condition if and only if $Y$ does.

articles.title: Unfolding the CAT(0) four-point condition
articles.statement:
A metric space $X$ satisfies the CAT(0)
four-point condition if and only if for all points $x, y, z, w \in X$,

$$d(x, z)^2 + d(y, w)^2 \le d(x, y)^2 + d(y, z)^2 + d(z, w)^2 + d(w, x)^2.$$

articles.title: CAT(0) four-point condition
articles.statement:
A metric space $X$ satisfies the CAT(0) four-point
comparison condition if for all points $x, y, z, w \in X$ (not necessarily distinct),

$$d(x, z)^2 + d(y, w)^2 \le d(x, y)^2 + d(y, z)^2 + d(z, w)^2 + d(w, x)^2,$$

that is, the sum of the squares of the diagonals of every quadrilateral $xyzw$ is at most the
sum of the squares of its sides.

For geodesic metric spaces this is equivalent to the usual Euclidean comparison-triangle
definition of a CAT(0) space.

articles.title: The CAT(0) four-point condition passes to isometrically embedded spaces
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$
be metric spaces and let $f : X \to Y$ be an isometry, that is, $d(f(a), f(b)) = d(a, b)$ for
all $a, b \in X$. If $Y$ satisfies the CAT(0) four-point condition, then so does $X$.

articles.title: Spaces with at most one point satisfy the CAT(0) four-point condition
articles.statement:
Every metric
space with at most one point (including the empty space) satisfies the CAT(0) four-point
condition.

articles.title: Closed geodesic
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a pseudo-extended metric space. A curve
$\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to X$ is a closed geodesic if it is a geodesic defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$,
it is periodic with some period $T > 0$ (that is, $\gamma(t + T) = \gamma(t)$ for all
$t \in \mathbb{R}$), and it is not constant: $\gamma(t_1) \ne \gamma(t_2)$ for some
$t_1, t_2 \in \mathbb{R}$.

Periodicity of a geodesic defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$ encodes both $\gamma(0) = \gamma(T)$ and
the matching of the velocities at $0$ and $T$. For a closed geodesic of speed $1$, every period
$T > 0$ is the length of $\gamma$ traversed over one period; its smallest positive period is the
length of the underlying prime closed geodesic.

articles.title: Constant curves are geodesics
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a pseudo-extended metric space. For every point
$p \in X$, the constant curve $\mathbb{R} \to X$, $t \mapsto p$, is a geodesic.

Its speed is $0$.

articles.title: Straight lines are geodesics
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a real normed space. For all $p, v \in F$, the
straight line $\mathbb{R} \to F$, $t \mapsto p + t v$, is a geodesic.

articles.title: Straight lines are geodesics of constant speed
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a real normed space and
$p, v \in F$. For every set of times $s \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, the straight line
$t \mapsto p + t v$ is a geodesic of speed $\|v\|$ on $s$.

articles.title: Geodesics of a given speed on a set of times
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a pseudo-extended metric space
with extended distance $d$, let $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to X$ be a curve, $s \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ a
set of times and $c \ge 0$ a real number. The curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic of speed $c$ on $s$ if
every $t \in s$ has some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $d(\gamma(t_1), \gamma(t_2)) = c\,|t_1 - t_2|$
for all $t_1, t_2 \in s$ with $|t_1 - t| < \varepsilon$ and $|t_2 - t| < \varepsilon$.

articles.title: Geodesic on a set of times
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a pseudo-extended metric space. A curve
$\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to X$ is a geodesic on a set of times $s \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ if, for some
real number $c \ge 0$, it is a geodesic of speed $c$ on $s$.

On a Riemannian manifold without boundary, with its Riemannian distance, every Riemannian geodesic
is a geodesic in this sense, and the piecewise $C^1$ geodesics in this sense are the Riemannian
geodesics.

articles.title: Geodesics defined for all times
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a pseudo-extended metric space. A curve
$\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to X$ is a geodesic if it is a geodesic on the set of all times
$\mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Closed geodesics are not constant
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a pseudo-extended metric space. If
$\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to X$ is a closed geodesic, then for every $p \in X$, $\gamma$ is not the
constant curve $t \mapsto p$.

articles.title: Constant curves are not closed geodesics
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a pseudo-extended metric space. For
every point $p \in X$, the constant curve $\mathbb{R} \to X$, $t \mapsto p$, is not a closed
geodesic.

articles.title: Four-point inequality of a $\delta$-hyperbolic space
articles.statement: The defining four-point inequality of a `δ`-hyperbolic space.

articles.title: A space with at most one point is $0$-hyperbolic
articles.statement:
Every pseudometric space $X$ with at
most one point is $0$-hyperbolic.

articles.title: Gromov $\delta$-hyperbolic space
articles.statement:
A pseudometric space `X` is `δ`-hyperbolic (in the sense of Gromov) if `0 ≤ δ` and the
Gromov product satisfies the four-point inequality
`(x ∣ z)_w ≥ min (x ∣ y)_w (y ∣ z)_w - δ` for all points `w x y z`, where
`(x ∣ y)_w = Metric.gromovProduct w x y` (basepoint first, as in Mathlib).

articles.title: Gromov-hyperbolic spaces
articles.statement:
A pseudometric space $X$ is Gromov-hyperbolic if there is a
real number $\delta$ such that $X$ is $\delta$-hyperbolic.

articles.title: Hyperbolicity is monotone in the constant
articles.statement:
If a pseudometric space $X$ is
$\delta$-hyperbolic and $\delta \le \delta'$, then $X$ is $\delta'$-hyperbolic.

articles.title: The hyperbolicity constant is nonnegative
articles.statement:
If a pseudometric space $X$ is
$\delta$-hyperbolic, then $\delta \ge 0$.

articles.title: Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma
articles.statement:
There is a constant $C > 0$ with the following property. Let
$\varepsilon > 0$, let $m$ and $N \ge 2$ be natural numbers, let $X$ be a set of exactly $N$
points of $\mathbb{R}^m$ with the Euclidean norm, and let $d$ be a natural number with
$d > C \varepsilon^{-2} \log N$. Then there is a map $f : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^d$ such
that $(1 - \varepsilon) \|x - y\| \le \|f(x) - f(y)\| \le (1 + \varepsilon) \|x - y\|$ for all
$x, y \in X$, where $\mathbb{R}^d$ also carries the Euclidean norm.

The map $f$ is not required to be linear, and $\varepsilon \ge 1$ is allowed (there the zero
map works). The proof takes $C = 64$ and uses a Gaussian random projection with a union bound
over pairs of points.

## Sources

- W. B. Johnson and J. Lindenstrauss, "Extensions of Lipschitz mappings into a Hilbert space," Contemporary Mathematics 26, Conference on Modern Analysis and Probability, American Mathematical Society (1984), 189--206, DOI 10.1090/conm/026/737400. ATLAS source-to-API map, item N147; ATLAS adds the hypothesis that N is at least 2.

articles.title: Microscopic weighting is not equivalent to finite concentration
articles.statement:
It is not true that every
nonempty finite metric space $X$ has a microscopic weighting if and only if it has finite
concentration. Here, for real $t$, $Z_t$ is the $X \times X$ matrix with entries
$e^{-t\,d(x,y)}$ and $w_t = Z_t^{-1}\mathbf{1}$ is its weighting, where $\mathbf{1}$ is the
all-ones vector and the inverse of a singular matrix is taken to be $0$. The space $X$ has a
microscopic weighting if $w_t$ converges to some $w \colon X \to \mathbb{R}$ as $t \to 0^+$. It
has finite concentration if there are $g \colon X \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\sum_{x \in X} g(x) = 1$
and $c \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\sum_{y \in X} d(x,y)\,g(y) = c$ for every $x \in X$.

Kenta Kitamura (assisted by ChatGPT) gave an explicit 10-point metric space with finite
concentration but no microscopic weighting.

## Sources

- Kenta Kitamura, microscopic-weighting-counterexample, Lean formalization of the 10-point counterexample, https://github.com/KitaKen1/microscopic-weighting-counterexample/blob/eff8979/lean/MicroscopicWeightingCounterexampleFC.lean#L886-L894.

articles.title: No compact set is congruent to a proper subset of itself
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a compact subset of
a metric space $X$. Then there is no map $f : X \to X$ with $d(f(x), f(y)) = d(x, y)$ for all
$x, y \in X$ such that $f(K) \subseteq K$ and $f(K) \neq K$.

The underlying fact is that an isometric embedding of a compact metric space into itself is
surjective.

## Sources

- S. Banach and S. Ulam, Problem 3 of the Scottish Book, stated and proved in the Scottish Book typescript.

articles.title: Constant sequences converge in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff sense
articles.statement:
For every
pseudometric space $Y$ and every point $q \in Y$, the constant sequence $(X_n, p_n) = (Y, q)$
converges to $(Y, q)$ in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff sense.

articles.title: Pointed Gromov–Hausdorff convergence with strict distortion
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ and
$Y$ be pseudometric spaces with base points $p_n \in X_n$ and $q \in Y$. Then $(X_n, p_n)$
converges to $(Y, q)$ in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff sense if and only if for all $R > 0$ and
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ there are a map $f$ from the open
ball $B(p_n, R)$ to $Y$ and a real number $\delta < \varepsilon$ with $f(p_n) = q$, with
$|d(f(x), f(y)) - d(x, y)| \le \delta$ for all $x, y \in B(p_n, R)$, and such that every point
of the open ball $B(q, R - \varepsilon)$ is at distance less than $\varepsilon$ from some point
of the image of $f$.

That is, the distortion of $f$ may be required to be strictly less than $\varepsilon$, as in
arXiv:2602.04826, Def. 2.12.

articles.title: Pointed Gromov–Hausdorff convergence with measurable maps
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be
separable pseudometric spaces, each with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra, with base points
$p_n \in X_n$, and let $Y$ be a pseudometric space with any $\sigma$-algebra and a base point
$q \in Y$. Then $(X_n, p_n)$ converges to $(Y, q)$ in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff sense if and
only if for all $R > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ there is
a map $f$ from the open ball $B(p_n, R)$ to $Y$, measurable for the subspace $\sigma$-algebra on
the ball, with $f(p_n) = q$, with $|d(f(x), f(y)) - d(x, y)| \le \varepsilon$ for all
$x, y \in B(p_n, R)$, and such that every point of the open ball $B(q, R - \varepsilon)$ is at
distance less than $\varepsilon$ from some point of the image of $f$.

So for separable spaces the approximating maps can be taken Borel, as Gigli–Mondino–Savaré
require.

articles.title: Pointed Gromov–Hausdorff convergence
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ and $Y$ be pseudometric
spaces with base points $p_n \in X_n$ and $q \in Y$. The sequence $(X_n, p_n)$ converges to
$(Y, q)$ in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff sense if for all $R > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ there is
$N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ there is a map $f$ from the open ball $B(p_n, R)$ to $Y$ with
$f(p_n) = q$, with $|d(f(x), f(y)) - d(x, y)| \le \varepsilon$ for all $x, y \in B(p_n, R)$, and
such that every point of the open ball $B(q, R - \varepsilon)$ is at distance less than
$\varepsilon$ from some point of the image of $f$.

No measurability or continuity is required of $f$, and the spaces need not be complete or
separable, so this extends the metric part of the pointed measured Gromov–Hausdorff convergence
of Gigli–Mondino–Savaré, who use Borel maps on complete separable spaces. Open balls are an
implementation choice for their unspecified balls $B_R$.

articles.title: Circle covering theorem (Erdős Problem 1121)
articles.statement:
Both parts of Erdős Problem 1121 hold. For
every natural number $d$, and in particular in the plane ($d = 2$): if $B(c_1, r_1), \dots,
B(c_n, r_n)$ are closed balls in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ with centres $c_i$ and radii
$r_i > 0$ such that every hyperplane meeting none of the balls has all the centres $c_i$
strictly on the same side, then some closed ball of radius $r_1 + \dots + r_n$ contains all of
the balls.

Goodman and Goodman [GoGo45] proved this in the plane and in higher dimensions; Hadwiger [Ha47]
extended it to convex bodies.

## Sources

- Goodman and Goodman [GoGo45] (planar case and higher dimensions), per erdosproblems.com/1121, https://www.erdosproblems.com/1121.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 1121 (circle covering)
articles.statement:
Write $B(c, r)$ for the closed ball with centre
$c$ and radius $r$ in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$. Call balls $B(c_1, r_1), \dots,
B(c_n, r_n)$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ *nonseparable* if for every nonzero vector $v$ and every real
$t$ such that no point $p$ of any of the balls satisfies $\langle v, p \rangle = t$, either
$\langle v, c_i \rangle < t$ for all $i$ or $\langle v, c_i \rangle > t$ for all $i$. The
statement is the conjunction of two parts. First, for every natural number $n$, all points
$c_1, \dots, c_n \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and all reals $r_1, \dots, r_n > 0$ such that the discs
$B(c_i, r_i)$ are nonseparable, there is a point $z$ such that the closed disc
$B(z, r_1 + \dots + r_n)$ contains every $B(c_i, r_i)$. Second, the same holds in
$\mathbb{R}^d$ for every natural number $d$, with closed balls in place of discs.

articles.title: Covering the cube by translates of its interior needs $2^n$ translates
articles.statement:
Let
$C_n = [-1, 1]^n$ be the coordinate cube in $\mathbb{R}^n$. If $C_n$ is contained in the union of
$q$ translates $v_1 + \operatorname{int} C_n, \dots, v_q + \operatorname{int} C_n$ of its interior,
then $2^n \le q$.

articles.title: The coordinate cube as an absolute-value box
articles.statement:
For every $n$, the coordinate cube in
$\mathbb{R}^n$ equals the set of points $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $|x_i| \le 1$ for every
coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Interior of the coordinate cube
articles.statement:
A point $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ lies in the interior of
the coordinate cube $[-1, 1]^n$ if and only if $-1 < x_i < 1$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: The coordinate cube is centrally symmetric
articles.statement:
For every $n$, the coordinate cube
$[-1, 1]^n$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is centrally symmetric: there is a point $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such
that for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $x$ lies in the cube if and only if $2c - x$ does.

articles.title: The coordinate cube is a convex body
articles.statement:
For every $n$, the coordinate cube $[-1, 1]^n$ in
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is a convex body: it is compact and convex, and its interior in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is
nonempty.

articles.title: Eight translates of the interior cover the three-dimensional cube
articles.statement:
Let
$C_3 = [-1, 1]^3$ be the coordinate cube in $\mathbb{R}^3$. There are vectors
$v_1, \dots, v_8 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $C_3$ is contained in the union of the translates
$v_1 + \operatorname{int} C_3, \dots, v_8 + \operatorname{int} C_3$ of its interior.

articles.title: Eight is the least number of interior translates covering the three-dimensional cube
articles.statement:
Let $C_3 = [-1, 1]^3$ be the coordinate cube in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Then $8$ is the least natural
number $q$ such that $C_3$ is contained in the union of $q$ translates of its interior
$\operatorname{int} C_3$.

articles.title: Translate covering number of the three-dimensional cube by its interior
articles.statement:
Let
$C_3 = [-1, 1]^3$ be the coordinate cube in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The translate covering number of $C_3$
by its interior $\operatorname{int} C_3$, the least number of translates of $\operatorname{int} C_3$
whose union contains $C_3$, equals $8$.

articles.title: Coordinate cube
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the coordinate cube is the set $[-1, 1]^n$ of
points $x$ of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $-1 \le x_i \le 1$ for every coordinate
$i$.

articles.title: Interior-translate covers unfold to translate covers
articles.statement:
For every set $K$ in the Euclidean
space $\mathbb{R}^n$ and every natural number $q$, $K$ has a cover by $q$ interior translates if
and only if $K$ is covered by $q$ translates of the set $L = \operatorname{int} K$, the interior
of $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: Covering by interior translates
articles.statement:
A set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered
by $q$ interior translates, for a natural number $q$, when there are vectors
$v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that
$K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{q} (v_i + \operatorname{int} K)$, where $\operatorname{int} K$ is the
interior of $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $v + S = \{v + y : y \in S\}$.

articles.title: Covering by smaller positive homothets
articles.statement:
A set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is
covered by $q$ smaller positive homothets, for a natural number $q$, when there are real numbers
$r_1, \dots, r_q$ with $0 < r_i < 1$ for every $i$ and vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$
such that every point of $K$ lies in $v_i + r_i K = \{v_i + r_i y : y \in K\}$ for some $i$.

The homothets are indexed by $i$, so the same homothet may occur more than once.

articles.title: Pointwise form of covering by translates
articles.statement:
For sets $K$ and $L$ in the Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and a natural number $q$, $K$ is covered by $q$ translates of $L$ if and only if
there are vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that every $x \in K$ lies in
$v_i + L = \{v_i + y : y \in L\}$ for some $i$.

articles.title: Covering by translates
articles.statement:
For sets $K$ and $L$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ and a
natural number $q$, $K$ is covered by $q$ translates of $L$ when there are vectors
$v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{q} (v_i + L)$, where
$v + L = \{v + y : y \in L\}$.

articles.title: Uniform interior-translate bounds in dimension three are at least eight
articles.statement:
If $q$ is a
natural number such that every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is contained in the union of
$q$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$, then $8 \le q$.

articles.title: Illumination by a direction
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a set and let
$v, x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The direction $v$ illuminates $x$ with respect to $K$ when $x$ lies on
the boundary of $K$, $\|v\| = 1$, and $x + tv$ lies in the interior of $K$ for some real
$t > 0$.

articles.title: Directional and exterior-point illumination are equivalent
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, let
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex body and let $q$ be a natural number. Then some $q$ unit
vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q$ illuminate $K$ if and only if some $q$ points $p_1, \dots, p_q$ outside
$K$ illuminate $K$. Here the vectors illuminate $K$ when every boundary point $x$ of $K$ has an $i$
and a $t > 0$ with $x + t v_i$ in the interior of $K$, and the points illuminate $K$ when every
boundary point $x$ of $K$ has an $i$ and a $t > 1$ with $p_i + t (x - p_i)$ in the interior of $K$.

## Sources

- Bezdek and Khan, arXiv:1602.06040v2, introduction.

articles.title: Directional and exterior-point illumination numbers are equal
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$ and
every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, the directional illumination number of $K$ equals
its exterior-point illumination number. These are the least $q$ such that some $q$ unit vectors,
respectively some $q$ points outside $K$, illuminate $K$, with the value $\infty$ when no finite
family does.

## Sources

- Bezdek and Khan, arXiv:1602.06040v2, introduction; follows from its finite-count equivalence, whose Lean proof is also requested here.

articles.title: Directional illumination is equivalent to covering by smaller homothets
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$,
let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex body and let $q$ be a natural number. Then some $q$
unit vectors illuminate $K$ if and only if $K$ is covered by $q$ homothets
$v_1 + r_1 K, \dots, v_q + r_q K$ with $v_i \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0 < r_i < 1$, repetitions
allowed.

## Sources

- Bezdek and Khan, arXiv:1602.06040v2, introduction.

articles.title: Directional illumination number
articles.statement:
The directional illumination number of a set
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is the least natural number $q$ such that $K$ is illuminated by $q$
directions, and $\infty$ if there is no such $q$.

articles.title: Directional illumination number equals the interior-translate covering number
articles.statement:
For every
$n \ge 1$ and every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, the directional illumination number of
$K$ equals the least $q$ such that $K$ is covered by $q$ translates of its interior
$\operatorname{int} K$. Both sides take the value $\infty$ when no finite family exists.

## Sources

- Arman, Kaire and Prymak, arXiv:2510.25968v3, introduction; follows from the finite-count equivalence, whose Lean proof is also requested here.

articles.title: Directional illumination is equivalent to covering by interior translates
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$,
let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex body and let $q$ be a natural number. Then some $q$ unit
vectors illuminate $K$ if and only if $K$ is covered by $q$ translates
$v_1 + \operatorname{int} K, \dots, v_q + \operatorname{int} K$ of its interior, repetitions
allowed.

## Sources

- Arman, Kaire and Prymak, arXiv:2510.25968v3, introduction.

articles.title: Illumination by an external point
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a set and let
$p, x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The point $p$ illuminates $x$ with respect to $K$ when $p \notin K$, $x$
lies on the boundary of $K$, and $p + t(x - p)$ lies in the interior of $K$ for some real $t > 1$;
that is, the ray from $p$ through $x$ meets the interior of $K$ at a point beyond $x$.

articles.title: External-point illumination number
articles.statement:
The external-point illumination number of a set
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is the least natural number $q$ such that $K$ is illuminated by $q$
external points, and $\infty$ if there is no such $q$.

articles.title: A least uniform bound is the Hadwiger covering number
articles.statement:
If $q$ is the least natural number
such that every convex body $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $q$ translates
of its interior, then the Hadwiger covering number of dimension $n$ equals $q$.

articles.title: Hadwiger covering number
articles.statement:
The Hadwiger covering number of dimension $n$, an element of
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, is the least natural number $q$ such that every convex body $K$ in
the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $q$ translates of its interior
$\operatorname{int} K$, and it is $\infty$ if no such $q$ exists.

articles.title: Two equivalent formulations of Hadwiger's covering conjecture
articles.statement:
The following statements
are equivalent: for every $n \ge 1$, every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by at
most $2^n$ homothets $v_i + r_i K$ with $v_i \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0 < r_i < 1$; and for every
$n \ge 1$, every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $2^n$ translates of its
interior $\operatorname{int} K$, repetitions allowed.

## Sources

- Bezdek and Khan, arXiv:1602.06040v2, introduction; Arman, Kaire and Prymak, arXiv:2510.25968v3, introduction.

articles.title: Illumination by $q$ directions
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is illuminated by $q$
directions, for a natural number $q$, if there are unit vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$
(not necessarily distinct) such that for every boundary point $x$ of $K$ there are an index $i$
and a real $t > 0$ with $x + tv_i$ in the interior of $K$.

articles.title: Illumination by $q$ external points
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is illuminated by $q$
external points, for a natural number $q$, if there are points
$p_1, \dots, p_q \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus K$ (not necessarily distinct) such that for every
boundary point $x$ of $K$ there are an index $i$ and a real $t > 1$ with $p_i + t(x - p_i)$ in the
interior of $K$.

articles.title: Every convex body has a finite illumination number
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$ and every convex
body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ there is a least natural number $q$ such that some $q$ unit vectors
$v_1, \dots, v_q$ illuminate $K$: every boundary point $x$ of $K$ has an $i$ and a $t > 0$ with
$x + t v_i$ in the interior of $K$.

## Sources

- Arman, Kaire and Prymak, arXiv:2510.25968v3, introduction's illumination-number definition; finite existence is the standard compact-convex-body qualification.

articles.title: Affine cube
articles.statement:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an affine cube if $K = e([-1, 1]^n)$ for
some affine bijection $e : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$, where $[-1, 1]^n$ is the coordinate cube
$\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : -1 \le x_i \le 1 \text{ for all } i\}$.

articles.title: Central symmetry about some center
articles.statement:
A set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is
centrally symmetric when there is a point $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that for every
$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $x \in K$ if and only if $2c - x \in K$.

articles.title: Convex bodies in Euclidean space
articles.statement:
A set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a
convex body when it is compact and convex and its interior in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is nonempty.

articles.title: Lassak's theorem for centrally symmetric bodies in dimension 3
articles.statement:
The number $8$ is the least
natural number $q$ such that every centrally symmetric convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is
covered by $q$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$, repetitions allowed. Here $K$ is
centrally symmetric when there is a point $c$ with $x \in K$ if and only if $2c - x \in K$.

## Sources

- Lassak (1984), reported in Arman, Bondarenko and Prymak, arXiv:2404.00547v1, introduction.

articles.title: Papadoperakis's bound for Hadwiger's covering problem in dimension 3
articles.statement:
Every convex body
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is covered by $16$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$,
repetitions allowed.

## Sources

- Papadoperakis (1999), reported in Arman, Bondarenko and Prymak, arXiv:2404.00547v1, introduction.

articles.title: Prymak's bound for Hadwiger's covering problem in dimension 3
articles.statement:
Every convex body
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is covered by $14$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$,
repetitions allowed.

## Sources

- Prymak (2023), arXiv:2112.10698; reported in Arman, Bondarenko and Prymak, arXiv:2404.00547v1, introduction.

articles.title: A least uniform bound is the symmetric Hadwiger covering number
articles.statement:
If $q$ is the least
natural number such that every centrally symmetric convex body $K$ in the Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $q$ translates of its interior, then the symmetric Hadwiger
covering number of dimension $n$ equals $q$.

articles.title: Symmetric Hadwiger covering number
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the symmetric Hadwiger
covering number in dimension $n$ is the least natural number $q$ such that every centrally
symmetric convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact convex set with nonempty interior that
is symmetric about some point) is covered by $q$ translates of its interior, and it is $\infty$
if no such $q$ exists.

articles.title: Lower bound $2^n$ for centrally symmetric interior-translate covering
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $q$ be
natural numbers. If every centrally symmetric convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact
convex set with nonempty interior that is symmetric about some point) can be covered by $q$ not
necessarily distinct translates of its interior, then $2^n \le q$.

The coordinate cube $[-1, 1]^n$ is such a body and already needs $2^n$ translates.

articles.title: The translate covering number is the least covering count
articles.statement:
Let $K, L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
and let $q \in \mathbb{N}$. If $q$ is the least natural number $r$ such that $K$ is covered by $r$
translates of $L$, then the translate covering number of $K$ by $L$ equals $q$.

articles.title: Translate covering number
articles.statement:
For sets $K, L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, the translate covering
number of $K$ by $L$ is the least natural number $q$ for which there are vectors
$v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $K \subseteq (v_1 + L) \cup \dots \cup (v_q + L)$, and it
is $\infty$ if no such $q$ exists.

articles.title: Uniform covering by interior translates and uniform directional illumination
articles.statement:
For
integers $n \ge 1$ and $q \ge 0$, every convex body in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact convex set with
nonempty interior) can be covered by $q$ translates of its interior if and only if every convex
body $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is illuminated by $q$ directions: there are unit vectors
$v_1, \dots, v_q$ such that each boundary point $x$ of $K$ has some $i$ and some $t > 0$ with
$x + t v_i$ in the interior of $K$.

## Sources

- Arman, Kaire and Prymak, arXiv:2510.25968v3, introduction; follows from the finite-count equivalence, whose Lean proof is also requested here.

articles.title: Lower bound $2^n$ for uniform interior-translate covering
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $q$ be natural
numbers. If every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact convex set with nonempty
interior) can be covered by $q$ not necessarily distinct translates of its interior, then
$2^n \le q$.

The coordinate cube $[-1, 1]^n$ already needs $2^n$ translates.

articles.title: Uniform bound for covering convex bodies by interior translates
articles.statement:
For $n, q \in \mathbb{N}$,
the uniform interior translate bound holds when every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a
compact convex set with nonempty interior) is covered by $q$ translates of its interior
$\operatorname{int} K$, that is, $K \subseteq (v_1 + \operatorname{int} K) \cup \dots \cup
(v_q + \operatorname{int} K)$ for some $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

This is one bound $q$ for all bodies at once, not a minimum over bodies.

articles.title: Uniform covering of symmetric bodies and uniform illumination by external points
articles.statement:
For
integers $n \ge 1$ and $q \ge 0$, every centrally symmetric convex body in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (a
compact convex set with nonempty interior that is symmetric about some point) can be covered by
$q$ translates of its interior if and only if every centrally symmetric convex body $K$ in
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is illuminated by $q$ external points: there are points $p_1, \dots, p_q$ outside
$K$ such that each boundary point $x$ of $K$ has some $i$ and some $t > 1$ with
$p_i + t(x - p_i)$ in the interior of $K$.

## Sources

- Arman, Kaire and Prymak, arXiv:2510.25968v3, introduction, and Bezdek and Khan, arXiv:1602.06040v2, introduction; follows from the two finite-count equivalences.

articles.title: Uniform bound for covering centrally symmetric convex bodies by interior translates
articles.statement:
For
$n, q \in \mathbb{N}$, the uniform symmetric interior translate bound holds when every convex body
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact convex set with nonempty interior) that is centrally
symmetric, meaning that there is $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$,
$x \in K$ if and only if $2c - x \in K$, is covered by $q$ translates of its interior, that is,
$K \subseteq (v_1 + \operatorname{int} K) \cup \dots \cup (v_q + \operatorname{int} K)$ for some
$v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: Covered fraction of a ball
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a set $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a
real number $R$, the covered fraction of $X$ at radius $R$ is

$$\frac{\operatorname{vol}\bigl(B_R(0) \cap \bigcup_{x \in X} B_1(x)\bigr)}
{\operatorname{vol}(B_R(0))},$$

where $B_r(y)$ is the open ball of radius $r$ about $y$ and $\operatorname{vol}$ is Lebesgue
measure; it equals $0$ when $R \le 0$.

articles.title: Density of a sphere packing
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, the density of a set
$X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is the limit superior, as $R \to \infty$, of the covered fraction of $X$
at radius $R$: the fraction of the open ball of radius $R$ about the origin covered by the open
unit balls centred at points of $X$.

articles.title: Euclidean space for sphere packings
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, $\mathbb{R}^d$ denotes the
$d$-dimensional real Euclidean space: $d$-tuples of real numbers with the Euclidean norm.

articles.title: Unit sphere packing
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, a set $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is the
centre set of a unit sphere packing if the open balls of radius $1$ centred at any two distinct
points of $X$ are disjoint.

articles.title: Kepler conjecture
articles.statement:
Let $\Delta(3)$ be the supremum of the densities of all unit sphere
packings in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Then $\Delta(3) = \pi / \sqrt{18}$.

## Sources

- Kepler conjecture 1611 (J. Kepler, *Strena seu de Nive Sexangula*); proof T. Hales, 'A proof of the Kepler conjecture', Ann. of Math. (2) 162 (2005) 1065–1185; formal verification in HOL Light + Isabelle by the Flyspeck project (T. Hales et al., completed August 2014), Forum Math. Pi 5 (2017) e2. Wiedijk-1000 #209; listed as §96 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `kepler_conjecture` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Optimal sphere packing density
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, $\Delta(d)$ is the supremum of
the densities of all unit sphere packings in $\mathbb{R}^d$.

articles.title: Klartag's lattice packing theorem
articles.statement:
There is a real constant $c > 0$ such that for every
integer $n \ge 1$ there is a linear map $\varphi : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ for which the
ellipsoid $E = \varphi(B)$, the image of the open Euclidean unit ball $B$ about the origin, has
volume exactly $c n^2$ and the origin is the only point of $E$ whose coordinates are all integers.

The map $\varphi$ is not required to be invertible; a degenerate $\varphi$ would give volume $0$.

## Sources

-. Problem `klartag_packing` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Areas of universal convex covers
articles.statement:
The set of admissible cover areas is the set of all
$a \in [0, \infty]$ for which there is a universal convex cover $\Omega$ in the plane (a nonempty
convex set containing a congruent copy of every nonempty convex planar set of diameter $1$) whose
Lebesgue area is $a$.

articles.title: Baez–Bagdasaryan–Gibbs upper bound
articles.statement:
There is a real number $b$ with
$0.844115297128419059 \le b < 0.844115297128419060$ such that the Lebesgue universal covering
constant (the infimum of the areas of universal convex covers) is at most $b$.

## Sources

- Baez, Bagdasaryan and Gibbs, The Lebesgue universal covering problem (2015).

articles.title: Statement of the Baez–Bagdasaryan–Gibbs upper bound
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that there
is a real number $b$ with $0.844115297128419059 \le b < 0.844115297128419060$ such that the
Lebesgue universal covering constant (the infimum of the areas of universal convex covers) is at
most $b$.

The 18 printed digits are a truncation of the bound, not its exact value.

articles.title: Brass–Sharifi lower bound
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue universal covering constant (the infimum of the
areas of universal convex covers) is at least $0.832$.

## Sources

- Brass and Sharifi, A lower bound for Lebesgue's universal cover problem (2005).

articles.title: Statement of the Brass–Sharifi lower bound
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that the Lebesgue
universal covering constant (the infimum of the areas of universal convex covers) is at least
$0.832$.

Brass and Sharifi obtained this bound by a rigorous computer-aided argument.

articles.title: Covering a congruent copy
articles.statement:
A planar set $\Omega$ covers a congruent copy of a planar set
$K$ when some isometry $e$ of the plane onto itself satisfies $e(K) \subseteq \Omega$.

Isometries include reflections.

articles.title: Directional width
articles.statement:
For a planar set $K$ and a vector $u$ in the plane, the width of $K$
in direction $u$ is $\sup_{x \in K} \langle u, x \rangle - \inf_{x \in K} \langle u, x \rangle$,
where the supremum and infimum are taken in $\mathbb{R}$, with the convention that each is $0$
when the set of values $\langle u, x \rangle$ is empty or unbounded on that side.

It is only applied to nonempty compact $K$, where both extrema are attained.

articles.title: Elekes's disk-and-triangle lower bound
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue universal covering constant (the
infimum of the areas of universal convex covers) is at least $0.8257$.

## Sources

- Elekes (1994), disk and equilateral triangle lower bound.

articles.title: Statement of Elekes's disk-and-triangle lower bound
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that the
Lebesgue universal covering constant (the infimum of the areas of universal convex covers) is at
least $0.8257$.

The bound comes from simultaneously covering a disk and an equilateral triangle of diameter $1$.

articles.title: Existence of a minimal universal cover
articles.statement:
There is a universal convex cover $\Omega$ (a
nonempty convex planar set containing a congruent copy of every nonempty convex planar set of
diameter $1$) whose Lebesgue area equals the Lebesgue universal covering constant, the infimum of
the areas of all universal convex covers.

## Sources

- Elekes, Generalized breadths, circular Cantor sets, and the least area UCC (1994).

articles.title: Statement of the existence of a minimal universal convex cover
articles.statement:
This proposition states
that some nonempty convex set $\Omega$ in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a universal convex
cover, that is, for every nonempty convex set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of diameter $1$ some
isometry $e$ of the plane onto itself satisfies $e(K) \subseteq \Omega$, and that the area (planar
Lebesgue measure) of $\Omega$ equals the Lebesgue universal covering constant, the infimum of the
areas of all universal convex covers.

The existence of such a cover follows from the Blaschke selection theorem.

articles.title: Elekes's regular-polygon lower bound for Lebesgue's covering problem
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue universal
covering constant, the infimum of the areas of the nonempty convex sets in the Euclidean plane that
contain a congruent copy of every nonempty convex planar set of diameter $1$, is at least $0.8271$.

## Sources

- Elekes (1994), additional regular polygon lower bound.

articles.title: Statement of Elekes's regular-polygon lower bound
articles.statement:
This proposition states that the Lebesgue
universal covering constant, the infimum of the areas of the nonempty convex sets in the Euclidean
plane that contain a congruent copy of every nonempty convex planar set of diameter $1$, is at
least $0.8271$.

This is Elekes's finite-decimal lower bound, obtained using regular $3^j$-gons as well.

articles.title: Gibbs's upper bound for Lebesgue's covering problem
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue universal covering
constant, the infimum of the areas of the nonempty convex sets in the Euclidean plane that contain a
congruent copy of every nonempty convex planar set of diameter $1$, is at most $0.8440935944$.

## Sources

- Gibbs, An Upper Bound for Lebesgue's Covering Problem (2018).

articles.title: Statement of Gibbs's upper bound
articles.statement:
This proposition states that the Lebesgue universal
covering constant, the infimum of the areas of the nonempty convex sets in the Euclidean plane that
contain a congruent copy of every nonempty convex planar set of diameter $1$, is at most
$0.8440935944$.

articles.title: Hansen's upper bound for Lebesgue's covering problem, as corrected
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue universal
covering constant, the infimum of the areas of the nonempty convex sets in the Euclidean plane that
contain a congruent copy of every nonempty convex planar set of diameter $1$, is at most
$0.844137708398$.

## Sources

- Hansen (1992), corrected in Baez, Bagdasaryan and Gibbs (2015).

articles.title: Statement of Hansen's corrected upper bound
articles.statement:
This proposition states that the Lebesgue
universal covering constant, the infimum of the areas of the nonempty convex sets in the Euclidean
plane that contain a congruent copy of every nonempty convex planar set of diameter $1$, is at most
$0.844137708398$.

This is Hansen's finite-decimal upper bound, as corrected by Baez, Bagdasaryan and Gibbs.

articles.title: Sets of constant width one
articles.statement:
A set $K$ in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ has constant
width $1$ when it is nonempty, compact and convex and, for every unit vector $u$, its width in
direction $u$, namely $\sup_{x \in K} \langle u, x \rangle - \inf_{x \in K} \langle u, x \rangle$,
equals $1$.

articles.title: Convex sets of diameter one
articles.statement:
A set $K$ in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a
unit-diameter convex set when it is nonempty and convex and its diameter
$\sup_{x, y \in K} \lVert x - y \rVert$ is exactly $1$.

articles.title: Universal convex covers
articles.statement:
A set $\Omega$ in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a universal
convex cover when it is nonempty and convex and, for every nonempty convex set
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of diameter $1$, some isometry $e$ of the plane onto itself satisfies
$e(K) \subseteq \Omega$.

articles.title: Lebesgue universal covering constant
articles.statement:
Call a set $\Omega$ in the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$ a universal convex cover if it is nonempty and convex and, for every nonempty
convex set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of diameter exactly $1$, some isometry of the plane onto
itself maps $K$ into $\Omega$. The Lebesgue universal covering constant is the infimum, taken in
$[0, \infty]$, of the Lebesgue areas of all universal convex covers; the infimum of an empty
family would be $\infty$.

The definition does not assume that a universal convex cover of minimal area exists.

articles.title: Pál's hexagon bound
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue universal covering constant is at most $\sqrt{3}/2$.

## Sources

- Pál, Über ein elementares Variationsproblem (1920), hexagon bound.

articles.title: Statement of Pál's hexagon bound
articles.statement:
The proposition that the Lebesgue universal covering
constant is at most $\sqrt{3}/2$, the bound given by Pál's regular hexagon.

articles.title: Pál's truncated hexagon bound
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue universal covering constant is at most
$2 - 2/\sqrt{3}$.

## Sources

- Pál, Über ein elementares Variationsproblem (1920), truncated hexagon bound.

articles.title: Statement of Pál's truncated hexagon bound
articles.statement:
The proposition that the Lebesgue universal
covering constant is at most $2 - 2/\sqrt{3}$, the bound given by Pál's truncated hexagon.

articles.title: Planar area
articles.statement:
The area of a set $S$ in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$
is its Lebesgue measure (outer measure if $S$ is not measurable), a value in $[0, \infty]$,
so infinite area is allowed.

articles.title: The Euclidean plane of Lebesgue's covering problem
articles.statement:
The ambient space is the Euclidean
plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, with the Euclidean distance.

articles.title: Sprague's bound
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue universal covering constant is at most $0.844137708436$.

## Sources

- Sprague, Über ein elementares Variationsproblem (1936).

articles.title: Statement of Sprague's bound
articles.statement:
The proposition that the Lebesgue universal covering
constant is at most $0.844137708436$.

articles.title: Jung's bound for the Lebesgue covering problem
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue universal covering constant
is at most $\pi/3$.

## Sources

- Jung's theorem, quoted in Elekes (1994), catalogue constant 13b.

articles.title: Jung's upper bound for Lebesgue's universal covering constant (statement)
articles.statement:
The proposition
that Lebesgue's universal covering constant is at most $\pi/3$.

articles.title: Covering sets of constant width one suffices
articles.statement:

the Euclidean plane that contains a congruent copy (an image under an isometry of the plane,
reflections allowed) of every nonempty compact convex planar set of constant width $1$. Then
$\Omega$ contains a congruent copy of every nonempty convex planar set of diameter $1$, that is,
$\Omega$ is a universal convex cover.

articles.title: Wetzel's sector covers every unit arc
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be the closed circular sector of radius $1$
and angle $30^\circ$ with apex $0$ and symmetric about the positive real axis, that is, the set of
complex numbers $z$ with $|z| \le 1$, $\operatorname{Re} z \ge 0$ and
$|\operatorname{Im} z| \le \tan(\pi/12)\operatorname{Re} z$. Then for every continuous curve
$\gamma : [0,1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length (total variation) exactly $1$ there are an angle
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a point $c \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $e^{i\theta}\gamma(t) + c \in S$
for all $t \in [0,1]$.

## Sources

- Optimization Problems, constant 13a, closed claim `wetzelSectorCovers`.

articles.title: Wetzel's sector covering claim
articles.statement:
The proposition that the closed circular sector $S$ of
radius $1$ and angle $30^\circ$ with apex $0$ and symmetric about the positive real axis, that is,
the set of complex numbers $z$ with $|z| \le 1$, $\operatorname{Re} z \ge 0$ and
$|\operatorname{Im} z| \le \tan(\pi/12)\operatorname{Re} z$, covers every unit arc: for every
continuous curve $\gamma : [0,1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length (total variation) exactly $1$ there are
an angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a point $c \in \mathbb{C}$ such that
$e^{i\theta}\gamma(t) + c \in S$ for all $t \in [0,1]$.

articles.title: Wetzel's sector
articles.statement:
This is the closed circular sector of radius $1$ and opening angle
$30^\circ$ with apex at the origin, placed symmetrically about the positive real axis: the set
of complex numbers $z$ with $|z| \le 1$, $\operatorname{Re} z \ge 0$ and
$|\operatorname{Im} z| \le \tan(\pi/12) \operatorname{Re} z$.

## Sources

- Optimization Problems, constant 13a; source-specific interval-arc adaptation.

articles.title: Center density in four dimensions
articles.statement:
The center density of sphere packings in
$\mathbb{R}^4$ is $\delta_4 = \Delta_4 / \operatorname{vol}(B)$, where $\Delta_4$ is the
sphere-packing density of $\mathbb{R}^4$ and $B$ is the open unit ball of $\mathbb{R}^4$ centered
at the origin; the quotient is taken in $[0, \infty]$.

## Sources

- dLOV2014 Section 1.4, `δ₄ = Δ₄ / vol(B)` for unit spheres.

articles.title: Center-density upper bounds as packing-density upper bounds
articles.statement:
For every real number
$a \ge 0$, the center density $\delta_4$ of sphere packings in $\mathbb{R}^4$ is at most $a$ if
and only if the sphere-packing density $\Delta_4$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$ is at most $\pi^2 a / 2$.

## Sources

- exact conversion between a nonnegative center-density upper bound and its `π²/2`-scaled volume-density bound.

articles.title: The density at a fixed radius is at most one
articles.statement:
For every packing $P$ of congruent balls
in $\mathbb{R}^4$ and every radius $R > 0$, the density of $P$ at radius $R$ (the supremum over
all centers $p \in \mathbb{R}^4$ of the density of $P$ in the open ball of radius $R$ about $p$)
is at most $1$.

## Sources

- taking the observation-center supremum preserves the bound by one.

articles.title: Density of a packing at a fixed radius
articles.statement:
For a packing $P$ of congruent balls in
$\mathbb{R}^4$ and a radius $R > 0$, the density of $P$ at radius $R$ is the supremum, over all
centers $p \in \mathbb{R}^4$, of the density of $P$ in the open ball of radius $R$ about $p$;
it is a value in $[0, \infty]$.

## Sources

- CE2003 Appendix A, supremum over all observation centers at fixed radius.

articles.title: A packing has countably many centers
articles.statement:
For every packing of congruent balls in
$\mathbb{R}^4$, the set of centers of its balls is countable.

## Sources

- packing admission conditions; disjoint nonempty open balls have countably many centers.

articles.title: The density in a ball is at most one
articles.statement:
For every packing $P$ of congruent balls in
$\mathbb{R}^4$, every point $p \in \mathbb{R}^4$ and every radius $R > 0$, the density of $P$ in
the open ball of radius $R$ about $p$ is at most $1$.

## Sources

- a covered-volume fraction cannot exceed one.

articles.title: Density of a packing in a ball
articles.statement:
For a packing $P$ of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$, a
point $p \in \mathbb{R}^4$ and a radius $R > 0$, the density of $P$ in the open ball $B(p, R)$ of
radius $R$ about $p$ is $\operatorname{vol}(U \cap B(p, R)) / \operatorname{vol}(B(p, R))$, where
$U$ is the union of the closed balls of $P$ and $\operatorname{vol}$ is Lebesgue measure; the
quotient is taken in $[0, \infty]$.

## Sources

- CE2003 Appendix A, `vol(P ∩ B(p,R)) / vol(B(p,R))`.

articles.title: Periodic packings
articles.statement:
A packing $P$ of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$ is periodic if there
are a basis $b_1, b_2, b_3, b_4$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$ and a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}^4$ such
that the set of centers of $P$ equals $\{c + w : c \in F, w \in \Lambda\}$, where $\Lambda$ is the
set of integer linear combinations of $b_1, b_2, b_3, b_4$.

## Sources

- CE2003 introduction, finite union of translates of a full-rank lattice. The lattice is the integer span of a real basis, not an arbitrary periodicity oracle.

articles.title: Lower bound for sphere packing in dimension four
articles.statement:
The sphere packing density $\Delta_4$
of $\mathbb{R}^4$, the supremum of the upper densities of all packings of congruent balls in
$\mathbb{R}^4$, satisfies $\frac{\pi^2}{16} \le \Delta_4$.

## Sources

- dLOV2014 Table 1. Known literature bound; no Lean proof supplied.

articles.title: Statement of the lower bound for sphere packing in dimension four
articles.statement:
The proposition that
the sphere packing density $\Delta_4$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$, the supremum of the upper densities of
all packings of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$, satisfies $\frac{\pi^2}{16} \le \Delta_4$.

articles.title: The four-dimensional packing density is nonnegative

articles.title: Balls of positive radius in $\mathbb{R}^4$ have finite volume
articles.statement:

articles.title: Packed ball
articles.statement:
For a packing $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^4$ with radius $r$ and a point
$c \in \mathbb{R}^4$, the packed ball of $P$ at $c$ is the closed ball
$\{x \in \mathbb{R}^4 : \|x - c\| \le r\}$, boundary included.

articles.title: The region covered by a packing is measurable
articles.statement:

the region covered by $P$, the union of its packed closed balls, is a Borel set; in
particular it is Lebesgue measurable.

## Sources

articles.title: Region covered by a packing
articles.statement:
For a packing $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^4$ with radius $r$ and set

closed balls $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^4 : \|x - c\| \le r\}$.

## Sources

articles.title: Packings of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$
articles.statement:
A packing in $\mathbb{R}^4$ consists of a
real radius $r > 0$ and a set $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^4$ of centres such that for any two distinct
centres $c, c' \in C$ the open balls of radius $r$ about $c$ and $c'$ are disjoint.

## Sources

- CE2003 introduction, congruent positive-radius balls with disjoint interiors.

articles.title: Periodic packings approach the optimal density in dimension four
articles.statement:
For a packing $Q$ of
congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$, let its upper density $\overline{\delta}(Q)$ be the limit
superior, as $R \to \infty$, of the supremum over all points $p$ of the fraction of the volume of
the open ball $B(p, R)$ covered by the closed balls of $Q$, and let the sphere packing density
$\Delta_4$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$ be the supremum of $\overline{\delta}(Q)$ over all such packings $Q$.
Then for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a periodic packing $P$ of congruent balls in
$\mathbb{R}^4$, meaning that its set of centers is a finite union of translates of the lattice
$\mathbb{Z}b_1 + \mathbb{Z}b_2 + \mathbb{Z}b_3 + \mathbb{Z}b_4$ for some basis $b_1, \dots, b_4$ of
$\mathbb{R}^4$, such that $\Delta_4 \le \overline{\delta}(P) + \varepsilon$.

## Sources

- CE2003 introduction and Appendix A. Known periodic approximation; no Lean proof supplied and no exact optimum-attainment claim.

articles.title: Statement that periodic packings approach the optimal density in dimension four
articles.statement:
For a
packing $Q$ of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$, let its upper density $\overline{\delta}(Q)$ be
the limit superior, as $R \to \infty$, of the supremum over all points $p$ of the fraction of the
volume of the open ball $B(p, R)$ covered by the closed balls of $Q$, and let the sphere packing
density $\Delta_4$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$ be the supremum of $\overline{\delta}(Q)$ over all such
packings $Q$. This is the proposition that for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a periodic
packing $P$ of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$, meaning that its set of centers is a finite
union of translates of the lattice $\mathbb{Z}b_1 + \mathbb{Z}b_2 + \mathbb{Z}b_3 + \mathbb{Z}b_4$
for some basis $b_1, \dots, b_4$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$, such that
$\Delta_4 \le \overline{\delta}(P) + \varepsilon$.

## Sources

- CE2003 introduction and Appendix A, periodic packings come arbitrarily close to the greatest density. Positive error does not assert attainment.

articles.title: Positive radii
articles.statement:
A positive radius is a real number $R$ with $R > 0$; the positive radii

articles.title: Four-dimensional Euclidean space
articles.statement:
The ambient space is $\mathbb{R}^4$, the space of real

articles.title: Sphere-packing density of $\mathbb{R}^4$
articles.statement:
The sphere-packing density
$\Delta_4 \in [0, \infty]$ is the supremum, over all packings $P$ of congruent balls in
$\mathbb{R}^4$, of the upper density of $P$. Here the upper density of $P$ is the limit superior,
as the real radius $R > 0$ tends to infinity, of the supremum over all points
$p \in \mathbb{R}^4$ of the ratio of the volume of the part of the open ball $B(p, R)$ covered
by $P$ to the volume of $B(p, R)$.

## Sources

- catalogue C36, supremum over all congruent-ball packings in `ℝ⁴`.

articles.title: The unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^4$ has volume $\pi^2/2$
articles.statement:
The Lebesgue measure of the open unit
ball centred at the origin of $\mathbb{R}^4$ equals $\pi^2/2$.

## Sources

articles.title: The unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^4$ has finite volume

articles.title: The unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^4$ has nonzero volume

articles.title: Volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^4$
articles.statement:

articles.title: Trivial upper bound for the sphere-packing density of $\mathbb{R}^4$

articles.title: The upper density of a packing is at most one
articles.statement:
For every packing $P$ of congruent balls in
$\mathbb{R}^4$, the upper density of $P$ is at most $1$.
